#6341. October broke a global heat record, and El Niño is still strengthening

October 2026 was the warmest October on record, as an intensifying El Niño added to global warmth and ocean temperatures reached new highs.

The global average surface air temperature in October 2026 was 15.35°C.

That’s 0.90°C above the 1991–2020 average and enough to make it the warmest October in the ERA5 record, beating October 2023 by 0.05°C.

It was also 1.75°C above the estimated pre-industrial baseline.

The data come from the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the European Union’s climate monitoring service. And the numbers keep stacking.

Before August 2026, the last individual month above 1.5°C was November 2025. Then August, September and October crossed it.

The last streak of three or more consecutive months above 1.5°C ended in April 2025.

The rolling twelve-month average – November 2025 through October 2026 – now sits at 1.51°C above pre-industrial levels.

January through October 2026 ranks as the second-warmest such period on record, 0.07°C below the same stretch in 2024 and 0.05°C above 2023.

A statistical model trained on 1979–2025 data gives 2026 a greater than 99% chance of exceeding 1.5°C for the full calendar year. That would make it only the second calendar year above that level after 2024.

There’s roughly an 80% probability it finishes as the second-warmest year on record and about a 20% chance it ties or exceeds 2024 for the top spot.

If 2026 does exceed 1.5°C, the four-year average for 2023–2026 would also cross that line.

An intensifying El Niño is adding to the global warmth. Sea surface temperatures across 60°S–60°N hit 20.95°C in October.

This is the highest October value ever recorded. The previous October record was set in 2023 during a developing El Niño. This one is considerably stronger.

The Niño 3.4 region – the patch of equatorial Pacific used to define El Niño intensity – averaged 29.94°C in October. That’s an all-time high for the region in any month, surpassing the record set just one month earlier in September.

The anomaly was +3.21°C, also a record, above September’s +2.99°C. For context, this exceeds the peaks of the monster El Niños of 1982–83, 1997–98, and 2015–16.

Across much of the central equatorial Pacific, temperatures ran more than 3°C above average. Along the Peruvian coast and west of the Galápagos, the anomalies reached 6 to 7°C.

The World Meteorological Organization expects this El Niño to peak in December 2026 and to persist through at least February 2027.

The ocean heat isn’t confined to the Pacific. Record October sea surface temperatures were also logged in parts of the northern Indian Ocean, the South Atlantic, and the subtropical North Atlantic.

Around Europe, records fell along the Atlantic coast and in the central and western Mediterranean.

The largest land-based anomalies on the planet were over West Antarctica.

There, temperatures ran more than 7°C above the October average and reached up to 11°C above normal in some areas.

The Copernicus report links this to high pressure over the Drake Passage and a wave pattern typically associated with El Niño. Siberia, the central United States, northern Canada, eastern Africa, and the Middle East also ran warm.

Cold anomalies showed up across much of southern South America, Greenland, northern Africa, parts of central Asia, and western Australia.

The warmth was not everywhere. But it was dominant.

European land temperatures averaged 11.08°C – 1.49°C above normal and the second-warmest October in the ERA5 record, behind only October 2022.

But unlike the record-breaking summer and September, the warmth was unevenly distributed.

Northern Fennoscandia and far-eastern Europe saw the most extreme departures, with Ukraine reaching up to 6°C above average.

Western Europe, by contrast, hovered closer to normal. Southern Italy, the southern Balkans, Greece, the eastern Mediterranean, and western Türkiye were actually about 2°C below average.

Individual months above 1.5°C are not the same as the sustained, multi-decadal average the Paris Agreement refers to. But the frequency with which individual months are crossing the threshold keeps increasing.

The first calendar year above 1.5°C happened in 2024. The second is almost certainly happening now.

A four-year average above 1.5°C would be another sign that the world is nearing the Paris Agreement’s long-term warming limit.

El Niño is expected to strengthen further before peaking in December, keeping attention on how this exceptional year will end.

#6340. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

#6338. Protecting cities from floods can come with a hidden cost for renters

Flood protection projects in Copenhagen may raise rents and water bills unevenly, placing a heavier burden on lower-income tenants.

A city can become better protected against flooding while becoming more expensive for its poorest residents.

New research shows how drainage projects can leave tenants paying disproportionately through higher rents and water bills.

The study, led by researchers at the University of Copenhagen, examined how flood protection costs reach households across the Danish capital.

Lead author Natalie Marie Gulsrud and her colleagues combined geographical analysis with a detailed look at the Hørgården housing development.

Their findings show why a policy applied equally on paper can feel very different depending on where someone lives.

At Hørgården, roughly 60 percent of residents have incomes below the Danish average. The development also appears on the Ministry of Social Affairs and Housing’s Prevention Areas list.

Its aging sewers need repairs, and a planned cloudburst route brings another obligation. Rainwater draining from roofs must be separated from wastewater and connected to the new system.

The paper projects rent increases of 17%–29% for the combined work. For a 75-square-meter apartment, that would add 967–1,292 Danish kroner to the monthly bill.

Stormwater separation accounts for about 22% of that increase, or 213–284 kroner each month. Most of the increase comes from sewer repairs.

The loans will be repaid over 30 years. Residents moving into Hørgården years after the work is finished will therefore help pay for it.

Copenhagen is investing in cloudburst tunnels and drainage improvements to keep heavy rain from overwhelming its sewers. Separating stormwater from wastewater is part of that effort.

The work protects the city, but apartment residents and not-for-profit tenants can bear a disproportionate share of its financing.

“Climate adaptation is not only about flooding and sewer capacity. It is also about rising rents,” Gulsrud said.

“Your type of housing determines how much of the bill you pay. Our case study shows that one-size-fits-all climate adaptation policies worsen urban injustice.”

“Stormwater costs fall disproportionately on not-for-profit housing residents, despite Copenhagen’s reputation for climate leadership.”

The researchers compared adaptation plans with data on housing types and tenure. They found that not-for-profit housing often lies closer to priority areas for flood management.

That proximity matters because properties along a cloudburst route may have to change their drainage systems at their own expense.

“We can see that not-for-profit housing is often located where cloudburst routes are typically established,” Gulsrud explained.

“The problem arises when properties along these routes are required to separate stormwater from wastewater on their own land to connect it to the cloudburst system. This makes sense from a water-management perspective, but it can also impose substantial costs.”

For an older development such as Hørgården, connecting to the new infrastructure involves extensive work. Those expenses ultimately reach households through their rents.

Water bills introduce a separate problem. Stormwater charges are based on drinking water consumption in each dwelling, rather than the rainwater leaving the property.

Imagine a detached house beside a four-storey block containing four apartments. Both buildings have a 100-square-meter roof.

If every household uses the same amount of drinking water, the apartment block pays four times the stormwater charge. Its roof is no larger.

This arrangement disadvantages buildings where many households share a roof. Not-for-profit developments commonly have four to six storeys.

“It would be fair if payment reflected the amount of stormwater each property actually discharges into the sewer system,” Gulsrud noted.

“At present, charges are tied to drinking water consumption instead. There is a fundamental inequity in the way water bills are allocated and in how residents pay for climate adaptation and cloudburst management.”

“As water charges continue to rise, the burden falls most heavily on the most marginalised members of society.”

The researchers also examined how these decisions are made. They found a divide between departments responsible for technical infrastructure and those dealing with social policy.

That leaves household finances poorly accounted for when drainage requirements are enforced. A project can satisfy engineering standards while putting residents under greater financial strain.

“In this paper we hope to introduce a human aspect to a highly technical topic involving stormwater pipes, housing tenure, and climate financing,” Gulsrud said.

In Hørgården, public records showed that officials knew housing costs would rise. Those costs nevertheless did not determine whether the separation requirement would go ahead.

The authors argue that closer cooperation between social and technical departments could help distribute costs more fairly. Housing circumstances and household resources would then become part of planning the work.

For residents, that would mean considering the rent bill alongside the drainage plan.

“Who gets protected as the climate changes, and who carries the cost? A just transition needs social and technical governance working together, not on separate tracks.”

“If we don’t fix this, we risk deepening socio ecological inequalities in the green transition. We hope this research moves us closer to a transition that is genuinely just and caring,” Gulsrud concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6336. Lucid Dreaming Was Once a Rare Gift. Now Scientists Say They Can Help You Learn It.

Researchers built dreamlike virtual worlds to teach people how to realize they’re dreaming—and it worked.

Some people don’t just dream. They often realize they’re dreaming and can even control the dreamworld, from giving themselves powers that defy the laws of physics to escaping a nightmare by waking themselves up. Lucid dreamers can go on adventures most of us can only dream about (pun intended). But is it possible to train yourself to do the same?

Dreams can happen during any stage of sleep, but they usually occur during REM sleep. When dreamers suddenly become aware that they’re dreaming, they’re in a lucid state. However, people who frequently have lucid dreams are rare. Researchers from the University of Trento in Rovereto, Italy, wanted to find out whether standard exercises, meditation, and virtual reality could teach people to have lucid dreams. Participants in the experimental group practiced open monitoring meditation, which is meant to sharpen sensory awareness and perception through nonjudgmental observation. They then did VR training that took them into virtual worlds full of bizarre, dreamlike scenarios. For comparison, a control group used VR that had nothing to do with dreaming, while a third group did only the standard training, without VR.

All participants started with the same baseline training, which they did while awake to practice dream recall and reality checks. They were told to keep a dream diary, noting each morning whether they remembered any dreams and, if so, what the dreams were about. Participants were also told to do reality checks, such as pinching themselves, to test whether they were awake or dreaming. They did these checks whenever they ran into something strange or simply thought of something strange. On top of that, phone alarms went off every hour for 12 hours each day to prompt more checks. The idea was that the habit would eventually carry over into their dreams. On top of this training, the experimental group did open monitoring meditation sessions in the lab to prepare for their VR training. During these sessions, participants observed their breathing, bodily sensations, thoughts, and emotions without reacting to them. Each session also included a guided exploration of an environment designed to look like a scene from a dream.

“Through repetition, [reality checks] are intended to become habitual and to transfer into dreams via ‘dream residue,’ where they may be triggered by dream signs that are unusual, surprising, or incongruent events, and thereby precipitate insight into the dream state,” the researchers wrote in their study, recently published in Frontiers in Psychology.

To build these scenes, the researchers created LucidDreamingVR, a program inspired by Tibetan dream yoga. Unlike the VR control group, whose content had nothing to do with dreaming, the experimental group completed eight sessions that grew steadily more elaborate, taking participants from recognizing a dream to controlling one. The early tasks taught them to spot dream signs: the virtual surroundings would suddenly shift, cueing a reality check, much as an odd detail might inside a dream. Later sessions drew on dream yoga techniques to let participants rehearse what they might do once they became lucid. With a single spoken command, they could fly, leap to incredible heights or, like Alice after tumbling down the rabbit hole, grow and shrink at will.

The researchers counted both lucid and semi-lucid dreams as “lucid-like” dreams. By the end of the experiment, 11 of the 13 participants who had trained with LucidDreamingVR had reported at least one lucid-like dream. By contrast, eight of 13 people in the control group without VR and only four of 12 in the VR control group reported one. Nearly 12% of the dreams the experimental group remembered were lucid-like, compared with about 3% for the control group without VR and about 1% for the VR control group. Surprisingly, the LucidDreamingVR group remembered the fewest dreams overall, so they also reported the fewest ordinary, non-lucid dreams. These results suggest that combining open monitoring meditation with dream-themed VR may increase lucid dreaming. However, because neither control group meditated, the study can’t show which part of the training mattered more.

“[Our] findings support the use of immersive environments as…cognitive-enhancement tools,” the researchers said. “Future work should combine VR-based rehearsal with objective sleep verification, factorial designs, and waking cognitive measures to clarify mechanism, specificity, and transfer.”

#6335. Lasers and robots using AI are launching a third revolution in farming by completely changing how we kill weeds

Lasers, robots and spot sprayers cut herbicide use, but two weed scientists explain why herbicide resistance will keep evolving around them.

In theory, a machine that rolls through a farm to zap or dig up individual weeds should be the perfect way to eliminate harmful chemicals and stop chemical-resistant weeds in their tracks.

However, two scientists recently warned that this high-tech farming dream is not yet the absolute cure everyone hopes it will be.

Resistance comes from the weeds that are hit and survive, not from how much herbicide the field gets. So a machine that treats only the weeds can cut herbicide use sharply and still favor resistant plants just as strongly.

The warning comes in a commentary by Lynn Sosnoskie of Cornell University and Stephen Duke of the University of Mississippi.

It’s an assessment of what the new machines have done so far, with no new field experiments of its own. It weighs the benefits against the trouble that the two scientists expect will follow.

“In the last 100 years, there have been two revolutions in weed management: synthetic herbicides and herbicide-resistant crops,” said Duke, a research professor at the University’s National Center for Natural Products Research.

“It looks to me like AI-driven precision weed management will be the next revolution.”

The machines come in three kinds, and all start with a camera. Software picks weeds out from crop plants and bare soil as the machine moves. Most carry their own lights under a hood, so they can work at night.

A sprayer then hits each weed with a nozzle, a laser burns its growing point, or a cultivator pulls it out.

The savings can be real. In U.S. trials of the one spot-spraying system, herbicide savings averaged about $50 an acre ($123 a hectare) in soybeans and $17 an acre ($43 a hectare) in corn.

In vegetable trials that Sosnoskie ran, laser weeding caused almost no crop injury, left the crop plants at least 30 percent heavier, and matched the yields of weed-free plots.

Sosnoskie, an associate professor in Cornell’s School of Integrative Plant Science, works on fruit and vegetable crops, and she said herbicides can damage or stunt them.

“But what we’re finding is that with precision technology, we can keep some, and sometimes even all, of the herbicide off the crop,” she added.

Some commercial robotic weeders run about $75,000 or more, and laser systems can cost over $1 million.

One U.S. analysis estimated that a spot-sprayer pays for itself in saved herbicide only after treating about 53,000 to 116,000 acres (21,500 to 47,000 hectares). Where the area falls, within that range, depends on weed density and herbicide prices.

Duke described an organic farmer in the Netherlands who bought a laser weeder for more than a million dollars. It saved the farmer so much hassle that he bought a second one, Duke said, but that won’t be true for everyone.

“Some of these farmers who are working with high-value crops can spend that much, but many can’t.”

Organic growers have a particular reason, Duke said. They can’t use synthetic herbicides, so they depend on hand weeding, and that labor is getting harder to find.

Prices are expected to fall as production scales up, the authors wrote, and some systems may be retrofitted onto existing equipment.

Farmers worldwide spend an estimated $35 billion to $47 billion a year on herbicides, and the authors wrote that wide adoption of these machines could shrink that market.

Fewer sales could mean less money for finding new herbicides, which are already scarce. Few substances with a new mode of action have reached the market in four decades, even as public pressure builds against chemicals such as glyphosate, the most widely used of them.

The weed resistance problem is subtler. A weed becomes resistant when a treated plant survives and reproduces, so what matters is what happens to each sprayed plant, not how much herbicide the field gets.

A camera that misses a weed leaves it untreated, and a nozzle that only partly covers one gives it a low dose. The authors wrote that both could speed up resistance rather than slow it down.

Fast growers such as Palmer amaranth and waterhemp can quickly outgrow the size a sprayer handles after a missed pass, and each plant can drop hundreds of thousands of seeds.

“That doesn’t mean every weed is resistant to every herbicide, but there are a lot of herbicide-resistant weeds out there,” Duke said. “It’s become a really big problem.”

The second warning is about the camera itself. A weed that sprouts under the crop canopy, grows in an unusual shape or looks enough like the crop stands a better chance of being left alone. Over many seasons, that could select for weeds that are harder to spot.

Weeds have done this before. Under generations of hand weeding, a barnyard grass that grows in rice paddies evolved a more upright shape and a white central vein on its leaf.

Both are features of cultivated rice, so farmers pulled it less often. The authors called a repeat under machine vision speculative but plausible.

Lasers and cultivators favor a different set of weeds, because both attack only the part of the plant above ground. Perennials that regrow from roots, tubers or underground stems could come to dominate fields where those machines do most of the work.

“What I’ve been arguing is just because we have this technology, that doesn’t free us from weeds,” Sosnoskie said. “With weed control, we always have to think about how the weed is going to respond or try to ‘win.'”

The software is only as good as the pictures it learned from. Dust, crop residue, odd lighting and a stressed crop that looks like a weed can all throw off the system.

“I worked with a company whose original algorithm kept missing one specific weed species: common ragweed,” Sosnoskie said. “Well, it turns out they don’t have the same ragweed species in California.”

The authors’ own conclusion is blunt. Weeds evolved around herbicides, and they expect weeds to evolve around the new machines too. Which traits, and how fast, is still speculation.

The systems will also need better sensors and more varied training images to hold their accuracy from one region to the next, they wrote.

Furthermore, the old, soil-applied herbicides that stop weeds before they sprout are likely to stay in use alongside the farm AI. Fewer weeds coming up means fewer for a camera to miss.

The full study was published in the journal Engineering.

#6334. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

#6333. Top-ranking parakeets face a hostile welcome after time away

Monk parakeets change their fighting habits when dominant birds leave, often bullying them when they return to the flock.

When a high-ranking monk parakeet disappears from its flock, the other birds adjust to its absence. But a new study shows that its return can trigger a shift toward bullying.

Researchers kept some high-ranking birds away from their flocks for eight days.

When they returned, most were bullied by the other birds. They were attacked much more often than they attacked others.

The work was led by Annemarie van der Marel while she was a postdoctoral researcher in Elizabeth Hobson’s lab at the University of Cincinnati.

Van der Marel now works at the Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity in Chile.

Monk parakeets are highly social parrots. They ease into friendships and they spend much of their time squabbling.

Every bird in the study was held in captivity. The researchers counted fights over space. In each one, a parakeet moved in on another bird, which then gave up its spot.

Between 2020 and 2022, 51 monk parakeets were observed in four flocks. The birds were kept in flight pens in Gainesville, Florida. The pens belong to the USDA National Wildlife Research Center.

Most of the birds had been caught in southern Florida. The species comes from South America but now lives wild in that region.

Observers logged more than 118,000 contests over about 1,460 hours.

“Each bird received a color mark so that we could identify them individually. We all had our favorites. They have a lot of personality,” van der Marel said.

Every three days, the wins and losses were used to rank the birds. In this way, the researchers worked out each flock’s pecking order.

In three of the flocks, one bird at a time was then removed. Each bird was chosen for its rank and housed apart for eight days. It was then returned to the same pen.

Fifteen birds went through that cycle. Nine of them ranked at or near the top of their flock. The other six held middle or lower ranks.

Three fighting patterns were described in a 2021 study by Hobson and two colleagues. Each pattern reflects how the members of an animal group pick their opponents.

In the first pattern, an animal attacks any lower-ranked group member.

In the second, it mostly attacks rivals ranked just below it. The third pattern, called bullying, involves mostly attacking group members ranked much lower.

Each undisturbed flock maintained its existing fighting pattern. One flock showed bullying for as long as it was watched.

Another flock attacked any bird of lower rank during the month before its removals. That pattern was not changed by a thunderstorm.

It was also not changed when two injured birds were taken out for care. A change of partner by the top-ranked bird had no effect either.

The patterns began to change once the removals started. Sixteen switches were recorded immediately after a bird was removed or returned.

Other switches were recorded between those events. No switch was recorded after some of the removals and returns. A group changing its pattern over time had not been documented before, the authors wrote.

A returning bird loses its rank according to the team’s earlier study.

The researchers therefore expected the other birds to have little reason to change how they fought.

The flock’s fighting pattern changed after six of the nine top-ranked birds were removed and after six of their returns.

However, the patterns adopted afterward differed. Any lower-ranked bird was most often attacked after a top bird was removed. That result was recorded in five of the nine cases.

Bullying was recorded in eight of the nine cases after a top bird was returned.

On average, each of the 15 returning birds was the target of about 530 contests.

Those contests were counted over the three days after its return. Birds of similar rank had been targeted about 220 times over the three days before.

The flocks were not fighting more overall. About the same number of contests was recorded in each three-day period of the experiment. The birds had simply changed their targets.

“When removing a top-ranked bird, all the remaining birds have updated their rank in the other bird’s absence,” van der Marel said.

“And when the absent bird returns, the group shifts toward a bullying dominance pattern, maybe because they don’t want to lose their new rank position.”

Returning top-ranked birds received much more aggression than returning lower-ranked birds did.

The researchers compared responses by rank in the two flocks studied in 2022. Bullying was recorded in eight of 12 cases after a top bird was removed or returned.

The flock attacked any lower-ranked member in eight of 12 cases after a lower-ranked bird was removed or returned.

Removing a top-ranked bird also changes the flock’s mix of ranks. The experimental design therefore could not fully distinguish between two possible responses.

The flock may have reacted to the loss of that bird or to the new mix of ranks.

Memory may play a part, the authors suggested.

Earlier work by Hobson found strong evidence on this point. Monk parakeets remember whom they fought, who won, and how fights between other birds turned out.

Flock members that remember a former top bird may gain from bullying it, the authors wrote. Such bullying could stop the bird from retaking the top rank.

The authors also suggested that bullying could work as a signal to other birds that are watching.

The birds were handled differently during removals and returns. The whole flock was netted and handled on removal days. Only the returning bird was handled on return days.

The effect of handling could not be fully separated from the effect of the return, the authors wrote. They gave two reasons for thinking that handling was not the main cause.

Bullying was rarely recorded after the return of a lower-ranked bird. The storm and other unplanned events did not change the flock’s fighting pattern.

The birds were also captive. Wild flocks of monk parakeets split apart and merge again often.

A wild flock can contain between one and 95 birds, and the average flock size is about four.

A wild bird may be separated from its flockmates more often than the captive birds were. Those separations may also be shorter or longer than eight days.

What a flock or its members gain by switching patterns is still not known.

The team is now splitting and merging flocks in ways closer to wild conditions. The fighting patterns of those flocks will then be checked for changes.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Computational Biology.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) officially announced its decision to revoke the United States' measles elimination status on Nov. 17, 2026. The week prior, the Wall Street Journal reported that the PAHO had reached that decision.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6330. Lightning lights up towering storms above the South China Sea

Lightning illuminates towering thunderstorms over the South China Sea in an astronaut photo that also captures Singapore and fishing boat lights.

Today’s Image of the Day captures the South China Sea after dark, where city lights and scattered offshore glows surround towering thunderstorms.

Lightning briefly illuminates the clouds from within, revealing rounded storm tops that rise above the surrounding cloud cover.

These domes mark places where strong updrafts have pushed parts of the storms above their broad, flattened tops.

An astronaut aboard the International Space Station captured the scene near Borneo on October 28, 2026.

The photograph brings together several sources of nighttime light, each with a different explanation.

Thunderstorms begin with rising air. When warm, moist air moves upward, it cools, and water vapor condenses into cloud droplets.

With a continuing supply of moisture and upward motion, a cloud can grow into a towering storm.

That growth eventually encounters an atmospheric boundary called the tropopause. It separates the troposphere, the lowest layer where most weather develops, from the stratosphere above.

At this boundary, rising air generally spreads sideways. The result is the broad, flattened cloud canopy known as a thunderstorm’s anvil.

A particularly strong updraft can briefly push beyond that canopy, producing a rounded bulge called an overshooting top.

These protrusions reveal the force of the rising air inside a storm, even when much of its internal activity remains hidden.

Several overshooting tops appear in the astronaut’s photograph. Lightning illuminates two of them, helping expose their shapes against the dark surroundings.

Such domes can sometimes extend into the stratosphere.

Their presence signals vigorous storm development, although the photograph alone does not establish the precise height of these particular clouds.

The light inside a thunderstorm begins with interactions among tiny particles.

High in the cloud, rising air supports a mixture of ice crystals, supercooled water droplets, and soft ice pellets called graupel. Collisions among these particles transfer electrical charge.

The storm’s air currents help separate the charged particles.

Smaller ice crystals can travel upward, while heavier particles remain lower, allowing regions with different electrical charges to develop.

When the electrical field becomes strong enough, a lightning discharge occurs.

That discharge can remain inside a cloud or connect different clouds, rather than reaching the ground.

From below, an observer may see a branching bolt or a sudden brightening overhead. From orbit, clouds can scatter the light into a much broader glow.

The storm briefly reveals its contours, giving astronauts a view of cloud structure that people beneath it cannot see.

The photograph freezes one of those fleeting moments. It records the illuminated cloud tops alongside lights that were already shining across the surrounding land and sea.

Singapore appears on the left side of the image. The Singapore Strait separates the city-state from the Indonesian islands of Batam and Bintan to its south.

Elsewhere, clusters of light interrupt the darkness offshore.

NASA identifies the blue lights west of Singapore as likely fishing vessels using powerful lamps to attract squid or schooling fish, including anchovies and sardines.

Scattered orange points farther offshore to the northwest are likely gas flares.

Those identifications carry some uncertainty.

Color and location help interpret the scene, but a distant point of light does not reveal its source as clearly as a close-up photograph would.

Together, the lights show how much activity continues after sunset.

Urban areas form concentrated patches, while offshore operations produce isolated points and clusters across otherwise dark water.

The setting also helps explain why storms are a prominent part of the view.

Singapore experiences thunderstorms throughout the year. They become more frequent during the transition periods between monsoons, generally in April and May and again in October and November.

During these periods, light and variable winds favor the development of local thunderstorms, particularly during the afternoon and evening.

Warm, humid air supplies the ingredients for clouds to build upward.

This seasonal pattern provides context for the photograph, though it does not establish how each storm in the frame formed.

The image captures the region at 14:20 UTC, well after sunset locally. A member of the station’s Expedition 75 crew took the photo with a Nikon Z9 camera and a 14-millimeter lens.

The published photograph was cropped and enhanced for contrast, with lens artifacts removed.

For a moment, lightning made the atmosphere itself part of the illuminated landscape.

Beneath the station, the lights of a city, people working at sea, and towering tropical storms shared the same frame.

Image Credit: NASA/JSC, Expedition 75. Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-250951

#6328. Bigger armies will not stop climate change, and may make the world less safe

Military emissions stay out of national climate tallies, and two BMJ authors say bigger defense budgets may leave people less safe, not more.

Many governments are raising their military budgets, and climate change is now one of the reasons they give for doing so. The thinking is that regions turning dangerously hot, wet, or dry will grow unstable and may go to war, so a bigger military is a precaution.

Two articles in a medical journal’s climate issue say that logic has it backwards.

War and the daily running of armies are themselves a large and mostly uncounted source of the gases heating the planet, their authors wrote. Spending more on them may leave people less safe, not more.

The articles are opinion pieces, not data studies, and they appeared in The BMJ on October 21. Neta Crawford, a professor of international relations at the University of St Andrews, is the author of the first. The journal commissioned it and didn’t send it for outside peer review.

Mohammed Abba-Aji of Washington University in St. Louis and Nason Maani of the University of Edinburgh are the authors of the second article.

In an interview with Earth.com, Abba-Aji described the comparison behind that article. “What struck me most was the contrast,” he said. The contrast is between what the world spends on weapons and what it gives away as aid.

Security officials describe climate change as a “threat multiplier,” Crawford wrote. The phrase means a warming climate could stress societies until they fight. The U.S. military, the U.K. Ministry of Defence, NATO, and the U.N. Security Council have all used it.

Crawford reversed the claim: war, she wrote, is a climate change multiplier.

The steadiest source of military emissions is the ordinary running of a military, from powering bases to the fuel burned in training and in moving troops. U.S. and NATO military doctrine stresses long-range air strikes, which produce more emissions than defensive doctrines do.

Everyday military emissions don’t appear in national greenhouse gas inventories. Crawford traced the gap to the Kyoto Protocol talks of the 1990s, when the U.S. Department of Defense pushed for a military exemption.

The department was the country’s largest petroleum user and feared being required to cut its emissions. The Pentagon is still the largest user, she wrote, and its annual emissions are larger than those of most countries.

Arms makers add to the total. BAE Systems, the biggest defense company in the U.K., reported about 377,000 tons (341,686 metric tons) of carbon dioxide equivalent for 2025 from its own operations and purchased energy.

Fighting raises the numbers fast. Crawford cited an accounting group’s estimate for the first four years of the war in Ukraine. Military operations alone produced about 126 million tons (114 million metric tons) of emissions in the form of carbon dioxide equivalent.

Destroyed forests and airliners rerouted around the war zone added more, and rebuilding will add more again. Those three sources come to roughly 190 million tons (170 million metric tons).

Strikes on oil and gas sites are worse still. The Nord Stream pipelines under the Baltic Sea were sabotaged in September 2022, and an estimated 513,000 tons (465,000 metric tons) of methane escaped, a 2025 study published in Nature found.

Crawford put that at about 15 million tons (13.85 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide equivalent, three times what Albania emitted during the whole of 2024.

Ukrainian drones hit Russian oil facilities this September, Crawford wrote, and strikes hit oil and gas infrastructure in the Middle East during the war with Iran this year.

The fuel shortages and price jumps were tracked. In contrast, the greenhouse gases released have gone essentially uncounted.

The second article is about the money. World military spending reached $2,887 billion in 2025, Abba-Aji told Earth.com. This is close to 2.5 percent of everything the world’s economies produced.

Official development assistance, the aid that richer governments send to poorer ones, fell to $174 billion the same year, the largest one-year drop on record.

Abba-Aji and Maani describe a cycle. Climate stress can make conflict more likely, through competition over resources or by making it easier for armed groups to recruit.

“Conflict in turn justifies more military spending, and that spending draws money away from the measures that could break the cycle,” Abba-Aji said.

Wealthier governments may stay out of the fighting, the two wrote, and still help create the conditions for it. They supply the weapons that keep a conflict going while cutting aid to the countries affected.

Crawford also objects to the idea that a hotter world leads to war on its own. The link between climate change and armed conflict is neither strong nor necessary, she wrote, citing a 2017 study that re-examined the Syrian civil war.

Governments can support their populations instead, she wrote, and neighboring governments can negotiate over shared resources. Those are political choices, not unavoidable consequences of climate change.

Climate change is already killing people without any war at all. In some regions, heatwaves, wildfires, storms, and floods made worse by warming now kill more people a year than armed conflict does, Crawford wrote.

By the Met Office‘s estimate, more than 1,100 deaths in England and Wales during the May and June heatwaves of 2026 were due to climate change.

The threat-multiplier frame has also changed where militaries operate. For years, Crawford wrote, armed forces have worried that a melting Arctic Ocean will open shipping lanes and a contest for minerals.

The U.S., NATO, Russia, and China have all increased their Arctic operations, at the same time as the region’s climate has become less stable and those operations harder to run.

Some armed forces present themselves as green, Crawford wrote. The U.S. Navy publicized a “great green fleet” in 2016, and the U.S. Army promoted its investments in green technology until mention of climate change was all but banned under the Trump administration.

Moving bases off coal does cut emissions, she wrote. But even forces that use fuel-efficient vehicles, batteries, solar power, and microgrids remain major emitters.

When spending grows, so do training, operations, and purchasing, and the emissions grow with them.

“Substantial emission reductions will occur only when armed forces reduce their overall size and footprint and transition to lower emitting doctrines, including those that do not require long range aircraft missions,” Crawford wrote.

Asked by Earth.com what governments should do first, Abba-Aji said they should “weigh the trade-offs between military and social spending for their health and climate consequences and set aside a share of security funding for climate adaptation, especially in the most vulnerable regions.”

Crawford’s own answer is to spend more on health, the environment, and the energy transition rather than take money from them.

“While some form of defense is required, the focus should shift to how to ensure effective defense at lower emission levels and reduced costs,” she wrote.

The size of the source that both articles describe is still unknown. Day-to-day military emissions are left out of national greenhouse gas inventories, and the gases released by this year’s strikes on oil and gas facilities haven’t been added up either.

Counting them would be the first step toward knowing its magnitude.

The full study was published in the journal The BMJ.

#6327. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

#6326. Uranus and Neptune’s strange magnetic fields may be getting stranger

New simulations suggest Uranus and Neptune’s magnetic fields could shift dramatically within decades, driven by conditions deep inside the planets.

Earth’s magnetic field is fairly simple. It has one strong north pole and one strong south pole, both lined up close to the axis the planet spins on, and that’s why a compass points north.

The magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are far messier.

Both planets’ magnetic fields are strongly tilted relative to their rotation axes.

A new study suggests the reason lies deep inside both planets, and that their fields may look quite different today from the last time a spacecraft measured them.

The study focuses on how well material deep inside the planets conducts electricity. In the computer models, conductivity increased with depth.

With that one change, the simulated fields matched the broad features measured during Voyager 2’s flybys in the 1980s.

The work was led by Chi Yan, a research associate at the Jackson School of Geosciences at The University of Texas at Austin.

Yan’s study is built on simulations, not new measurements. Each planet’s magnetic field has been measured up close only once.

NASA’s Voyager 2 flew past Uranus in 1986 and past Neptune in 1989. It’s still the only spacecraft to have visited either planet.

Earth’s magnetic field is tilted about 11 degrees from the axis it spins around. Voyager 2 found that Uranus’ field is tilted 59 degrees and Neptune’s is tilted 47 degrees.

On every other planet with a known magnetic field, the simple north-south pattern accounts for 74% to 98% of the magnetic energy at the surface.

For Uranus and Neptune, the figure is only 12%. The rest of their magnetic energy comes from smaller, more complicated patterns.

A planet makes a magnetic field when fluid that can carry electric current moves around deep inside it. Scientists call this process a dynamo.

Earth’s outer core is liquid iron, surrounded by a mostly solid layer of rock. As the molten iron moves, shaped by Earth’s spin, it produces a field with strong north and south poles.

Uranus and Neptune are about four times wider than Earth.

Scientists think they are made mostly of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane and rocky material, though the exact makeup is still unknown.

They’re called ice giants because water, ammonia and methane are classified as ices in planetary science.

Yan said the planets’ large size and chemistry could explain the tilted fields. Under enough pressure, water molecules can split into charged pieces called ions, which let electricity flow.

“Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high,” said Yan.

“Under these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.”

The researchers simulated fluid moving inside an ice giant and tracked how the flow, the heat and the magnetic field changed together.

The team tested several interior layouts, with thicker and thinner layers of moving fluid.

In some runs, the fluid conducted electricity equally well at every depth. Those runs made strong, upright fields much like Earth’s, and the poles never flipped.

When the fluid conducted better with depth, the result changed in every layout the team tried. The fields became messy, with several poles, and they flipped direction at irregular times.

Near the top of the moving layer, where the fluid conducted less well, magnetic forces had less control over the flow. The motion there broke into smaller, more vigorous swirls.

The runs that looked most like Uranus and Neptune had a fairly thin layer of moving fluid. The authors wrote that the effect doesn’t need finely tuned conditions.

That flexibility matters because the two planets differ sharply in heat.

Uranus gives off little heat beyond the sunlight it absorbs. Neptune gives off nearly twice the energy it receives from the Sun.

In two runs, the simulated fields closely resembled those measured at Uranus and Neptune, then looked clearly different 32 simulated years later.

More than 30 years have passed since Voyager 2’s visits.

“Earth’s magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years,” said Yan.

“Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.”

In one run that resembled Uranus, the tilt moved 84 degrees over 40 years. In another, it moved 13 degrees. Fast and slow change both showed up in runs resembling Uranus.

A 13-degree shift would fit what telescopes have seen at Uranus. Its auroras have appeared in roughly the same places as in 1986, give or take 10 to 20 degrees.

The slow periods didn’t last, though. In the 13-degree run, the field soon started changing faster.

Auroras are one way to check. They form when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases high in a planet’s atmosphere, and where they show up can hint at whether the planet’s magnetic tilt has moved.

Some recent telescope studies, including one that estimated Uranus’ rotation rate by tracking its auroras, assumed its magnetic field had remained unchanged since 1986.

At Neptune, the southern aurora appears to have moved about 30 degrees in latitude between 1989 and 2023.

Researchers aren’t sure yet whether that move reflects a change in the magnetic field.

They are now studying sharp infrared images of both planets’ auroras from the James Webb Space Telescope.

Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University, led that observing campaign and reviewed the new paper for the journal.

Both planets also have an ionosphere, an electrically charged layer high in the atmosphere.

“We are busy working on what’s contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone,” said Stallard.

Yan’s group plans to combine the Webb aurora images, Voyager 2’s magnetic readings and the simulations to estimate how the two fields are arranged today.

Uranus’ magnetic field could also turn out to change slowly over a long period.

If it does, the models suggest the planet’s deep interior carries electricity about 10 times better than standard estimates.

That could mean the inside of Uranus is hotter than scientists thought. Or it could mean the interior holds materials that carry electricity more easily.

Understanding the interiors properly will take new missions back to the ice giants, the researchers wrote.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Physics.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications.

After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World" (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King, director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov?

I was sitting in a lecture theatre at Cambridge University in 1994 when one of my lecturers, Erika Hagelberg, spoke about a new study she had just been involved in. It was the first major case to combine both mitochondrial DNA and DNA fingerprinting to identify human remains: those of the Russian imperial family.

But first I need to take you back to Russia in 1917 and the abdication of the tsar following the Russian Revolution.

The Russian royal family, the Romanovs, had been the reigning imperial dynasty since 1617, and three centuries later, Tsar Nicholas II was on the throne. Nicholas was the cousin of George V, king of the United Kingdom, their mothers being sisters, and had married George's cousin Princess Alix (Alexandra) of Hesse, who was apparently Queen Victoria's favourite grandchild. Nicholas and Alix had five children, four daughters (Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia) and a son, Alexei.

The tsar and his wife were not well liked by the Russian population and political unrest culminated in the revolution of 1917, when Nicholas was forced to abdicate. The family were kept under house arrest and in 1918 they were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg with the royal physician, Dr Botkin, and three of their staff. On the night of 16 July, the family, their doctor and staff were herded into the cellar together and executed. Their bodies were then taken to a secret location and placed in a hastily dug communal grave, doused in sulphuric acid in an attempt to disfigure them and hinder identification, and then covered over, the location of the grave being lost for more than 70 years.

The Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, 1919.

Ironically, the new Russian government had wanted to get the Romanovs out of Russia due to the risk of their becoming a rallying point, but a plan to grant asylum to the Romanovs in the U.K. because of their links with the British royal family fell through, owing to a reluctance on the part of George V to grant it. Yet those links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial in their identification.

Fast-forward to 1991, when several skeletons were found in a shallow grave some 20 miles from Yekaterinburg. Many of the bones were badly damaged but it was possible to determine, based on examination of the skeletal remains, that there were nine individuals — two short of the 11 killed that night. The faces of the skulls were badly damaged in all of the skeletons, all of them showing evidence of violence either in the form of bullet holes or bayonet wounds or both. Before the genetic study, Russian forensic scientists had used numerous techniques alongside historical data to tentatively identify the remains as some of the members of the Russian royal family, their doctor and servants.

These included examining the bones, to determine approximate age and sex, and some of the teeth, the expensive dental work, incorporating gold, platinum and porcelain, indicating that certain remains must belong to members of an aristocratic family. The team worked out that the two missing individuals would have been two of the children, one of the daughters (while it was hard to determine which one it would be, given how close in age they were, it was thought that it was either Maria or Anastasia) and the son, Prince Alexei.

The Russian chief forensic medical examiner then contacted a team in the U.K., which included Erika, to see if genetic evidence could be used to confirm the identification. The U.K. team used the amelogenin genetic sex test, now part of standard forensic DNA testing, which confirmed the sex of the skeletons (four male and five female bodies), while an early form of DNA profiling showed that there was a family group here — two parents and three children — and four unrelated individuals. So far, so good.

Next, they needed to prove that this was the Russian royal family, and they did this using mitochondrial DNA analysis. As you'll remember, mitochondrial DNA is passed down by a mother to all her children, male and female, but only daughters can pass it on — so if female-line family members of Tsar Nicholas and Tsarina Alexandra could be found and would agree to give a DNA test, their mitochondrial DNA should match that of their royal ancestors. It just so happened that the late Prince Philip, husband of the late Queen Elizabeth, was related to the tsarina through the female line: she was his great-aunt, his maternal grandmother being the sister of the tsarina. He kindly gave a DNA sample.

The testing that they did was standard for the time in that they looked at two regions known as hypervariable regions 1 and 2 (HVR1 and HVR2). You'll remember that mitochondrial DNA has 37 rather crucial genes on it where any "typo" that occurs as the DNA is being copied could have serious consequences if the mutation is deleterious. By contrast, in those parts of the mitochondrial genome that don't code for anything, such as these two hypervariable regions, mutations can occur more freely without necessarily causing issues, meaning that these regions contain much more genetic variation. These are the sections of mitochondrial DNA that scientists began analysing for identification purposes. While it's not as precise as DNA profiling because many thousands of people will all have the same mitochondrial DNA type, it can be very helpful in a case such as this.

Prince Philip's DNA was eventually used to confirm the identities of the lost Romanov family.

When the team sequenced these two regions, Prince Philip's mitochondrial DNA was found to match that of the putative remains of the tsarina and her daughters. Next they found two living female-line relatives of the tsar, descended from his maternal grandmother: a great-great-niece, Princess Xenia Cheremeteff Sfiris, and a first cousin twice removed, James Carnegie, 3rd Duke of Fife. The mitochondrial DNA from these two matched each other perfectly, and they, in turn, matched that of the tsar, except at one base where there was both a match and a mismatch.

This is because the tsar had what's known as a heteroplasmy at this position: some of the mitochondrial DNA sequences showed a T and others showed a C, his maternal relatives showing a T. Heteroplasmy is known to take place primarily through mutations occurring when the DNA is copied to make new cells in a person's lifetime, but it can be inherited from a maternal ancestor with heteroplasmy. Extremely rarely, it can come from paternal mitochondrial DNA making it into the cell. So the fact that heteroplasmy existed in the DNA sample didn't negate the match, and the probability that these were the Romanovs was still between 70 to 1 through to 840,000 to 1 in favour. But, it did sow some seeds of doubt. Incidentally, we now know that heteroplasmy is fairly common, with potentially over half of the human population having at least one heteroplasmy, albeit at a low percentage in terms of their mitochondrial DNA carrying it.

So, to be doubly sure, in 1996 the remains of the tsar's brother, Georgij, who had died in 1899, were exhumed and he was found to have exactly the same mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Given the very low chance of two people having this particular heteroplasmy if they weren't related, this pointed to the mitochondrial DNA data the researchers obtained being 130,000,000 times more likely if these were the Romanovs than if they were an unrelated family.

The case was solved in terms of identifying the tsar, tsarina and three of their daughters, but the mystery still remained as to what had happened to the two other children. In the scientific paper reporting the results, the authors conjectured that possibly the two children had been buried separately, or that they could have survived the massacre. Incidentally, there was a woman living in the U.S. who claimed to be Anastasia, saying she had managed to escape being executed, and so the fact that two of the children were missing from the Romanov family group only fuelled the idea that maybe she truly was the missing princess.

Then, in 2007, a group of amateur archaeologists, digging a mere 70 metres away from the previously discovered mass grave, came across more human remains. Skeletal evidence showed that they were the remains of two bodies, a young woman aged 15-19 and a probable male aged 12-15. DNA analysis was brought to bear and again showed that the two individuals were siblings and related to the Romanovs already identified. As an extra DNA test, Y-chromosome testing was carried out, the Y chromosome being passed from father to son, to confirm that the Y chromosome of the newly found male skeleton was indeed male and that it matched the Y chromosome of the tsar. This also then matched male-line relatives — a second cousin once removed of the tsar (third cousin of Alexei) through Tsar Nicholas I. The missing Romanov children had been found.

From an award-winning expert on DNA, discover the myth-busting book that opens a dazzling window into the world of modern genetics.

Fascinating, compassionate, and entirely captivating, The Secrets of Our DNA is the essential book that explains how genetics has changed and transformed the world around us.

Turi King is renowned for presenting complex findings on DNA and genetic science in an accessible and compelling way and she has won awards for her public engagement in science. Turi is the director of the Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath. She is an honorary fellow of the British Science Association, a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London, a member of the Chartered Society of Forensic Sciences, and a member of the International Society of Forensic Geneticists. She is well known for her academic work leading the identification of Richard III; advising on the case of Mary Jane Kelly (the last victim of Jack the Ripper); leading the project on sequencing Hitler’s genome; as well as her media work co-presenting BBC’s DNA Family Secrets.
