#6323. Clouds block satellite cameras, so an AI learned how to redraw the ground beneath them

GeoCore-9B learned how to recreate the ground that is hidden beneath cloud cover in satellite photos.

A satellite picture of a flooded town is only worth something if the camera can see the town. On a cloudy day it can’t, and the picture shows cloud where the streets should be. A new AI model fills those streets back in.

It was built to know where on Earth it is looking and how much ground each pixel covers.

Jeonghyeok Do and Munchurl Kim of KAIST in South Korea built the model, called GeoCore-9B. Their paper is a preprint that has been accepted for presentation at NeurIPS 2026, an artificial intelligence conference. It has not yet been published in a journal.

The ground the model draws under a cloud is a reconstruction, not a photograph. Do and Kim make that point themselves, and they warn that realistic fake satellite imagery could be used to spread disinformation about disasters or geopolitical events.

Ordinary satellite pictures work like a camera. They record sunlight bouncing off the ground, so thick cloud or nighttime leaves them with nothing to record.

That matters most during floods and wildfires, when the weather is often bad and the ground is exactly what people need to see.

A radar satellite sends radio waves down and measures the echoes that come back. The method is called synthetic aperture radar, and it works at night and through cloud.

But its images don’t look like photographs, because brightness and texture in them mean different things. Do and Kim wanted one model for both problems.

Earlier attempts started with an AI built to generate ordinary photographs and then taught it about satellites. Do and Kim wrote that this builds in biases.

Ordinary photos are taken from eye level with a subject in the middle, while a satellite looks straight down at a scene with no center.

So they trained their AI model from scratch on satellite views alone, adjusting about 9 billion internal settings, known as parameters, as it learned.

The training set was 10 million satellite images, each paired with a sentence describing it. The note for a port mentioned ships and warehouses; the note for farmland mentioned a road between fields.

Each image also carried its latitude, longitude, and how much ground one pixel covers. A building looks very different when each pixel covers about 3 feet (1 meter) than when each covers about 105 feet (32 meters).

Without that number, a small building and a large industrial plant can have the same shape.

A model this large, trained from nothing, learns slowly and tends to produce scenes with no coherent layout. So Do and Kim brought in a second AI, already trained to recognize satellite imagery, as a teacher.

During training, the new model was scored on how well its internal picture of a scene agreed with the teacher’s picture of how roads connect and where field boundaries lie.

The teacher is switched off once training ends, so it adds no work when the model is in use. Without it, the team found, the model’s images had fragmented textures and distorted structures. With it, every score they tracked improved.

The team also tested what the model had absorbed about geography. Given only a latitude and longitude, with no text at all, it drew dense skyscrapers for the coordinates of New York City and ice fields for Antarctica. It drew sand dunes for the Sahara and forest for the Amazon.

The team checked 500 of these coordinate-only images generated by the model against all 10.5 million real world photos that were used as training images.

They found none that closely matched the real-world satellite images, suggesting that the AI was not simply copying existing photographs. However, they wrote that the test can’t rule out every form of memorization used by the AI model.

To put the model to work, Do and Kim froze it and trained a small set of extra settings for each task. This was far cheaper than retraining it.

On a public test set of cloudy and clear image pairs, GeoCore-9B outscored every program built specifically for cloud removal on two of three standard measures. Those were cover brightness and color accuracy, and how closely the structure matches the clear image.

On the third, how natural the image looks, it scored about the same as the best specialist. The roads and field boundaries in its reconstructions stayed where the clear images put them.

On a second public dataset, the model turned radar images into photo-like images. It scored best on the two measures of realism and fine detail, and it roughly matched the best specialist on structural similarity.

“By training the AI on where each satellite image was taken and the actual size of the terrain it shows, we made it possible to use a single model for multiple tasks such as cloud removal and image conversion,” said Kim, a professor in KAIST’s School of Electrical Engineering.

He added that he expects the work to make weather-limited satellite data more usable for assessing disasters and monitoring changes in forests and cities.

The model only produces ordinary color images. It can read a radar image but can’t generate one. In addition, it doesn’t handle the multispectral images, with light bands beyond visible color, that some Earth-observation satellites record.

One piece, the component that compresses each image before the model works on it, came from ordinary photography. On the cloud-removal images, it kept the main features but lost some faint local detail.

By their own account, the experiments can’t say how much of the gain came from the model’s size, its training data, or the teacher.

So far each task has been tested on a single public dataset. How the model performs on other satellites and regions is unknown, and that is the test Do and Kim plan next.

Do and Kim also want the model to predict changes on the ground: flooding, building damage, wildfire spread, and urban growth. The team plans to explore surveillance and reconnaissance as well.

The model’s code and weights are online, so other groups can run those tests.

The full study has been posted as a preprint on arXiv and accepted for presentation at NeurIPS 2026. It has not been published in a journal.

#6322. New hypothesis explains why the right side of the human brain controls the left side of the body

The brain's crossed wiring runs through every vertebrate group, and two neuroscientists trace it to the eyes of the first fishes.

A stroke on the right side of the brain weakens the left arm and leg. The brain is cross-wired that way, and for more than a century scientists have assumed there was an evolutionary reason for it.

Two neuroscientists have traced the crossing through every major group of living vertebrates. They now propose that evolution may never have selected it for the jobs it does.

On their reading, the crossed wiring may simply be inherited from the way the first fishes’ eyes were wired to their brains, some 500 million years ago.

Martin Wessendorf, an associate professor emeritus of neuroscience at the University of Minnesota, and Daniel Wang, a researcher in the University’s Department of Neuroscience, wrote the review.

It is a hypothesis built from more than a century of published anatomy rather than a new experiment. However, the authors wrote that it may be testable in fossils.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wang said the question reaches beyond his own field.

“This’ll be relevant to anyone who wants to know more about why brain injury on one side of the head often leads to loss of function on the opposite side of the body,” he said.

The crossing begins at the eye. The lens flips the image, so whatever sits to your right lands on the left side of each retina. The nerve fibers carrying the right half of the view then sort themselves at a junction behind the eyes and run to the left side of the brain.

One place that information goes is a structure in the midbrain called the optic tectum. It holds a map of the opposite half of visual space, and it fires fast turning and escape movements.

Every vertebrate examined appears to have one, lampreys and hagfish included, along with the crossing junction behind the eyes.

Living jawless fish carry both, so the authors conclude that the last common ancestor of all vertebrates probably did too. That puts the first crossed wiring in the Cambrian period, among jawless fishes that lived roughly 538 to 486 million years ago.

Anatomists call crossed wiring contralateral organization, and its age is what struck Wang.

“What surprised me the most was likely just how old the contralateral organization of the optic tectum is for vertebrates – spanning even to the Cambrian,” he told Earth.com.

Body senses crossed next. Two pathways carry touch, pain, temperature and body position from the spinal cord up to the brain, and both cross the midline in amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

The one for light touch and body position is missing in fishes, so the authors trace it to the last common ancestor of the four-limbed animals.

Movement pathways cross too. One runs from the optic tectum down to the spinal cord and turns the body toward whatever just appeared at the edge of vision.

Lampreys and bony fish appear to have no such pathway. Sharks have one that mostly stays on its own side, and rays and lungfish have a crossed one.

Reptiles appear to have lost that pathway. A second crossed pathway, from a cluster of midbrain cells called the red nucleus, is thought to help control limbs.

True mammals appeared about 165 million years ago. By then, those crossed senses and movement pathways had already existed for almost 200 million years.

The pathway that lets you move one finger at a time is the special case. It runs from the cerebral cortex, the six-layered outer sheet found only in mammals, down to the spinal cord, and it crosses in the lower brainstem.

In most mammals, it ends where touch signals enter the cord and adjusts those signals. Few mammals besides primates, raccoons and kinkajous have a version that reaches the nerve cells that drive muscles.

So the circuit that gives humans fine control of their hands appears to be a sensory circuit put to a new use. Wang said that was the finding that surprised his co-author most.

“This demonstrates that circuitry that’s involved in one function can, with just a change or two, become a function that’s entirely different.”

The crossing isn’t universal in this pathway. In goats and elephants, it runs down both sides of the spinal cord, and in hedgehogs and moles it mostly stays on its own side. Even in humans, an estimated 10 to 25 percent of its fibers don’t cross.

Wang pointed to the goats and elephants, “so there’s a decent amount of diversity there,” he said. The authors read that variety as a sign that natural selection wasn’t strongly favoring the crossing in this pathway.

Isaac Newton proposed in 1704 that the junction behind the eyes sorts nerve fibers by visual field.

Ramón y Cajal, who later won a Nobel Prize for his work on the structure of the nervous system, went further in an 1898 paper. Once the visual map crossed, he proposed, it would pay for the maps of hearing, touch and movement to match it.

In computer models published in 2014, an animal controlled by the opposite side of its brain was likelier to survive a blow to one side of the head or body.

At least two other research groups have blamed a twist in the body plan, dating to the split between vertebrates and their invertebrate ancestors. That argument goes back to an 1822 dissection of a crayfish.

The authors see a problem with the twist. The visual system was probably crossed in the first vertebrates, but the pathways for touch, limb control and finger control didn’t exist yet.

So the authors doubt that a single ancient twist can explain them.

The authors’ own answer starts with the optic tectum. Its map of the opposite half of visual space sits on top. Beneath it, in register, sit maps of touch and hearing from the same half, and at the bottom sit the cells that fire movements.

Wessendorf and Wang propose that this stack biased the sensory and motor pathways that evolved later toward crossing.

When the cortex evolved, most of the pathways carrying signals into it were already crossed. A cortex wired to its own side would have needed extra crossings to collect vision, touch and hearing from the far side, or a rewiring of every older circuit.

The authors argue that either change would have carried a “wiring cost,” leaving mammals that were less energy-efficient, less intelligent, or both.

Not everything crosses. Smell and taste mostly stay on the same side, and the authors note that neither sense maps space the way vision, hearing and touch do.

The cerebellum, which coordinates movement, works the same side of the body it sits on.

“We propose that contralateral organization didn’t necessarily evolve as an adaptation, but because evolution is an engineer that builds with the foundation and materials it has at hand,” Wang and Wessendorf wrote.

The authors list what would test the idea. Their first prediction is that the last common ancestor of vertebrates had both the crossing junction and an optic tectum.

Cambrian fossils of jawless fish exist, and a fossilized brain cast from one could show whether both were there.

Wang said the finding that would complicate the idea is an early fossil vertebrate whose optic tectum handled vision on the same side rather than the opposite one.

The authors also predict that crossed pathways from the forebrain to the spinal cord will prove widespread in birds. Unfortunately, relatively few bird species have been examined.

Crocodilians appear not to have been checked, and the authors predict they have one too.

Hearing is the one sense the authors treat with caution. It appears to have evolved partly on its own in different lines.

What remains unknown is whether any Cambrian fish skull preserves enough of its brain to show the crossing.

Until one does, the idea rests on living anatomy. The next checks are in the fossil record, and in the birds and crocodilians whose spinal pathways have yet to be mapped.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Neuroanatomy.

#6321. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

#6319. Billions of trees grow beyond forests – and counting them could change restoration plans

A satellite study counted 5.25 billion trees in Rwanda and Tanzania, finding more than half outside forests, from farmland to towns.

Count a country’s forests and you’ve counted its trees, or so the thinking goes. In Rwanda and Tanzania, most of the trees aren’t in the forests at all.

Researchers counted about 5.25 billion trees across the two countries from 2019 satellite images, and more than half stood on farms, in grassland and shrubland, and in towns.

Countries and organizations have pledged to plant more than a trillion trees worldwide since the Paris climate agreement of 2015.

A pledge needs a count of what is already there, and that count has mostly come from forest surveys that often exclude farmland.

Maurice Mugabowindekwe and Martin Brandt of the University of Copenhagen led the team, with colleagues at the Rwanda Space Agency, the University of Rwanda, and the Tanzania Forest Services Agency.

Their count covers only trees big enough to see from space. That means a crown of at least 32 square feet (3 square meters), or a height of at least 10 feet (3 meters).

The team sorted its count by the land cover map that the European Space Agency’s WorldCover project publishes.

Only 48.8% of the trees fell inside the class that map calls tree cover, which is roughly forest and woodland.

The other 51.2% were spread across everything else: shrubland held 22.1%, grassland 16.4%, and cropland 12%.

The rest, under 1%, stood in towns, wetlands, bare ground and mangroves. Counting only trees in the tree-cover category would leave out more than half the total.

Tanzania accounted for about 5.04 billion of the trees and Rwanda for about 213 million. The typical acre in Tanzania carried 17 trees (42 per hectare) and the typical acre in Rwanda 15 (37 per hectare).

A typical acre of forest carried about 25 (61 per hectare). Forest holds trees more thickly, but there is far more land outside it.

In 2015, a team writing in Nature estimated about 19.9 billion trees in Tanzania, nearly four times this count.

The estimates are not directly comparable: the earlier study included small trees beneath the canopy, while the new study also counted trees outside forests.

Older tree maps worked from pictures sharp enough to outline each crown, taken by drones, aircraft or satellites. Those images cost money, and clouds spoil many.

The Planet satellites the team used have a 10-foot (3-meter) pixel.

The freely available Sentinel-2 optical images and Sentinel-1 radar data have 33-foot (10-meter) pixels.

So the team stopped trying to outline crowns. They stacked 20 bands of data from the three satellite systems into one image and cut it into squares 315 feet (96 meters) on a side.

Then they trained a deep learning model to estimate how many trees each square held, from the patterns of color, texture and radar echo inside it.

The model learned from about 12 million tree crowns in 2,832 sample areas across nine African countries and India. People had marked those crowns by hand or pulled them from laser-scanner height maps.

The team also found that dropping the sharper Planet images and using only the two Sentinel satellites gave nearly the same accuracy.

Rwanda and Tanzania both run national forest inventories, in which crews measure the trees in fixed plots.

The team compared its predictions with 196 of those plots in Rwanda and 19,664 in Tanzania.

It counted only trees at least 8 inches (20 centimeters) thick at chest height, the size most likely to show from above.

The model undercounted in most landscapes. Its raw estimate was about 179 million trees for Rwanda and 3.79 billion for Tanzania.

Matching the field plots raised those figures by about a fifth and a third, respectively, to the 213 million and 5.04 billion reported.

The authors’ explanation is that overlapping crowns in dense forest blur into one signal at a 10-foot pixel.

Built-up areas and mangroves in Tanzania were overcounted instead, and the authors suspect buildings and wetland plants were being read as trees.

Even after correction, the Tanzania figure could be anywhere from 4.6 to 5.6 billion.

A survey of East African farms found an average of 79 trees per acre (195 per hectare).

At that density, the two countries’ 37.6 million acres (15.2 million hectares) of cropland could take about 2.3 billion more trees.

That would be nearly half as many again as the two countries hold now, and trees among crops can raise harvests as well, the authors added.

Tanzania’s own census counts far more cropland than the satellite map does, about 99 million acres (40 million hectares), half of it on smallholder farms.

On that figure, the authors wrote, smallholders alone could add around 3.4 billion trees “if they access adequate support and incentives.”

That is more trees than the count found in all of Tanzania’s forests.

The authors’ point is that a baseline like this one can guide where a government puts its restoration money, and where planting new trees would crowd out naturally open land.

Restoration programs across Africa, from national pledges to the Great Green Wall, have mostly had no such baseline, because operational tree-count systems remain largely unavailable, the authors wrote.

The satellites can’t see under a dense canopy, so the authors treat their own estimates for closed forest with caution.

The count also leaves out every tree too small to show at a 10-foot pixel, so it can’t yet tell whether newly planted seedlings survive.

The correction factors came from Rwandan and Tanzanian field plots, so they may not apply elsewhere.

To use this method elsewhere, researchers would need local field measurements to check and adjust the satellite estimates.

The data and code are publicly available. The team plans to incorporate field measurements into the model to better account for trees hidden beneath the canopy.

The researchers also hope to test the method in other regions and with data from other satellites.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Remote Sensing.

Think that cows are the king of flatulence? There's another animal that likely blows the competition away.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Flatology, the study of flatulence, sounds more like a joke than a serious scientific discipline. But studying farts actually helps biologists understand an animal's diet and digestion.

We know that a host of creatures ‪—​​ from whales, to snakes, to sloths ‪— pass gas. But do we know which animal is the top tooter? Experts told Live Science the answer is blowing in the wind.

"Getting quantitative measurements for farts per animal is pretty difficult," Nick Caruso, a data scientist and co-author of '"Does It Fart?: The Definitive Field Guide to Animal Flatulence'' (Quercus Publishing, 2017), told Live Science in an email.

What we can do is hypothesize using the data we do have. Expelled gas is made partially of methane, so comparing methane emissions produced by different species may provide a clue. However, this method does have limitations, experts pointed out.

Researchers measure the methane animals produce by placing them inside respiration chambers, then inserting a capsule into the stomach that releases a tracer gas while strapping them with a harness that samples their breath. Alternatively, they capture their breath at stations where they feed or are milked.

Research points to livestock, especially cows, as major methane emitters. A recent report puts their total methane emissions at 117 teragrams per year. (One teragram is equal to 1 billion kilograms, or 2.2 billion pounds.) A buildup of cow-generated methane gas even caused a dairy shed in Germany to explode. However, contrary to what many people believe, the "overwhelming majority" of methane emissions from livestock is released through burping, not flatulence, Ermias Kebreab, a professor of animal science at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science in an email.

The reason comes down to where in the gut the gas is made. Herbivores can't break down plant material on their own; they rely on microbes in their guts to ferment it, and that fermentation releases gases such as methane and carbon dioxide, Dr. Marcus Clauss, head of research and co-director of the Clinic for Zoo Animals, Exotic Pets and Wildlife at the University of Zurich, told Live Science in an email. Some of this gas is absorbed into the bloodstream and exhaled. The rest tends to leave by the nearest exit ‪—‬ animals that ferment their food toward the front of the digestive tract mostly burp it out, while those that ferment it toward the back mostly pass it as wind, Clauss explained.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Cows and other ruminants ‪(such as buffalo, sheep, goats and camels)‬ ferment their food in a chamber called the rumen, located near the front of the digestive system, so most of the methane they produce is through belching, Matthew Hayek, an associate professor of environmental studies at New York University, told Live Science in an email.

So if it's not cows, which animal is the top farter based on their methane emissions? The best candidates are hindgut fermenters ‪—‬ herbivores that digest plant matter in the large intestine (the hindgut). Meat eaters, by contrast, typically produce far less methane than herbivores do, Clauss said.

Are cows really the top contender for animal farts?

One possible contender are termites, which break down wood and grass in their hindguts. Their global population is estimated to be around 27 quadrillion (that's 15 zeros) individuals, and they collectively emit 10 teragrams of methane per year.

But, per individual, the title might go to horses. According to a 2019 report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, horses have the highest methane emissions among hindgut fermenters — around 40 pounds (18 kg) of methane per horse each year.

However, Clauss is skeptical. "The ranking of horse as highest is only because it has been measured," he told Live Science in an email. "But there are so many hindgut fermenters not measured, like rhino ... Who knows?"

If we consider methane emissions per unit of bodyweight, the nutria (Myocastor coypus) ‪—‬ an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent ‪—‬ would have higher methane emissions than the horse, Clauss said.

Clauss also questioned the accuracy of using methane emissions data as an indicator of flatulence. "There is some methane in flatulence, but most likely the majority of methane produced by an animal is exhaled, i.e. it goes via blood to the lungs," he said.

So until scientists figure out how to measure animal farts, any ranking remains speculative. For now, scientists have developed ways to track intestinal gas in people, including swallowable electronic capsules that measure gases inside the gut and clip-on underwear sensors that detect hydrogen in farts.

Methane is a particularly potent greenhouse gas when released into the atmosphere, and the quantities that large herds of cows and other ruminants emit through burping are enough to contribute to climate change. Indeed, scientists are experimenting with ways to reduce methane emissions from cattle — for example, by adding seaweed to their diet.

But animal flatulence is not a major contributor to global methane increases, Hayek said.

Even methane emissions from termite flatulence, while large, do not have an impact, Stefan Arndt, a professor of physiological and ecosystem ecology at the University of Melbourne in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "A large proportion of that methane is then consumed by methanotrophic bacteria in the soil," he said. These bacteria use methane as an energy source, thereby reducing the net methane emissions from termites substantially.

"Their emissions are part of the natural cycle of methane that has always been there for millennia," Arndt added. "The increasing methane concentrations in the atmosphere that are leading to climate change are caused by humans."

#6317. A paleontologist hiking near Arches National Park may have found a new armored dinosaur

A new dinosaur bonebed discovered near Moab, Utah, may contain an unknown armored dinosaur species dating back 138 to 141 million years.

In mid-October 2026, the Utah Geological Survey (UGS) opened a new dinosaur excavation near Moab, in eastern Utah. The team calls the site the Ironstone Bonebed, and it lies north of Arches National Park.

The bonebed appears to contain the remains of a new species of armored dinosaur, the agency said. State Paleontologist Jim Kirkland is describing the animal and naming it in honor of Don DeBlieux, the Utah assistant state paleontologist.

The site is estimated at 138 million to 141 million years old. The UGS called it “currently tied as potentially the oldest Cretaceous dinosaur bonebed in North America.”

DeBlieux has said he spotted the first fossils while exploring the area on foot. They were a shoulder blade and an upper arm bone from an armored dinosaur.

He oversees the UGS field paleontology program and its fossil preparation lab. In 2002, he found a skull weathering out of sandstone near the middle of the Wahweap Formation, in southern Utah’s Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.

That skull became the horned dinosaur Diabloceratops eatoni. DeBlieux spent more than 800 hours over two years removing the rock from around the bone.

Kirkland has said the crew has identified about four kinds of dinosaurs at the new site so far.

Kirkland, who has held his post since 1999, is known for naming numerous dinosaur species, most notably Utahraptor. After 25 years of working side by side with him, DeBlieux will retire at the end of 2026.

Geologically, the new locality is nearly equivalent to Doelling’s Bowl, a UGS site some six miles (10 kilometers) to the east.

DeBlieux also found Doelling’s Bowl, in 2005, when he came across the vertebrae and a hip bone of a dromaeosaurid, a raptor-like predator.

A 2012 study of Utah raptors named it Yurgovuchia doellingi and reported a bone bed covering tens of acres (at least several hectares).

Plant-eating iguanodonts, including one compared to Iguanacolossus, dominate it, with at least ten individuals. At least three polacanthine ankylosaurs, a group of armored dinosaurs, were also found there.

The bonebed lies in the lower Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation, below a marker layer of calcrete. It yielded Mierasaurus bobyoungi, a long-necked sauropod descended from Jurassic turiasaurs of the Iberian Peninsula.

Kirkland and DeBlieux co-authored its 2017 description. By then, Doelling’s Bowl had also produced teeth from a large allosauroid predator and a new, still unnamed species of polacanthid ankylosaur.

“Ankylosaurs were so well protected that even their eyelids were armored,” Kirkland and Mark Loewen, then of the Utah Museum of Natural History, wrote in 2011.

At the time, the Cedar Mountain Formation had yielded more ankylosaur species than any other geologic formation in the world. Several more from it had been found but not yet described.

Gastonia burgei came from the basal Yellow Cat Member. It was closely related to Polacanthus foxi, from nearly age-equivalent rocks on England’s Isle of Wight.

Younger layers have produced other Cedar Mountain dinosaurs, including the ankylosaur Peloroplites cedrimontanus from the Ruby Ranch Member.

Utah’s first known nodosaurid, Animantarx ramaljonesi, was the first dinosaur discovered solely by technology. A radiological technician found it in 1994 by mapping low-level radiation across a quarry near the top of the formation.

Cedarpelta bilbyhallorum was then North America’s only known ankylosaurid from the Lower Cretaceous. Ankylosaurids are the branch of armored dinosaurs known for tail clubs and boxy skulls.

The UGS expects the new site to shed light on the transition from the Jurassic to the Cretaceous. A catastrophic event at the end of the Jurassic led to the near-complete extinction of Utah’s Morrison Formation dinosaurs, including Stegosaurus.

Across most of the western North American mountain belt, the gap between Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks spans 20 million to 25 million years.

In eastern Utah, microfossils, chemical signatures and uranium-lead dating of ancient soils cut it to five million to seven million years.

Kirkland, DeBlieux and two colleagues reported that revised dating in a 2025 conference abstract. In those rocks, an increase in larger coelurosaurs, a group of meat-eating dinosaurs, documents the extinction.

The ancient soils also point to a short wet interval after the drier Late Jurassic. Where Early Cretaceous wetlands formed in eastern Utah appears to have been controlled by movement of ancient salt deposits.

Kirkland has argued that the same salt tectonics explain why Utah’s oldest Cretaceous dinosaurs are restricted to northern Grand County.

As buried salt beds were squeezed into ridges, nearby ground subsided, and Lower Cretaceous sediments collected in the low areas.

Across much of the rest of North America, erosion was removing rock at the time. Salt movement peaked in the early Mesozoic, as reflected by the Salt Valley anticline at Arches National Park and the Moab fault.

The information was obtained from the Utah Geological Survey.

#6316. The Pentagon Is Planning for Blackouts That Last for Months. One Problem Could Doom the Strategy.

Generators could keep the lights on for months, but what happens when the base’s water runs dry?

Picture a military base on day thirty of a regional blackout. Its generators are still going strong, but the local utility has stopped pumping water to the base. Keeping the lights on won’t do much good if there’s no water to cool computers or fight a fire.

The Pentagon wants bases to keep working through outages like this. In September, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced FORTRESS America, a plan to help military bases withstand attacks and disruptions to civilian services. The goal was to keep essential operations going for at least three months without outside help. Pentagon installations official Dale Marks shared more details in October, explaining that power targets would range from 30 to 90 days, depending on the base, and critical supplies would need to be stocked for at least three months.

Paul Stockton, a former assistant secretary of defense for homeland defense and Americas’ security affairs, tells Popular Mechanics that many defense installations “depend on civilian-operated water utilities that lie outside installation fencelines.” Suppose the base keeps its power on for three months. Can it still do its job if the services outside the gate stop working?

Stockton puts water at the top of his concerns. Beyond drinking supplies, bases need it for fire suppression and computer cooling, uses he calls “absolutely vital for mission execution at most bases.” Sanitation depends on water, too. “Losing that electricity-dependent water utility support would have devastating effects in an extended conflict,” he says. Even if the base’s generators are running perfectly, that won’t matter if there’s a fire and there’s no water running through the hydrants.

Some missions need very little from the outside world. Stockton says bases that launch nuclear strikes with bombers or other nuclear forces depend relatively little on civilian services. Bases that send troops overseas are different. For them, keeping the base running is only the first step.

A unit heading to a conflict in the Taiwan Strait could start its trip at a base hundreds of miles from the coast. Getting troops and equipment to a ship would mean relying on civilian transportation and a working seaport, Stockton says. Keeping a base running through a blackout would be an achievement. But if its troops and equipment can’t get to the fight, the military still has a problem.

A reactor could help with the fuel trucks

Keeping generators supplied creates another outside dependency. Stockton says bases commonly run on natural gas or diesel, and an extended outage could disrupt deliveries. Bases may have room to store substantial diesel reserves, but replenishing them through a region with disabled infrastructure would be difficult.

Small nuclear reactors could help. A microreactor could power a base for a long time without regular fuel deliveries. In August, the Army said it would spend up to $2.2 billion on five companies to build reactors at five bases. It hopes to have the first one running by September 2028. Reactors won’t be the only answer, though. Marks has said bases will also use other energy sources, and the mix will vary by location.

“You park the reactor, turn it on, and it just sits there being hot,” says Brendan Kochunas, an associate professor of nuclear engineering and radiological sciences at the University of Michigan. Once engineers can get it running reliably, a base could go a long time without a fresh delivery of reactor fuel. Diesel generators, by contrast, would keep burning through their fuel supply.

The military microreactors are “very much still in development,” Kochunas says. Antares Nuclear, the company the Army chose to build a reactor at Fort Bragg, demonstrated a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in its Mark-0 reactor in June. Its follow-on Mark-1 is scheduled to demonstrate electricity production in 2027, according to the company’s congressional testimony.

That leaves a big question: can a reactor keep going on its own? Kochunas says the real test comes when a reactor runs at full power for a long stretch. That’s when engineers find out what needs fixing, “once you see everything heat up.” A single broken pump or sensor could leave a base waiting for outside help. That’s the same kind of help a blackout could cut off. For Kochunas, a reactor is only ready when it has shown it can run “without interaction, only observation, for the duration of the anticipated mission outage.”

Stockton says the first step in knowing whether a base could really survive a blackout is a surprise test called a blackstart exercise. Without warning, the base cuts itself off from the grid and starts its own generators. Then it has to get power to the equipment its mission depends on. That’s harder than it sounds. “Such blackstart operations are challenging,” Stockton says. But a successful start only answers the first question—the next is how long the base can continue operating if fuel deliveries become unreliable or the water utility fails. An exercise that assumes those services will keep working could give commanders too much confidence in what the generators have accomplished.

David Alexander, an emeritus professor of emergency planning and management at University College London, sees a similar issue in hospitals. They “function as part of the medical system. Hence, they do not work independently,” he says. Backup power keeps the building running, but it can’t replace everything else a hospital depends on to do its job.

The strongest fortress may extend beyond the fence

So where should the money go? Stockton says one of the best investments might not be on the base at all. The pumps that send water to the base sit at the local water utility. So if a blackout shuts them down, the base’s taps and hydrants will go dry. Helping the utility keep its own power on could do more for the mission than spending on the base itself. Stockton also wants planners to think bigger than one base and its town. In a 2026 report for the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, he proposed choosing large sections of the grid, some covering several states, that could cut themselves off when trouble started spreading elsewhere. He calls them “microgrids on steroids.”

First, utilities would need a plan to keep the power on inside each section. If that works, a region’s seaports could keep running along with its bases, and troops and equipment would have a real chance of reaching their ships. Hegseth has promised that if an adversary takes down the grid, “our bases stay lit.” That’s an important goal, but just keeping the lights on isn’t enough. The real goal is getting troops to where the fight is—and a base that can’t do that is just a well-lit place to wait.

#6315. City crows let people get closer, but country crows can be bolder in their own way

City crows tolerate people better than rural crows, but unfamiliar objects near food can make them more cautious.

City crows let people get closer than rural crows do. But when researchers put a lamp base in a pile of peanuts, city crows were less likely than rural crows to take a peanut.

The study of American crows around Ithaca, New York, suggests that a crow’s fears are shaped by its past experience.

Two experiments were run by Dave Colucci and Anne Clark, biologists at Binghamton University. In the first experiment, objects were left next to food on crow territories.

In the second, Colucci walked toward crows and measured how close he got before they flew.

The evidence for greater wariness in city crows comes from a single object.

It also comes from only one of the three measures used by the team. In addition, the city sites were closer to suburbs than to a downtown.

In crows, Colucci said, fear of anything new exists side by side with a great deal of curiosity. The fear does not always prevail, he added, so a new opportunity is sometimes seized.

Ten crow families were chosen from parking lots, parks, and dead-end streets near Ithaca.

Another 10 families lived on farmland and natural areas in the nearby town of Dryden.

American crows live in family groups that share a territory.

On most days of the week, Colucci scattered two cups of unsalted peanuts in the shell on each territory.

The same spot was used each time. He continued until the family had fed there three times in a row.

A single object was then set in the middle of the peanuts on four separate mornings. The crows were filmed by a hidden camcorder. Colucci watched from at least 164 feet (50 meters) away.

The trials were run in July and August of 2019 and 2020. Four objects were used: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a takeout box, and a lamp base.

The box was paperboard, and the lamp base was made to look like wood.

Every crow was expected to find the lamp base new. Bright colors, shiny surfaces and sharp angles are typical of human-made things.

These features are probably better known to crows living in cities. None of them was present on the lamp base.

When only peanuts were offered, nearly every crow that came within about 10 feet (3 meters) took one.

The team estimated the probability of eating at 99% for such city crows and 97% for rural crows.

With the lamp base in place, the estimated probability dropped to 76% among rural crows and 53% among city crows.

Wariness of new things is called neophobia by biologists. By this measure, the city crows had more of it.

The other two measures concerned only the first crow of each family to arrive and to eat. Their timing was compared with that on days when no object was present.

With the lamp base in place, the first crow to arrive and the first to eat were about as quick in city families as in rural ones.

To Colucci and Clark, that result suggests both places have some bold crows.

Results from earlier experiments on city and country birds have not agreed with one another. Lower wariness in cities has been reported in some of them, higher wariness or no difference in others.

Colucci and Clark wrote that some of those experiments used human-made objects, which city animals may know better.

A second idea was tested with the corn and the takeout box. An ear of corn should be ordinary to a crow that lives beside farm fields.

That ear of corn should seem strange to a crow whose home is beside a parking lot. For a takeout box, the reverse should be true.

More rural crows were put off by the takeout box, and more city crows were put off by the corn.

The team could be confident of that pattern only in the share of crows that ate. In how quickly the first crow arrived or ate, the pattern was too weak to be sure of.

A one-mile (1.6 km) stretch of road was also walked in each setting once a week for three weeks. Every human-made object was recorded.

A total of 341 objects was counted, with 169 along the city road and 172 along the rural road. A typical object nevertheless remained in place for a shorter time along the city road.

Objects turned over faster along the city road, but city crows were still more reluctant to eat beside the lamp base.

City crows are thus exposed to a constant turnover of objects, yet their wariness of new things hasn’t been reduced.

The authors suggested that most litter may be treated by city crows as one category.

In the second experiment, crows were approached on foot by Colucci 145 times over three summers. These approaches took place across upstate New York and Quebec.

During some approaches his gaze was fixed directly on the crow. During others his whole face was tilted toward the ground. A camera on his chest streamed video to a phone in his hand so that his direction could be maintained.

The average crow took flight while he was still about 150 feet (45 meters) away. A distance of 33 feet (10 meters) or less was reached in only eight approaches.

Closer approaches were tolerated by city crows than by rural crows, as is usual for city animals. Rural crows fled from far away regardless of the direction of his gaze.

In the most built-up areas, crows let him get about 82 feet (25 meters) closer when his face was down. The authors wrote that the true effect of his gaze could be either small or large.

A similar but smaller effect was found in a 2013 study of crows in Seattle. To the authors’ knowledge, a difference between two populations in the use of human gaze had not been shown before.

Hunting is one possible explanation for the behavior of the rural crows.

Within city limits in New York, crows may not be hunted. Hunting them in rural areas is legal from September 1 to March 31.

The rural response was described by Clark, an associate professor emerita of biological sciences, as a blunt defense against predators. “Don’t take any chances, don’t stop to assess; let’s just be safe,” she said.

Clark added that such a habit would not work for city crows. People pass by too often in a city for a crow to take flight every time.

The peanut experiment also provided evidence of greater caution among rural crows. With no object present, the first city crow reached the peanuts at about four times the rural rate.

The number of people living within about half a mile (800 meters) gave the best prediction of a crow’s reaction. When smaller or larger circles were used, the predictions were poorer.

A circle of that size is larger than the territory held by a crow family.

It was suggested by the authors that crows average their experience of people over a wide area. They then adjust to the person approaching them.

Individual people who have threatened them are also remembered by crows.

The study leaves open whether city crows gain any advantage from being more cautious around an unfamiliar object. Two possible explanations have been put forward by the authors.

One is that cities contain dangers which cannot be predicted even by a crow that knows its neighborhood well.

The other concerns the crows that first settled in towns about 70 years ago. Those birds may have had little fear of new things, with caution proving useful only later.

It is also uncertain whether the lamp base was equally new to both groups. Its shape is perfectly symmetrical, and such symmetry is rare in natural objects.

City crows might therefore have found it more familiar than the team had intended.

Were that the case, the authors wrote, the difference between city and rural crows could be underestimated.

Future research could test whether wariness slows crows down when new problems have to be solved. It could also test whether cities hold more unfamiliar threats.

For comparisons of urban wildlife with rural animals, a first step was recommended by Colucci and Clark. They wrote that the objects present in each environment ought to be identified first.

The full study was published in the journal Behavioral Ecology.

#6314. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

After nine days in space, the Artemis II crewmembers faced their final and riskiest challenge: splashdown. In this excerpt from the book "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space," astronaut Jeremy Hansen describes the moment from his chair.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After nine days in space, the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission looked out their capsule window on April 10, 2026, and saw the bright-blue Earth below them. The crew had traveled more than 250,000 miles (400,000 kilometers) from our planet — farther from Earth than any humans had ever gone — and now, home was just a few hundred miles straight down.

Only one milestone remained: splashdown, a fast and fiery plunge into the Pacific Ocean that would mark the end of humanity's first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years.Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, the lone Canadian Space Agency astronaut on the crew, had every reason to be confident that the team's Orion crew capsule would hold up just fine. But this was Hansen's first time in space, and his first time dropping through the sky like a fireball at 24,600 mph (39,600 kmh).

It wasn't that he was afraid for himself, Hansen explains in "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space" (Hanover Square Press, 2026), which he co-wrote with John Larsen). Rather, he knew that his wife Catherine and three children would be among the millions of Earthlings watching the most dangerous moment of his mission from below.

In this excerpt from the book, Hansen describes the thrilling intensity of splashdown and the euphoria of knowing that he and his crewmates were going to make it back safely — and make history.

CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen smiles inside the Orion crew capsule during the Artemis II lunar flyby.

Immediately after jettisoning the European Service Module, and exactly half an hour before we were due to splashdown, Mission Control initiated the crew module raise burn. This nineteen-second burn was the first and only burn using the small thrusters built into our Orion capsule. It slightly shallowed our entry trajectory to put us right in the sweet spot while also providing some added distance from the service module, as we'd be hitting the atmosphere in near succession. It, too, went flawlessly. I tightened my straps; it was time for the fireworks.

A re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere is absolutely on the short list of the most incredible experiences of my life. We slammed into it at 7:53 p.m., thundering down at over 10 kilometres [6.2 miles] per second. Per second.

The thrusters fired almost constantly to stabilize the capsule: loud thuds, as if Thor himself were hammering on our spacecraft, as the G-forces quickly began to build, aggressively scrubbing off the velocity we had added to our rocket nine days earlier. Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us. It started red and transformed into a bright, bluish-green, pulsating light. It was breathtaking, the bright colors igniting our senses.

It was insane to think about what we were doing. We all knew how this worked; we all knew the science. But deep inside, I also recognized that astronauts must have a screw loose to do this. Nobody in their right mind would strap themselves inside a metal canister that itself was sitting inside a giant fireball. But there was no other way down, and I had accepted the realities of this journey long in advance.

Although I was at peace, I felt guilty for the stress I was putting on my family. I had talked to them openly about the mission's risks, and this was the highest-risk moment. I tried to send my love telepathically, telling them it was going great.

The Orion capsule drops toward the Pacific Ocean with all parachutes successfully deployed.

As we continued our freefall, it looked like a thousand camera flashes were exploding inside Integrity. I lowered the sun visor on my helmet. There were only centimeters of heatshield and aluminum separating me from the more than 2500°C heat outside. Almost instantly, the heat inside our cramped home also began to rise, an increase that engineers refer to as "thermally benign." All I know is that I couldn't feel it, blissfully wrapped in my thermally controlled garments.

As we continued to fall, the G-forces built up to nearly four times the pressure we feel on Earth. I wasn't too worried, having endured more than five minutes of the same G-force, or more, in the NASA centrifuge trainer. I had half-expected the freefall back to Earth to seem short, but it was a long six minutes before the flames finally ceased and we re-established communications with Mission Control.

It had already been a wild ride, but I also knew another crazy part — parachute deployment and the actual splashdown — lay ahead. My adrenalin kept pumping.

Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us.

"Integrity, Houston. Comms check, post-blackout," we heard from Mission Control. It was music to our ears. It was exactly 8:00 p.m.

"Houston, Integrity," Reid [Wiseman, mission commander], replied. "We have you loud and clear."

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried. For the folks at NASA, it was clear that all had gone well during the descent — a small fleet of NASA and Air Force planes had captured it on high-resolution cameras. But, for me, it wasn't over yet. I wouldn't truly feel safe until our three main parachutes successfully deployed. If they didn't, we'd be a chunk of metal slamming into the ocean at incredibly high speed, and the chances of surviving that would be somewhere between minimal and non-existent.

I've watched many of my close friends return from space, and I find the minutes after surviving the re-entry heat until the parachutes deploy to be the hardest part to watch. When I see a capsule plunge through the clouds with no chutes, I always worry they might not appear at all. That's completely terrifying.

Jeremy Hansen arrives on the deck of the USS John P. Murtha after being recovered from the Orion capsule. All four crewmembers were in perfect health after splashdown.

I thought of Catherine and the kids, sending them a "don't worry, gang" message in my mind. Catherine later told me that she had a very bad feeling about the heatshield, so when we emerged from blackout, she began crying and didn't even focus on the parachutes.

Three minutes later, at an altitude of 7,100 metres, timed explosions released small chutes that pulled off the cover for two larger chutes, called drogues because they are intended to slow our acceleration to a speed that would allow our main parachutes to open without ripping. They did their job perfectly, but it was wild inside the capsule, jerking us back and forth like a ride at the fair.

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried.

One minute later, at only 1,500 metres above the ocean, the drogue chutes cut loose, and, for a few moments, we felt like we were falling backward. Then, in succession, the three main parachutes began deploying, blossoming slowly so they wouldn't tear apart. The rate of our fall slowed as the red-and-white nylon canopies, each 35 metres in diameter, filled with air. The thrusters kept firing, aiming the capsule's base directly toward the point of impact.

"Integrity, we see three good-looking parachutes," we heard from our CAPCOM. Within seconds, our splashdown speed had reduced to 27 kilometres per hour.

That's it, I said to myself. I'm pretty sure we can survive whatever else could be thrown at us now.

Christina [Koch, mission specialist] seemed to agree. We grabbed one another's hands in a moment of celebration.

Excerpted from "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, The Groundbreaking Human Mission Into Deep Space" by John Larsen with Jeremy Hansen. © 2026 by John Larsen, used with permission by HarperCollins/Hanover Square Press.

A riveting and intimate account of the iconic achievement of Artemis II, Earthrise—written by author John Larsen and based on extensive interviews he conducted with Hansen—is a testament to what can be achieved with unity, teamwork, and a bold belief in humanity’s ability to reach for the stars.

Earthrise is his second book.

#6312. Miles Below the Pacific, Rocks Litter the Abyss. Something Is Alive Inside Them—Thousands of Somethings.

Up to 245 lifeforms can live on a single nodule, but mining could wipe them out before we even name them.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

At first glance, polymetallic nodules don’t look like much. To the uninitiated, these strange potato-sized rocks look relatively unremarkable, but everything about them defies such a description—and that’s also why they’re central to a deep-sea controversy that’s been brewing for years.

The problem is twofold. First, these nodules contain metals vital to emerging technologies, including manganese, cobalt, copper, zinc, and iron. Second, most of them sit in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, in a region called the Clarion–Clipperton Zone, roughly 4,000 to 6,000 meters (about 2.5 to 3.7 miles) below the surface. Life in estuaries and tidal zones near the coast is adapted to constant change, from daily temperature swings to human interference. The deep ocean is far more fragile. That’s a problem, because there’s immense interest in mining these nodules, and doing so could be far more destructive down there.

Now, a new study published in the journal Scientific Reports has found that in addition to being part of a delicate ecosystem, the nodules are ecosystems themselves, home to dozens or even hundreds of tiny animals. That’s because of their porous internal structure. Each nodule begins as a bit of ancient debris on the seafloor, and dissolved metals slowly build up around it in layers, adding only a few millimeters of rock every million years. One scientist, speaking with Popular Mechanics in 2024 said the process is “like a super slow game of Tetris.”

The new study analyzed a total 244 nodules that contained more than 4,000 individual animals on their surfaces alone. While on average 17 animals lived on each nodule, some contained as many as 245 lifeforms, ranging from single-celled species to nematodes and small crustaceans. The various crevices found throughout the nodules provide the perfect habitat to harbor all these species.

“The crevices in the polymetallic nodules function as small shelters and provide home to animals that we do not encounter in the soft sediment of the seafloor,” said Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo, a co-lead author of the study from the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research (NIOZ), in a press statement.

The surrounding sediment held more life overall, but nodules hosted their own distinct communities. They were similar from one nodule to the next and noticeably different from those in the mud. And some of those residents seem to live nowhere else. One species, a single-celled organism called Thurammina sp. 1, appears perfectly adapted to life on the nodules. If the nodules were mined, it could disappear along with an ecosystem that took millions of years to build.

“Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules,” Sabine Gollner, also from the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research and senior author of the study, said. “This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining.”

But the creatures that depend on the nodules aren't the only reason to think twice about mining them. In 2024, a team of scientists from the Scottish Association for Marine Science and Northwestern University found possible evidence that the nodules produced “dark oxygen,” a rare form of oxygen production that doesn’t rely on sunlight. The Mining Company—which initially funded that research—and other scientists refuted those findings, while the initial research team stood behind their work. They’re currently undertaking another expedition to the CCZ to study this oxygen-producing phenomenon.

Dark oxygen or no, it’s increasingly clear that these nodules are part of a long-standing ecosystem whose history began long before the first hominin appeared on Earth—let alone Homo sapiens. Will this unique habitat fall prey to our insatiable hunger for progress? Well, that remains to be seen.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6310. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

#6309. Scientists Buried Sheep in a French Cemetery for a Year. What They Dug Up Could Change How We Bury Humans.

Half the corpses became bones and rich soil. The other half began turning into eerie ‘grave wax.”

When someone dies and is buried, it’s often described as “returning to the Earth,” and strictly speaking, that’s true. A body, typically pumped full of preservatives and chemicals in a traditional burial, is lowered into a perplexingly ornate casket, where it can take upwards of 15 years to fully decompose. However, a new kind of burial known as “terramation” or “human composting” does away with these attempts at preserving the body. Instead, it leans into the opposite strategy by creating favorable microbial environments that can decompose human flesh in just a month. The result is a more eco-friendly end of life that doesn’t pollute the air like cremations, or leach chemicals into the ground as decomposing caskets do.

This new approach to the afterlife is currently legal only in a dozen U.S. states, parts of Germany, and New South Wales in Australia. But France may be next, thanks in part to a strange experiment unfolding at a cemetery in Les Ulis. It’s here that Damien Charabidzé, an entomologist at the Université de Lille, is studying two types of burials side-by-side using sheep corpses. Last summer, Charabidzé teamed up with Humo Sapiens, a group campaigning to legalize terramation, to bury sheep in eight pits. Four sheep went straight into the soil, and four were packed in shredded plant matter.

“It's the same principle as composting,” Charabidzé said in a press release for the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS). “You need to strike a balance between a nitrogen-rich material to be broken down (in this case, a corpse) and carbon (wood shavings) through which oxygen can circulate.”

Then the team waited a year and returned on a sweltering summer day to unearth their decomposed specimens. In the pits filled with plant material, no odors issued forth when the burials were exhumed. Only bones remained in the graves, with all organic material transformed into humus—stable soil organic matter. The same could not be said of the other pits. There, the sheep had only lost only a quarter of their mass and many of them were in the process of saponification, in which fats from the body turn into a kind of wax (often referred to in human burials as “grave wax”).

“The flesh practically stops decomposing,” Charabidzé said in a press release. “And nothing grows above the pit….We don’t know to what extent this natural phenomenon is exacerbated by embalming fluids, by the ingestion of food packed with preservatives during life, or by the deterioration of the soil in cemeteries.”

Terramation solves several problems at once. Cremating a single body has roughly the carbon footprint of a round-trip flight, according to researchers, and composting could largely eliminate those emissions. It also keeps embalming chemicals out of the soil and takes up no permanent cemetery space. That matters because as land prices soar worldwide, burial leases are getting shorter, making a grave a less attractive way to ride out eternity. Terramation also has a spiritual appeal. Instead of harming the planet that sustained us, our final act can be a gift back to it.

Mortality is undergoing a reexamination of sorts as the ultra-rich are trying to cheat death, and AI companies are selling digital avatars of the dead. Terramation offers something humbler: a way to die that actually helps the planet.
