Ancient writers couldn't agree on how Egypt's last queen took her own life, and the famous snakebite story may owe more to her enemies than to the facts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The death of Cleopatra is among the most famous in history. In 31 B.C., the Egyptian queen and her Roman ally and lover, Mark Antony, lost the Battle of Actium to Octavian, who would later become Rome's first emperor, Augustus. The following summer, Cleopatra was captured during a Roman ambush inside her royal tomb in Alexandria.

According to Octavian’s account, rather than facing the disgrace of defeat, the queen allowed a venomous asp snake to bite her and quickly succumbed to its poison. Some Roman writers, such as the historian Velleius Paterculus, repeated that story without question.

But others were far less certain of this account, calling it Roman propaganda to cement Octavian's rise to power. And most historians today doubt that a snake was involved at all. So how did Cleopatra die?

Live Science spoke with experts, who told us that the queen's death is still shrouded in mystery.

"We cannot know for sure exactly how Cleopatra died," Prudence Jones, a professor of classics at Montclair State University in New Jersey and author of "Cleopatra: A Sourcebook" (University of Oklahoma Press, 2006), told Live Science in an email.

What historians largely agree on is that Cleopatra VII, the last queen of Egypt's Ptolemaic dynasty, took her own life and that she chose a method that left her body composed and dignified.

Physical evidence of Cleopatra's death is elusive. Much of Alexandria's royal quarter now lies underwater, and underwater archaeologist Franck Goddio, who has been excavating it, hasn't found the queen's mausoleum, Jones said. Even if Cleopatra's remains surfaced, bones would be unlikely to show evidence of snake venom, she added, noting that forensics is outside her area of expertise.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Divers celebrate as a crane pulls an artifact from the waters at Abu Qir bay in Alexandria, Egypt on Aug. 21, 2025.

The best witness may have been Olympus, Cleopatra's personal physician. "Unfortunately, nothing survives of Olympus' account," Jones said.

What does remain is a story told largely by Cleopatra's enemies. The earliest surviving account is a poem by the Roman poet Horace, whose patron was a close friend of Octavian, said Jane Draycott, a historian at the University of Glasgow. His Ode 1.37, written around the time of her death, celebrates Octavian's victory and already pictures the queen handling serpents — yet it ends with grudging admiration for a woman who refused to be paraded as a trophy.

Following her capture, Cleopatra was held under military guard. By then, she had already tried to end her life twice. Cleopatra had tried to stab herself when Roman soldiers broke into the mausoleum where she had barricaded herself, and she later tried to starve herself, stopping only after Octavian threatened her children.

To Draycott, those attempts leave little doubt that Cleopatra would rather die than live as a captive. "She does not want to be a prisoner; she does not want to be led through the streets of Rome in triumph as a defeated foe," she told Live Science.

In the Greco-Roman world, suicide didn't carry the stigma it later acquired under Christianity, she added. "It was a way of wiping the slate clean, removing any shame, any disgrace from yourself." After the defeat of his remaining forces at Alexandria and hearing a false report of Cleopatra's death, Antony was the first of the two lovers to die by suicide.

According to the Greek biographer Plutarch, who based his account on that of Cleopatra's personal physician, Cleopatra visited Antony's tomb, bathed, ate and sent Octavian a sealed letter asking to be buried beside Antony, signaling that she meant to die. Octavian realized what was happening and sent messengers rushing to her, but they arrived too late. They found her dead in her royal regalia, with her attendants Iras and Charmion dying beside her.

A statue depicting Cleopatra's suicide by asp, the most famous of several ancient theories.

Jones has compiled what ancient historians, biographers, geographers and physicians wrote about Cleopatra's death. Every source mentions a snakebite, but several also suggest other possibilities, including a poisonous ointment, poison hidden in a hollow hairpin, and snake venom poured into a wound the queen made by biting herself. Only one of these writers, the geographer Strabo, was alive when Cleopatra died, and the only people in the room with her died, too.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio wrote that the sole clue was a pair of faint pricks on her arm. That doesn't settle much, however. "A cobra bite can appear as two small puncture wounds, but not all cobra bites appear this way and not all double puncture wounds result from snakebites," Jones said.

Jones traces the snake version of the story to Octavian, who was in Alexandria when Cleopatra died. Plutarch reported that an image of Cleopatra with an asp clinging to her was carried in Octavian's triumphal procession in Rome. "Octavian, however, was Cleopatra's enemy and for that reason we may not want to accept his account uncritically," Jones said.

Draycott suggested another possible source of confusion: Snake-shaped jewelry was fashionable in Alexandria at the time, so Romans viewing an effigy of the queen may have mistaken a snake bracelet for a real snake.

Draycott doesn't think one snake could have killed all three women. Jones is less certain. Snakes don't inject the same amount of venom with every bite, and some "dry bites" deliver none at all, Jones said. "On the other hand, I don't think it is impossible, as the body of a cobra contains enough venom to kill multiple people," she added.

The general view among historians, Draycott said, is that Cleopatra took some kind of poison — one that worked quickly and didn't cause seizures or vomiting. The absence of these symptoms is telling: An asp is believed to be what is now known as the Egyptian cobra (Naja haje), whose venom causes a slow, agonizing death with respiratory failure.

A young Egyptian cobra (Naja haja) strikes a typical defensive pose in scrubland near Sidi Ifni, Morocco.

Cleopatra likely would have had other means, then. Alexandria was the Mediterranean's center of scientific study, and texts from the period, such as Nicander's "Theriaca," catalog venomous animals, Jones noted. Cleopatra's father, Ptolemy XII, even consulted the pharmacologist Zopyrus about antidotes. Plutarch claimed that Cleopatra personally oversaw experiments that observed the effects of deadly poisons on condemned prisoners.

Still, that claim and other poison stories should be read with caution, Draycott said, because they draw on Roman stereotypes about women. In the Roman view, "manly men will battle with swords," while women, seen as "deceitful and weak" at this time, were thought to kill in secret. "They'll sneak it into your food," Draycott said, summing up the stereotype.

Roman writers were equally suspicious. Poisoning allegations dogged the Hellenistic dynasties of ancient Egypt and the neighboring Seleucid kingdom, as well as Rome's own imperial family. Some were probably true, Draycott said, but others may have been foodborne illnesses or other health conditions people didn't understand.

The method may remain a mystery, but for most historians, the motive doesn't change: Cleopatra chose to die on her own terms.

Olivia Maule is a former Live Science intern and science journalist whose beats include space, biotechnology and the environment. She holds a B.A. in biology and a B.S. in anthropology from the University of Florida and completed a master's degree in science communication at U.C. Santa Cruz. A 2025 AAAS Mass Media Fellow, she wrote stories and produced videos during a summer at El Nuevo Día, Puerto Rico's largest newspaper, and has written for Eos, Mongabay, Science magazine and Stanford Report. Olivia is a native Spanish and English speaker.

#6307. Trump’s closing midterm argument, Reflecting Pool edition

President Donald Trump on Monday delivered an unconventional midterms closing argument after spending weeks dropping comments at rallies aimed at sowing doubts about the election — and what he might do to contest races Republicans lose.

After barnstorming states with competitive Senate races the last few weeks, Trump delivered his final message in Washington, D.C. He even chose the Reflecting Pool by the Lincoln Memorial — the site of a refurbishment he oversaw that was plagued by questionable work that continues to reverberate politically and legally.

There had been rumblings online last week that he would be in Michigan to close out his rally blitz alongside former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, who is in a Toss-up race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. That race was rocked Sunday when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost a primary to El-Sayed, endorsed the Republican nominee. Alas, Trump chose the nation’s capital and mused about pool liner colors, an issue that has not overtaken voter concerns about the cost of living, corruption, the Iran war and other issues, according to public polling.

“We resurfaced the bottom in a beautiful dark blue, very dark blue. They call it ‘American flag blue,’ but it's very dark,” he said, wearing a suit, tie and white baseball cap. “And if you had a regular blue, like I personally love the lighter color blue, but then you wouldn't have any reflectors.”

He also plugged his proposed arch, made questionable statements about crime rates and boasted about his other Washington, D.C., fountain and park projects. He did not mention Tuesday’s election —which he deemed “the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime” — until after the 22-minute mark. Once he moved on from boasting about his D.C. projects, Trump touted his second administration’s policy record. And himself.

“As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime. The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history,” he said. “These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

He noted he had held 29 rallies in recent weeks. He contended Iran’s military platforms and stockpiles were “way down.” He touted statistics about the economy.

“Personal incomes are the highest in history. The poverty rate is at an all-time record low,” he said, adding. “American exports are at an all-time high, and more people are working today than at any point in the history of our country. And the United States is now by far the largest supplier of oil and natural gas anywhere in the world.”

The Reflecting Pool event came after he spent weeks on the campaign trail making warnings about elections — specifically, ones Democrats have won and might win this week.

For instance, during an Oct. 20 campaign rally in North Carolina for former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, who is running against former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper, Trump returned to casting doubt on his 2020 loss.

“What a lot of people don’t know is that we got screwed in 2020,” Trump said that evening, referring to the presidential race he lost to Joe Biden. “We did great. But you know who … didn't allow it to happen was Michael Whatley. We were winning everything. You went to bed [at] 10:00. The race was over.

“Then all of a sudden, Georgia happened and some other things happened. Pennsylvania happened,” he said, continuing to cast doubt on his losses that year in both states despite no evidence of fraud.

“But we can’t forget,” he told loyalists in eastern North Carolina. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales lists the race as leaning toward Cooper.

Trump also offered the same crowd a preview of what his administration and political organizations have signaled for Tuesday at strategically selected polling stations with competitive House and Senate races.

“You know what didn’t happen? North Carolina didn't happen,” he said to cheers about the 2020 election. “Because he had 619 lawyers at every station watching, watching, watching.”

Democratic lawmakers and pro-voter groups have warned for months that they fear pro-Trump election monitors — or even federal agents — could try to intimidate anti-Trump voters from casting ballots. Some sources have even raised concerns the administration might try seizing ballots in places that could swing a close outcome toward Republican candidates.

Trump’s rally rhetoric also suggests he will raise doubts not just about the outcomes the votes produce, but how they were cast.

“The whole thing is corrupt,” he told rallygoers Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa. “Go to paper ballots, everybody. Nice, beautiful paper ballots. You know, the paper ballots cost 9 percent of what these crooked machines cost, so you’d save a lot,” he said, without offering evidence that electronically cast ballots are problematic.

He even set the stage for casting doubt over or challenging Democratic-won races in states with GOP chiefs executive.

“And even Republican governors, many of them, they, they just do it,” he said of using voting machines over watermarked paper ballots. “I don't know, it’s hard to believe. But you go to paper and you have the ballot there, and it’s so simple, and they put it in stacks.”

Still, Trump and his team have questioned the counting of paper ballots before — in 2020 in places like Arizona, Georgia and Pennsylvania, but to no avail. That didn’t stop him on Sunday, like at previous campaign stops, from alleging Democrats would still try shenanigans.

“It’s, look, they’ll try figuring something [out], but it’s much harder, because they have to cheat,” he said without providing evidence. “Because without, look, their policies are so bad.”

One GOP strategist, granted anonymity to be candid, said it was “normal” for any party to contest “some” election results.

Former Pennsylvania GOP Rep. Charlie Dent on Friday said Trump’s rally rhetoric appears mostly aimed at influencing public opinion and could be lacking a legitimate legal strategy.

“I’m not sure how he would intend to make a challenge to the certification of some members who may win by comfortable margins,” Dent said. “There might be circumstances where you have some contested outcomes shortly after the election that are very close. But then you’ll have a legal process and a recount process to go through to ultimately determine who the winner is.

“But once those winners are determined and the states certify those elections, then everything that’s done or said in Washington is merely ministerial at that point,” he added. “If there are objections to a particular outcome, there are legal remedies candidates can seek out.”

Mark Zaid, an attorney who has sued the Trump administration multiple times, said Monday that “the danger with his rhetoric is that he expects people to react to what he says and implement his words into action.

“He did that on Jan. 6 and he continues to do it now,” Zaid added, referring to the January 2021 Capitol riot by a pro-Trump mob following his fiery Ellipse speech that morning raising doubts about his loss to Biden.

“My own view is that post-Nov. 3 he will act far more like a cornered animal, more dangerous than when an avenue of escape is available — and implement a scorched-earth response to anything that is thrown at him,” he added. “I find it amazing that his rhetoric seemingly goes unchallenged by his base.”

Trump appeared in a relaxed mood on Monday, joking that he intended to rename the Reflecting Pool to include his name.

“I’m only kidding,” he said, looking toward assembled media members. “Please, don’t report it.” Later, about the midterms, he said the party of sitting presidents typically loses, adding matter-of-factly: “We gave this a very strong shot.”

#6306. Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical?

Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical shapes, such as ovals or pears, depending on composition?

Bodies large enough to be considered planets have enough mass that gravity molds them into a roughly spherical shape.

The key word here is roughly — other factors also come into play, such as a planet’s composition (rocky or gassy) and its rate of spin. The faster a planet spins, the more its rotation causes it to bulge outward at the equator. That’s because as a planet rotates, there’s a tug-of-war between the way material wants to fly off the planet due to rotation and the way gravity wants to pull all that planet’s material inward. The battle between these forces is most intense at the equator.

In our solar system, Mercury and Venus are slowly spinning rocky planets; therefore, they are the most spherical of the Sun’s worlds.

Earth and Mars spin a little faster, so they are about 0.3% and 0.6% thicker at the equator than the poles, respectively. This shape is called an oblate spheroid. However, because these planets have a solid surface that is higher in some places than others, they are not perfect oblate spheroids — they are minutely lumpy and bumpy, as data from orbiting satellites have detailed. In fact, the surface area of Earth’s Southern Hemisphere is very slightly larger than its Northern Hemisphere, making Earth marginally pear-shaped. It’s important to note, however, that despite these deviations, Earth is still almost spherical — if you used a basketball to represent the shape of our planet, its deviation from a perfect sphere would be only about 0.03 inch (0.08 centimeter) at the middle.

The gas giants Jupiter and Saturn bulge outward the most — Jupiter is nearly 7% thicker at its equator than its poles, and Saturn is 10.7% thicker around the middle. Ice giants Uranus and Neptune have smaller central bulges, only 2.3% and 1.7% thicker at the equator, respectively.

What about exoplanets, though? Some planetary systems we’ve found experience much more extreme conditions, with large, gassy planets orbiting very close to their stars (called hot Jupiters). One of these hot Jupiters is WASP-121 b, which orbits a blazingly hot star. In fact, this planet orbits so closely to its star that gravitational forces have stretched it out into a football shape. Astronomers believe that if the planet were much closer to its star, it would be ripped apart entirely.

In addition to its stretched-out shape, WASP-121 b and other planets, including WASP-69 b and KELT-9 b, appear to have puffed-up atmospheres and cometlike tails. These tails form as their host stars blast the planets with high-energy radiation, knocking gas particles into space.

As for pear-shaped exoplanets, astronomers haven’t found anything to suggest they exist to the extent you’re likely picturing. Other terrestrial planets likely have deformations similar to Earth’s — or perhaps slightly more extreme — but even “extreme” in this case probably translates to a planet appearing essentially spherical from a great distance.

This question and answer were originally published online October 24, 2020.

#6305. Why Do Some People Feel Their Souls Leave Their Bodies at Night? The Answer May Lie in a Hidden Brain State.

Brainwave recordings reveal the strange neural overlap that can make you feel like you’re floating away.

When you have what is known as an out-of-body experience, you may feel as if your mind has left your body, though it hasn’t actually gone anywhere. Maybe you feel like you’re floating or flying. On the darker side, it might be an unsettling experience that makes you feel as if your body no longer belongs to you, or a nightmarish bout of sleep paralysis that leaves you panting and in a cold sweat. How can the brain conjure experiences that sound straight out of science fiction but are really nothing more than illusions?

To make sense of these intangible phenomena, neuroscientist Teresa Campillo-Ferrer of Radboud University in the Netherlands recruited participants for an experiment designed to capture what happens in the brain when the mind seems to wander from the body during sleep. Most of her subjects had already had an out-of-body episode or some other kind of unusual bodily experience (UBE). Some were lucid dreamers, people who can become aware that they are dreaming. Others had dealt with sleep paralysis, which is waking up while the body is still paralyzed as it is during dreaming sleep. Some had even felt that they left their physical body behind and passed through a portal to another realm. Although UBEs can occur during waking hours, Campillo-Ferrer reasoned that she would probably capture more of them in sleeping brains.

“Studying UBEs is essential for understanding the mechanisms underlying bodily awareness, self-perception, and the sense of ‘having a body’ (embodiment) or ‘owning a body’ (body ownership),” she wrote in a study recently published in Consciousness and Cognition. “As such, UBE research has the potential to expand current theories of human self-consciousness and multisensory perception.”

The participants’ main job was simply to relax. Before they drifted off to dreamland, they were fitted with EEG electrodes, practiced pre-sleep meditation, and were given visual stimulation that could help induce lucid dreams and UBEs. Researchers also asked them to move their eyes left and right several times if they noticed anything strange happening, whether or not they were lucid dreaming. This works because even in a semiconscious state, the brain can remember instructions and respond to something unusual. Participants then slept for three hours in soundproof chambers. If the recordings showed the left-right eye signal, participants were either spoken to over an intercom or woken up to describe their experiences. After the sleep session ended, participants also discussed their dreams with the researchers.

The reported UBEs fell into several categories. In vestibular-motor experiences, subjects felt as if they were moving or being moved, such as levitating, spinning, or falling. These sensations can also show up in the opposite way, as heaviness or a feeling of sinking deeper and deeper, like the harrowing scene in A Nightmare on Elm Street where Glen is sucked into his own bed. Flying and other movements that defy the laws of physics also belong in this category. In tactile UBEs, the person feels touch or vibrations from an outside source even though nothing is touching them. In UBEs involving distorted body boundaries, the outer limits of the body blur, so that the body seems to merge with the bed (another very Freddy Krueger moment), shapeshift into another form, or gain a duplicate.

Other UBEs are defined by a lack of bodily sensation or sense of position. These are often associated with feeling detached from the physical body or not knowing where the body actually is. They are similar, though not identical, to out-of-body UBEs, in which participants reported leaving their physical body or realizing, at least while dreaming, that they felt separate from it. Because out-of-body experiences often involve a feeling of levitation, they tend to overlap with the vestibular-motor category, though some involve no sense of movement at all. Sleep paralysis made up another category, and it may be the most frightening. The person is fully aware but can’t move, and sometimes it feels as if they can’t breathe. Still other UBEs stemmed from hallucinations or lucid dreams.

Exactly where UBEs arise in the brain is still unknown. After analyzing EEG patterns, however, the researchers suggest that they happen somewhere in the liminal space between waking and sleeping. In participants whose UBEs were confirmed by the eye-movement signal, slower brainwaves known as delta and theta waves decreased while faster beta and gamma waves surged, especially in the temporal lobes on both sides of the brain. These are the regions that process the sensory information that gives us a sense of existing in our bodies. What makes this pattern striking is that slower waves are linked to sleep, while faster waves are more typical of being awake. It is as if the sleeping and waking brain overlap.

Campillo-Ferrer explained the significance of these findings: “Specific EEG features associated with UBEs appear to reflect the reactivation of EEG activity from levels observed in baseline brain states in which UBEs emerge. [Our] models allowed for precise analysis of neural activity and individual variability, providing new insights into the neural correlates associated with UBEs and their role in bodily self-perception and consciousness.”

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6304. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

#6303. 15 moments that shaped the 2026 midterm campaign

Republicans began the 2026 election cycle on a high, with a governing trifecta in Washington and heavy optimism that the coalition that swept Donald Trump back into the White House represented a durable new voting bloc. They had a favorable Senate map and insisted there were opportunities to expand their narrow House majority.

But Trump’s policies, economic anxieties, historical trends and an unpopular war have upended  the calculus for the midterm elections. At the close of the campaign, the fight for Congress is taking place mostly on Republican turf, a striking shift in less than two years.

Here are 15 moments that shaped the 2026 midterm campaign:

Less than three months after taking office, Trump made good on a campaign promise: a 10 percent minimum tariff on all imports and higher duties on nations that run trade surpluses with the U.S. Since proclaiming “Liberation Day,” the on-and-off tariffs have injected uncertainty into the economy and hurt key sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing and consumer goods by driving up costs. Polls show the tariffs, which economists estimate have cost the average American household about $1,100, are viewed unfavorably by most voters, likely hurting Republican candidates in several states.

Republicans celebrated a key legislative achievement last summer, with the enactment of the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which they later sought to rebrand as the “Working Families Tax Cut.” The law’s tax provisions became a focal point for the GOP during the campaign, while Democrats slammed the included health care cuts. Before passage, North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis drew scorn from Trump for opposing the measure and soon announced his retirement, opening up a pivotal Senate seat that Democrat Roy Cooper is favored to flip.

Trump kicked the mid-decade redistricting wars into high gear when he directed Texas to redraw its congressional lines, resulting in five seats getting revamped in Republicans' favor. Other GOP-led states followed suit, though Democrats have remained competitive in several of these redrawn districts. Meanwhile, California voters approved a Democrat-drawn map aimed at helping the party flip five Republican seats, and a court-approved map in Utah gives the party a prime pickup opportunity.

Democrats had a big night in the off-year elections, with a pair of decisive gubernatorial victories: former Rep. Abigail Spanberger flipped the Virginia governor's mansion and Rep. Mikie Sherrill won in New Jersey. The two moderates focused their campaigns on cost-of-living issues, as did progressive Zohran Mamdani in his winning race for New York mayor, giving Democrats a blueprint for 2026.

The Trump administration began sending federal immigration agents to Minnesota in late 2025, but Operation Metro Surge picked up in January and ultimately led to the fatal shootings of two people by federal agents. That in turn intensified Democratic calls to “abolish ICE” and made immigration enforcement a defining issue in Democratic primaries across the country.

Not long after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran, Trump predicted that the conflict would last a few weeks. It didn’t play out that way, and the ongoing war has become a focal point of the campaign. Higher oil costs have led to higher prices, the blame for which Democrats have pinned on Trump and Republicans in Congress. While Trump’s job approval ratings had fallen before the start of the war, they’ve dropped further since then.

Facing serious sexual misconduct allegations, California Democrat Eric Swalwell, who was running for governor, and Texas Republican Tony Gonzales resigned from the House just as their colleagues were preparing to expel them from the chamber. Swalwell dropped his gubernatorial bid and Gonzales left behind an open seat that has grown increasingly competitive.

In invalidating Louisiana's congressional map, the Supreme Court pared back the Voting Rights Act and set off a new phase in the redistricting wars, as GOP-led Southern states sought to redraw districts with substantial Black populations. Not all attempts were successful, but Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee ended up with new maps.

A week before the Republican Senate primary runoff in Texas, Trump publicly backed scandal-plagued state Attorney General Ken Paxton’s challenge to Sen. John Cornyn. Paxton went on to win that contest, but has had a tougher general election fight against Democrat James Talarico. Two other incumbents the president targeted for defeat — Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy and Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie — also lost their May primaries to Trump-backed challengers. But Trump’s endorsement power had its limits: Several of his picks, including Iowa gubernatorial hopeful Randy Feenstra, lost primaries this summer.

June 23 was a big night for Mamdani as three House candidates he endorsed, including two fellow democratic socialists, won their primaries. Two of them ousted incumbent Democrats, Dan Goldman and Adriano Espaillat, and a third defeated the hand-picked successor of retiring Rep. Nydia L. Velázquez.  The New York primaries kicked off a strong summer for progressive candidates in states such as Colorado, Michigan and Minnesota.

Maine Democrat Graham Platner appeared to have weathered an array of controversies when he easily won his June primary to take on Republican Sen. Susan Collins. But about a month later, he ended his campaign following a report that he had sexually assaulted a woman he once dated, which he denied. That set off a weekslong scramble for Democrats to replace him on the ballot, culminating with a party convention at which former state Senate President Troy Jackson became Democrats’ new nominee.

The sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham shocked Washington but also touched off a scramble for South Carolina Republicans to replace him on the November ballot. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed the late senator’s sister, Darline Graham, to fill his seat, and she then won Trump’s support to seek a full term. Boosted by the president, Darline Graham went on to secure the nomination via a primary runoff, but her general election against Democrat Annie Andrews has tightened significantly.

Republicans gathered in Dallas for a first-ever midterm convention.  The two-day event offered them a chance to hone their message, fire up voters and lavish praise upon Trump, the gathering’s brainchild. Speakers, including Trump, stoked fears about democratic socialism, but polls showed the event didn’t provide the GOP with the bounce the party was anticipating. The president followed the convention with a series of rallies in red states, where he implored Americans to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

Alaska’s competitive Senate race features two candidates with the same name: Dan S. Sullivan, the GOP incumbent, and retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., listed on the ballot with no party affiliation. Former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, has said she was unaware of the effort to recruit the second Sullivan, but The New York Times reported that top aides to her campaign were closely involved in the ballot-stacking plan. The Trump administration is attempting to block certification of the results if the incumbent doesn’t win, but, on Sunday, a district judge dismissed the lawsuit.

Less than 48 hours before polls were set to open on Election Day, Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens served up a November surprise Sunday, endorsing Republican Mike Rogers for Senate over Abdul El-Sayed, who had narrowly bested her in an August Democratic primary. While it was unclear how much influence her late decision could have on the race, a high-profile intraparty fight was surely not how Democrats wanted to close out the campaign. Even so, the El-Sayed campaign said Sunday was its biggest fundraising day, bringing in $2.4 million.

#6302. Nov. 16, 1974: Arecibo sends a message

On Nov. 16, 1974, a group gathered at Arecibo Observatory in the rainforest interior of Puerto Rico, there for a reopening celebration after upgrades to the facility. After the requisite speeches, scientists used the radio telescope to send what would be known as the Arecibo message: 1,679 bits of data in 73 lines, each 23 characters long. To the assembled crowd, the dispatch sounded like nearly three minutes of two tones. But encoded in those tones was message crafted by a team of scientists led by Frank Drake and including Carl Sagan: a rough illustration of a human, the structure of a DNA double helix, and a map of the Earth’s position in the solar system.

The communication was aimed at M13, a globular cluster about 25,000 light-years away in Hercules. Since it would take thousands of years for the signal to arrive there – not to mention time for a signal to be sent back by any extraterrestrial civilization that intercepted it – the Arecibo message wasn’t so much an actual attempt at communication as it was a demonstration of how we might do so.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

As NASA's Voyager 1 probe reaches one light-day from Earth, we look back at its legendary photos of Jupiter that changed our view of the solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency announced its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

#6299. Falcon 9 flies national security doubleheader

On Wednesday, Nov. 18, China is expected to launch a Long March 2D from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province at 5:50 p.m. EST, according to NextSpaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later that night on Wednesday, Nov. 18, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 10:00 p.m. EST. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has said what the rocket carries. The Falcon 9 booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

On Friday, Nov. 20, a Long March 8A is slated to lift off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on Hainan Island at 6:00 a.m. EST, per NextSpaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed, but is suspected to be a batch of SatNet low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites for Guowang — a state-backed broadband megaconstellation meant to rival Starlink.

Closing out the week on Saturday, Nov. 21, the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) will launch NROL-136 on a Falcon 9 from SLC-4E at 7:30 a.m. EST. Rather than heading for a droneship, the booster will fly back to Landing Zone 4.

Last week opened on Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 6:41 a.m. EST, when a Long March 2D lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center carrying CAS Pathfinder-1. The Chinese Academy of Sciences built the satellite to test key technologies for its planned Origins space science program, CGTN reported. Later that night, at 11:36 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-627 mission from Vandenberg after two postponements. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:47 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched Starship Flight 15 from Starbase, Texas, aiming to catch both stages with its launch tower for the first time. SpaceX was unable to catch the Super Heavy booster after its onboard guidance system made the call to abort the attempt. Instead it exploded over the Gulf of Mexico just before reaching the water. The ship, on the other hand, reached orbit, the second Starship ever to do so, and released 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

Then on Saturday afternoon, after 14 trips around Earth, the rocket’s upper stage slowed over Starbase, dropped between the tower’s mechanical “chopsticks,” and was plucked out of the air. The catch was a first for SpaceX and spaceflight in general — no other spacecraft has ever entered orbit and then been caught at its launch site.

Russia launched a mission from the Vostochny Cosmodrome at 8:16 p.m. EST on Friday, Nov. 13. The Soyuz-2.1b carried a pair of high-resolution imaging satellites and a dozen smaller payloads.

Rocket Lab marked a milestone just after midnight on Saturday, Nov. 14. At 12:30 a.m. EST, its Electron rocket flew for the 100th time on The Mountain God Rises, lifting off from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula. The rocket placed a synthetic aperture radar satellite into orbit for the Japanese company iQPS. Synthetic aperture radar bounces microwaves off the ground to build images, letting it see through clouds and darkness.

The week ended in a loss. On Sunday, Nov. 15, at 12:40 p.m. EST, United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station carrying 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the company’s broadband constellation. It was Vulcan’s return to flight after the USSF-87 mission in February — which experienced a minor booster anomaly despite successfully delivering its payload — and the first of several dozen Vulcan launches Amazon has booked. About 10 minutes into the flight, ULA reported an anomaly, and the satellites never reached orbit.

Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit. Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us…

On Monday, Nov. 23, Arianespace is targeting 5:12 a.m. EST to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 more Amazon Leo satellites.

Later on Monday, Nov. 23, SpaceX is slated to launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the Space Force from Vandenberg at 11:04 a.m. EST.

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, China is slated to launch a Long March 12 from the commercial launch site at Wenchang on Hainan Island at 2:00 a.m. EST, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been confirmed, but is likely another batch of SatNet LEO satellites for Guowang.

On Thursday, Nov. 26, a launch window opens for the third flight of Isar Aerospace’s Spectrum rocket from Andøya Spaceport in Norway, according to European Spaceflight. Its payloads include AT-Astra, an Austrian technology-demonstration satellite built by Vienna-based R-Space. Spectrum reached orbit for the first time on its second flight in September.

On Sunday, Nov. 29, NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting 10:47 a.m. EST to launch the NG-25 Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. Named the S.S. James A. Lovell after the beloved Apollo 13 commander, the spacecraft will haul several tons of supplies to the space station.

#6297. Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Taking gender-affirming hormone therapy was the right decision for 97 percent surveyed

Demonstrators rally at the U.S. Supreme Court in 2025 in support of gender-affirming health care for transgender youth. The vast majority of transgender and gender diverse young people are satisfied with their decision to take hormone therapy, according the largest survey on the topic.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.

Almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, said they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”

Gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.

Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.

As per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.

The new research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.

But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

#6295. The Sky Today on Tuesday, November 17: Spotlight on the Pleiades

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Early this evening brighter targets are best, as the Moon doesn’t set until late. Ready for viewing as the winter constellations start to dominate earlier each day is the Pleiades, an open cluster cataloged as M45.

Known since antiquity and readily visible to the naked eye, the Pleiades contains several bright stars arranged in a tiny dipperlike shape. Located in northwestern Taurus, the cluster is sometimes mistaken for the Little Dipper, although that asterism is much larger and lies in the northern sky, anchored at the end of its handle by Polaris, the North Star. The Pleiades shines with a collective magnitude of 1.6 and spans roughly 110’ — a huge swath of sky. It lies above the sideways V-shape of Taurus’ face as the Bull rises in the east this evening, and is already 30° high by 7:30 P.M. local time. How many stars can you make out with the naked eye? Most observers see six or seven.

Once you’ve taken in the cluster without any optical aid, zoom in with binoculars or a finder scope. (Any higher magnification and you won’t see most of the cluster at once, but instead be limited to a smaller portion.) Many more stars will now pop into your field of view. If you do opt for high magnification, look for a faint grayish haze around the stars — this is nearby dust reflecting the stars’ light, and requires clear, dark conditions to make out.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight, with the best meteor viewing overnight into the early-morning hours of November 18, as the Moon sets around midnight and the radiant rises higher. Keep reading for more detail below on how to observe the shower.

Sunrise: 6:47 A.M.Sunset: 4:42 P.M.Moonrise: 12:56 P.M.Moonset: —Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (57%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early on the morning of the 18th, after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.

Two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.

To catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per second.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to correct an error in the speed of the meteors.

Recently, researchers used AI to "decode" segments of birdsong. In the wake of this, Live Science asks its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The idea of talking to animals like Dr. Dolittle might sound far-fetched, but researchers are making progress toward understanding how other species communicate. In a recent Live Science interview, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie explained how she used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the calls of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata). For instance, Elie was able to determine which calls the birds used to communicate over short distances versus longer distances.

Birds aren't the only animals scientists are hoping to understand. Researchers with Project CETI are using AI to decipher the clicks and calls of sperm whales, while a separate team (with the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI) conducted what they described as the first "conversation" between humans and a humpback whale. The whale, named Twain, responded to recorded calls played by researchers over a 20 minute period, a "conversation" scientists believe could help us figure out how to communicate with extraterrestrial life someday.

Closer to home, cats have already figured out how to use meows to get their human's attention, whether they're demanding food, affection or simply that we open the door for them (again). Whether this means they understand the human language or not is still up for debate, but it raises an interesting question: If we could understand what animals were saying, which species would you most want to talk to? Vote in our poll and let us know what you'd ask in the comments below!

#6293. 5 things to watch for in Tuesday’s midterm elections

Midterm elections are almost always referendums on the party in power. That’s especially true this year, when President Donald Trump has repeatedly directed Republican voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.”

But Trump’s sagging poll numbers, driven by cost-of-living concerns and an unpopular war, have helped create a political environment that favors Democrats.

Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales projects Democrats could net four to six seats in the Senate, a scenario considered highly unlikely at the start of the cycle. To succeed, Democrats need to flip seats in several red-leaning states, among them Alaska, Iowa and Kansas. The party would also need to hold its own vulnerable seats in New Hampshire, Minnesota and Georgia.

On the House side, the question seems to be not whether Democrats will take the majority, but rather how big their margin will be. The party needs a net gain of three seats; Inside Elections projects Democrats could wind up winning 20 to 30 seats, a significant number of them in districts that voted for Trump by double digits two years ago.

Here are five things we’ll be watching for as the votes are tallied:

Republicans appeared to win the redistricting wars that defined much of the 2026 election cycle, especially after the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act, which led to new maps in several Southern states. Democrats gained favorable lines in California and Utah, but Republicans redrew more seats in their favor. The overall GOP effort put new districts on the board in places such as Florida and Louisiana but also sought to boost Republicans’ chances of ousting longtime targets, including Reps. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio and Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez of Texas.

While some redrawn districts are clear pickups, many redrawn seats are considered Toss-ups, forcing the GOP to deploy significant resources. Still, if Republicans make the gains they hoped to make in places such as Florida and Texas, it could go a long way in helping them either somehow keep the majority or narrow a Democratic one.

Historic gains among Latino voters helped Trump win the White House in 2024 and boosted GOP candidates in swing districts across the nation. Those victories also influenced Texas Republicans’ redraw of the state’s congressional map, betting that Latino voters would stick with the party. But anger over the president’s immigration policies, coupled with economic anxiety, has driven Trump’s approval numbers among Latinos to historic lows.

Across the South, the Trump-led redistricting push that dismantled House districts with sizable Black populations has fired up Black voters in states such as North Carolina and Louisiana. Black voters could also be key to determining the winner of Michigan’s hard-fought Senate race.

Democrats’ initial midterm target list, released in April 2025, included a few Republican incumbents who represented seats that Trump had carried by double digits the previous year. The number of “reach” battleground races in traditionally red terrain that fit that description has only grown since then. One of the biggest questions heading into election night is how many of those districts Democrats will be competitive in. Wins in those districts would translate into a larger Democratic majority or, at the very least, could help offset losses by Democratic incumbents in redrawn seats.

But flipping these districts would put a bull's-eye on the Democratic winners, since their seats would likely rank among Republicans’ best pickup opportunities in 2028.

At the start of the midterm cycle, few could have predicted that the Senate battlefield would run through states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024. But concerns over rising prices driven by Trump’s tariff policy and the war in Iran have put several red-state seats in play. In the farm belt states of Iowa and Kansas, soaring diesel and fertilizer costs have GOP candidates on defense. In South Carolina, a divisive Republican primary and an untested first-time candidate have made the race unexpectedly competitive. And in Ohio, the return of a Democratic former senator, coupled with a national environment that is increasingly inhospitable to the GOP, suggests the state could shift from red to purple.

Recent surveys have shown Democrats with the advantage heading into Election Day and Trump’s job approval rating underwater, meaning more voters disapprove of the job he’s doing than approve. All signs point to Democrats retaking the House and potentially winning the Senate majority. That wouldn’t be unexpected — after all, the president’s party almost always loses seats in midterm elections. But polls have been wrong before. In August, some surveys predicted progressive Abdul El-Sayed would notch a double-digit win over Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, but El-Sayed wound up winning by less than a point. Throughout the campaign, Republicans have cautioned against reading too much into the polls, asserting that they typically undercount GOP voters.

#6290. We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI worms could spread like octopuses or slime molds, exploiting smart devices

Common forms of cyberattack include viruses and worms. Researchers recently added new styles of attack to the twisted menagerie: worms that act more like octopuses or slime molds.

VICTOR HABBICK VISIONS/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

AI is already powering new, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a new worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”

Here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, says Guan, of the University of Toronto.

That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments showed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

And there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.)

Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan says. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

“The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

The Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan says.

Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

The octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a new device, the head would use AI to plan how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler says. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover new places to copy itself (third image).

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.)

The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan says they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

Meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers showed another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan says the company’s work shows that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

And that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

Anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that showed it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

Whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan says. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still big programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma says. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

Ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler says.

Guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”

Anthropic. AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter. 2026.

J. Guan et al. AI agents enable adaptive computer worms. arXiv.org. 2026. doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2606.03811

O. Çetin et al. Cleaning up the internet of evil things: real-world evidence on ISP and consumer efforts to remove Mirai. Network and Distributed Systems Security (NDSS) Symposium, San Diego, 2019.

#6288. At the Races: It's almost over

By Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

Voters are weighing in on whether to keep Republicans in control of Congress or give some power to Democrats amid mounting signs of dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump.

Democrats, who have expanded both the House and Senate battleground maps, are optimistic about their chances, while Republicans are hoping their base voters turn out — and help them defy the polls once again.

The expanded battleground map was evident in our final rankings of the most vulnerable senators, which included Sens. Roger Marshall of Kansas, Darline Graham of South Carolina and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi, three states that weren’t exactly expected to be part of the battleground at the beginning of the year.

Some of House Republicans’ best pickup opportunities come in districts that were redrawn in their favor, which is reflected in our final list of the most vulnerable House incumbents. Just two Democrats— Florida’s Darren Soto and Alabama’s Shomari Figures — rank among the 10 most endangered House members, while Republicans from the nation’s most competitive swing seats occupy most of the other spots.

Speaker Mike Johnson has spent the past several weeks crisscrossing the country hoping to save his narrow majority. He appeared Monday night with Rep. Jen Kiggans in the same Virginia district where Hakeem Jeffries, the top House Democrat, campaigned on Saturday. Earlier in the day, Johnson returned to Eastern North Carolina, home to a costly rematch between Democratic Rep. Don Davis and Republican Laurie Buckhout. Johnson also held a rally in a neighboring district that Trump would have carried by 14 points, a sign of GOP vulnerabilities even in conservative terrain. The speaker will begin Election Day in South Texas, where Republicans are hoping to flip two House seats while preserving another.

To mark Election Day, we’ve taken a look back over the past two years and identified 15 key moments that shaped the midterm campaign. We also have five questions we hope the election results will help us answer, including whether redistricting pays off for Republicans and how key constituencies that supported Trump and Republicans two years ago vote this time. And Roll Call photojournalists Bill Clark and Tom Williams shared the most memorable and striking images from their time on the trail this cycle.

Of course, it hasn’t been a quiet end to the campaign. Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens, who unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for Senate this year, sent shockwaves across both parties Sunday when she appeared with and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over primary rival Abdul El-Sayed.

That followed a major development in the Alaska Senate race, after The New York Times reported that aides to Democrat Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate who shares a name with Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. A federal judge on Sunday rejected a lawsuit from the Trump administration, which sought to delay certification of the Senate election if the incumbent Sullivan loses, as our colleague Michael Macagnone reported.

If your preferred way to watch results roll in is with a crowd, CQ Roll Call’s Nina Heller has a rundown of D.C. bars that will be airing election night results, many of which are offering deals on drinks and food.

Stay tuned to the Roll Call website for results and immediate takeaways. At the Races will be back in your inbox as usual on Thursday as we break the results down and look ahead to the next Congress.

After all, 2028 is right around the corner.

#6287. Nov. 17, 1966: A phenomenal Leonid meteor storm

On Nov. 17, 1966, the Leonids put on one of the greatest meteor shows in recorded history, during which eyewitnesses reported a sky that seemed to “rain shooting stars.” Observers in North America witnessed a peak of thousands of meteors per minute; Kitt Peak National Observatory reported 40 meteors per second. This peak occurred around 12:00 Universal Time, and lasted for about 15 to 20 minutes. As the requisite rate of 1,000 meteors per hour was not just met but superseded dozens of times over, the event was firmly classified as a true meteor storm.
