#6274. The 7 Best Electric Chainsaws of 2026

Cordless battery-powered chainsaws are quiet, light, and fast—everything you need for a spring refresh.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you own a home with trees on your property, an electric chainsaw is a must-have tool in your yard care arsenal. Electric chainsaws have come a long way and, in most cases, closed the gap to their gas-powered cousins—they’re easy to start (just push a button or two in most cases), generate little noise, produce no fumes, and simplify maintenance. We’ve tested electric saws as big as 20 inches and they’re powerful enough to bring down a mature tree.

Saws with 24-inch bars or more are still considered gas engine territory, but that’s overkill for most homeowners. For cleaning up after storms, felling small to medium-size trees, and regular pruning or arboreal maintenance, an electric chainsaw is the ideal choice.

We noted how well each chainsaw endured prolonged use. Making repeated cuts can cause a chainsaw, and its battery, to heat up. If it gets too hot, it will trigger a thermal limit and the saw’s overload protection will shut it down. We also considered comfort, vibration, saw balance, and ease of use to make our final recommendations.

Stihl’s new battery-powered MSA 260 C-O tops our list of chainsaws for two main reasons: run-time and constant, consistent power. These are the two most common concerns or complaints we hear from people when it comes to electric saws. The MSA 260 C-O made significantly more cuts on one battery charge than any other saw tested. But that’s only partly attributable to the saw—it’s also due to Stihl’s new AllPro 300.0 battery. Working in concert, the battery and saw deliver power at a constant level, maintaining a chain speed through most of the saw’s runtime.

Aside from run-time and consistent power delivery, the MSA 260 C-O has the ability to chew through big, tough logs. Note that Stihl positions the MSA 260 C-O “for professional applications” so the performance does come at a cost, $770 for the 18-inch model we tested, plus another $350 for the battery. While that might seem like a lot, it’s in line with other pro battery and gas saws. So, if you’re a frequent chainsaw user, the investment is going to be worth it.

Husqvarna may not have been the fastest-cutting electric chainsaw we tested, but it’s at the top of our list because it does just about everything well—it operates smoothly, cuts fast (enough), and is easy to use. With the boost button engaged, it blazed through our cutting tests, slicing through an 8-inch log in about 5 seconds. It also had the fastest windup speed of any electric chainsaw that I personally tested—it was ready to cut as soon as I pulled the trigger. Even with its impressive power, this chainsaw is surprisingly quiet, producing 67 decibels at 60 feet. The Power Axe isn’t particularly light at 14.5 pounds with battery, but it’s well balanced. I had no problem holding it steady even when making cuts at waist-level height.

The Power Axe also comes with a suite of well-designed, user-friendly features. The power button and boost button are located just above the handle so they’re easier to access on the fly. You also have the ability to adjust the chain tension by hand, loosening a dial to release the tension, then rotating a dial to tighten it back up. The whole process takes seconds. There’s also a built-in chain brake to protect from injuries. It’s a well-built, high-performing electric chainsaw that still manages to come in at a reasonable price.

Echo’s DCS-5000 gives you what you want most out of a chainsaw: raw cutting power. It may lack some of the bells and whistles you’ll find on pricier models, such as tool-less chain tensioning and power-saving settings, but its base performance is right up there with the Power Axe 350i. The DCS-5000 cut through 8-inch hardwood in less than 4 seconds. That's saying something considering that the DCS-5000 costs at least $100 less than any other saw that can do the same.

Along with its impressive cutting speed, the Echo is also relatively light at just over 12 pounds. I could feel the difference whenever I had to lift it up above shoulder-height to cut higher limbs, or while crouching down to cut a fallen 8-inch beech tree.

There is a trade-off with the DCS-5000, though, in that it lacks any kind of quality-of-life-related features. You won’t find tool-less chain tensioning or ECO settings that conserve battery life here. It’s pretty loud, too, producing 76 decibels at 60 feet. And, finally, while I appreciated the lighter weight, I could also feel the vibrations in my arm more than electric chainsaws with more refined builds.

Still, if you don't mind the rougher feel, higher noise level, and lack of a few user-friendly features you’ll find on pricier electric chainsaws, the Echo DCS-5000 offers exceptional value.

The newest saw from Makita, the 40V Max XGT 20-inch chainsaw, is a beast. The brand claims it offers the power of a 50-cc gas saw, and we’re inclined to agree. The first pull of the trigger surprised us with the speed and sound of the chain whizzing around. And it wasn’t just the noise that was impressive—in testing, it positively tore through logs.

Using the 40V Max XGT for practical tasks like felling trees, or cleaning up fallen trees after a storm, confirmed its power. I tackled logs as big as 18 inches, and the saw left nothing to be desired—it handled everything I used it on, without faltering. The 40V Max XGT chainsaw, at 20-inches, is among the biggest battery powered chainsaws we test. Our test unit came as a kit, with everything you need, including an 8.0Ah battery and charger. The kit isn’t cheap, but if you’re already on the Makita 40-volt XGT platform, you can save $500 and buy the chainsaw as a tool only.

The Stihl MSA 80 is an easy-to-use chainsaw that also packs impressive cutting power. Its compact build—the 14-inch saw weighs about 10 pounds—gives it a balanced feel in hand. It features a narrow bar that makes it easier to fit it into the crotches of trees for pruning than other electric chainsaws we tested like the Ego 20-inch chainsaw or Husqvarna Power Axe 350i. Likewise, it comes equipped with a thinner chain that cuts more smoothly through wood, producing less vibration. Lastly, its variable speed trigger allows you to adjust the speed of the blade to suit the job at hand.

There are several user-friendly features worth noting. Chain adjustments are effortless: Simply loosen a knob, turn the adjuster, and tighten the knob. There’s also a lubrication system to keep the chain moving with a minimal amount of bar oil.

Stihl’s chainsaws come at a premium price, and this one is no different. At $500, the MSA 80 is the most expensive electric chainsaw we tested, despite having a relatively short bar. Even so, it’s an ideal choice for homeowners who are looking for professional-grade build quality and performance out of an electric chainsaw.

If you already have other Echo tools, like a leaf blower or trimmer, then you can save a little cash and purchase the DCS-2500T as a tool only.

There’s a price for the CS-2005’s cutting power and capacity, though—its weight. While we liked its buttery smooth operation, it weighs an arm-burning 19.3 pounds with a battery. Making cuts on limbs above the head or below the knees was a far more challenging experience than with electric chainsaws we tested that were 4 to 5 pounds lighter. The Ego CS-2005 also lacks a tool-free chain tensioning system. If you don’t mind the extra heft, the Ego CS-2005 is the high-powered electric you’ll want for really big jobs.

As new models come out, we can’t keep all the models we test on our recommended list. But some of these older models and runners-up are still worth considering. Here are a few:

Milwaukee M18 Fuel 18V 16-Inch Electric Chainsaw: Don’t be fooled by the Milwaukee’s lower voltage, this saw has plenty of power for quickly cutting up large limbs or felling medium-sized trees. It’s a good saw, but we’d mostly recommend it to folks already on Milwaukee’s M18 platform, so you can buy it as a tool only and save some money.

Stihl GTA 26: While folks often refer to tools like this as “mini chain saws”, Stihl bills the GTA 26 as a garden pruner. Intended specifically for pruning shrubs and small branches, the GTA 26 combines light weight and a pistol-like configuration to make an easy-to-handle tool. Think of it as a power loppers, with greater size capability.

Worx Nitro WG385 40V 16-Inch Chainsaw: At less than $300, the Worx Nitro WG385 can get the job done. It’s lighter and easier to maneuver than other similarly sized saws, but it’s also a little less powerful, with a little less run-time. Still, with some patience we were able to find it useful for basic property maintenance. For the price, the Worx Nitro WG385 is a good cost-effective option for occasional use.

At the heart of an electric chainsaw is its motor and battery, which need to work in concert to perform well. The longer the chainsaw bar, the bigger the log or tree you can cut. So, the motor has to have enough torque and speed, while the battery has to be able to deliver the power needed to sustain that torque and speed. This is one reason why bigger saws can cost a lot more than smaller ones. Batteries are a significant factor in the price of a saw, and bigger batteries cost more. Battery size is typically measured in amp-hours (Ah), and larger saws will typically have 8 to 12 Ah batteries.

Mini chainsaws, made for pruning and other small jobs, feature a one-handed design with a small cutting bar—4 to 8 inches—and a small battery. If you need to break down large branches from trees, opt for a smaller full-size chainsaw with a 12- to 14-inch cutting bar. For something professional-grade, consider a large chainsaw with a 16- to 20-inch cutting bar and larger battery.

Among electric chainsaws with comparable bar lengths, those with larger batteries will typically have more ripping power, which means they’ll cut through limbs and logs more quickly, allowing you to get the job done faster. Just keep in mind that a more powerful chainsaw is also often a heavier chainsaw.

An electric chainsaw’s runtime depends on the capacity of its battery, in amp-hours. Broadly speaking, more capacity means more juice, but larger saws draw more power per second, so it’s not uncommon to find large chainsaws with large batteries getting comparable battery life to their smaller, more efficient counterparts.

Since your chainsaw only uses power when you’re using it to cut, its true runtime comes down to how many cuts it can make on a single charge. The Popular Mechanics test team tests runtime by checking how many times each model cuts through a 6-inch log on a single charge. Depending on battery size and chainsaw power, that number can vary quite a bit—from as low as 50 to as high as 300.

The “cutting bar” is the business end of the chainsaw—the long, rounded metal guide that the chain spins around to create a blade. The length of the bar, which is measured from the base of the chainsaw’s head to the tip of the cutting bar, determines the maximum thickness of the wood that your chainsaw can cut through in a single pass. Generally speaking, your chainsaw can safely cut through limbs with a diameter up to 2 inches less than the length of the bar. For example, a 12-inch chainsaw can cut through a limb up to 10 inches in diameter in a single pass.

For a long time, going electric meant settling for a chainsaw with a shorter bar, but that’s no longer the case. While gas engines offer more power, especially in larger saws, there are electric options with professional-length cutting bars. For instance, a 20-inch electric chainsaw has the power to bring down mature trees.

Need is an important distinction here. We don’t recommend picking the most powerful saw with the longest cutting bar within your budget. A longer bar will give you more cutting capacity, but it’s also heavier and more difficult to handle safely. We recommend buying the tool that’s just big enough for the cutting tasks you’ll perform regularly. If you’re looking to trim small limbs and branches, a pruning saw with a 4- to 8-inch bar such as the Stihl GTA 26 is going to be the best choice. If you’re taking down trees and breaking them down for firewood, you may need something longer.

It’s important that you feel comfortable handling the weight of your chainsaw. If it’s too heavy to hold at chest height, then you can’t use it safely.

With electric chainsaws, weight is directly related to the length of the cutting bar. The longer the cutting bar, the heavier the chainsaw. A mini chainsaw with an 8-inch bar will weigh around 5 pounds, while a large 18-inch chainsaw can weigh as much as 15 pounds.

One thing to keep in mind: Many manufacturers list the “bare” weight of their cordless chainsaws without the battery, so when you do add that in, it can mean an extra 1 to 3 pounds to the load.

Chainsaws are among the most dangerous power tools you can put your hands on: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), some 36,000 people ends up in the hospital with chainsaw-related injuries each year.

That is why it’s crucial to always take every step you can to ensure the safest possible conditions when using a chainsaw. A good electric chainsaw should have built-in safety features to minimize the possibility of an accident: First, look for a trigger lock, which requires you to maintain pressure on a button near the handle to keep the chain spinning. Most will also have a chain brake at the front of the handle, which disengages the chain if the chainsaw kicks back.

That depends on the size of the tree. Even the largest electric chainsaws with a 20-inch cutting bar only have the torque necessary to cut down moderately tall trees. You’ll want a gas chainsaw that brings the extra power to bring down an older, larger tree, or if you’re bringing trees down regularly.

Electric chainsaws don’t require much maintenance. Use a brush or cloth to remove sawdust and other debris that’s caught in the chain and sprocket area after each use.

You should also clean any debris that’s fallen into the air intake slots: Brush it away material on the outside with a clean paintbrush, then blow the valves out with compressed air.

Lastly, electric chainsaws have an auto-lubrication mechanism, but we recommend checking the chain oil reservoir before each use, and refilling it if necessary.

Many cordless electric chainsaws are water resistant and will work fine in the rain. Before you take one for a spin, check its Ingress Protection rating (IP), which measures dust and waterproofing. If your chainsaw features an “IPX3” rating, it can handle “sprays of water” and should be fine in light rain. An “IPX4” rating can withstand moderate to heavy rain.

All that said, we don’t really recommend operating a chainsaw in the rain. Even with work gloves, rain makes every chainsaw-related job less safe, so hold off until the sun comes out if you can.

You should never use a corded electric chainsaw in the rain. Doing so presents a significant electrocution risk. (It’s one of many reasons we generally don’t recommend them.)

#6273. Voyager 1 reaches 1 light-day from Earth

At 5:16 a.m. EST on Wednesday, Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will become the first spacecraft to reach a distance of 1 light-day from Earth. A command radioed from home will need 24 hours to arrive, and a reply another 24 to come back. NASA is asking the public to celebrate by sending the spacecraft a signal on the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17.

NASA launched the twin Voyager spacecraft in 1977 to tour the giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn, while Voyager 2 went on to Uranus and Neptune and is still the only spacecraft to visit either one. Both then kept going. They’re now the only probes ever to study interstellar space directly, the region beyond the Sun’s magnetic field.

Each spacecraft runs on a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, the same kind of power source that drives NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars. Plutonium-238, the fuel source, gives off heat as it naturally decays, and the generators turn that heat into electricity. But because the output fades by about 4 watts every year, engineers have spent years shutting off components and instruments to stretch the spacecraft’s lives. This year, a risky maneuver nicknamed the “Big Bang” turned off several devices in one coordinated move to buy the spacecraft and their remaining instruments several more years of operation. Today, Voyager 1 only runs two of its original 10 instruments, and Voyager 2 runs three.

Voyager 1 is closing in on 1 light-day from Earth (about 16.1 billion miles [25.9 billion kilometers]) — farther than any spacecraft has ever gone. Its twin is about 2 billion miles (3.2 billion km) closer to Earth, near enough that a signal takes about 20 hours to reach Voyager 2.

Voyager 1 lifted off Sept. 5, 1977, two weeks after Voyager 2 but on a shorter trajectory as it was traveling to Jupiter. After visiting Saturn in 1980, it drifted away from the solar system’s planets for good. A decade later, it captured the famous photograph of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot. In August 2012, it became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space, and Voyager 2 followed in 2018. Voyager 2 won’t reach the light-day mark until November 2035. You can see both missions’ exact locations on NASA’s mission status page.

A light-day is a distance measuring how far light travels in 24 hours. At about 186,000 miles per second (299,792 km per second), that adds up to roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion km). For scale, the Moon is just 1.3 light-seconds away, the Sun about 8.3 light-minutes, and Neptune a bit over 4 light-hours. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, lies more than 1,500 light-days away.

At a speed of nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), Voyager 1 is anything but slow. Still, it needed more than 49 years to cover the distance light crosses in a single day.

Astronomy usually asks readers to dim their lights. But tomorrow night is an exception: To celebrate Voyager 1’s accomplishment, NASA invites everyone to flash Voyager’s call sign, V-G-R, skyward in Morse code on Tuesday evening. Use NASA’s automated flasher on your smartphone or tablet. Or grab a plain flashlight and do it manually: V: dot-dot-dot-dash; G: dash-dash-dot; R: dot-dash-dot. Dots are quick blinks of the light, and dashes are long flashes of about a second. Pause between letters.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6272. The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The virus, eliminated in 2000, has now been circulating for more than a year

Flyers provide information about a Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic in Lancaster County aiming to curb an ongoing outbreak.

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO announced; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

That won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

Measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” said epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

“To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo said. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”

PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

But widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

That measles made a comeback is not a surprise, says Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and quickly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”

What’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, said in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”

But surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo said. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health

Efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

Homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States showed that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, says Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

Measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento says. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

Local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer said in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive plan at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in new states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo says. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

There’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

“The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo says. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has said the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”

Eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo says. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”

Public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in New Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also announced that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

“It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo said. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”

#6271. Man charged in spree of powder-filled letters that rattled Congress

Federal officials unsealed charges Tuesday against an Oklahoma man accused of mailing hundreds of letters containing suspicious substances to members of Congress and other officials last month and ahead of the 2024 election.

The court records, unsealed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma, show officials filed a complaint against Robin Martin with two charges: conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications. Martin is set to make his first court appearance Tuesday; information for an attorney was not immediately available.

The complaint alleges Martin sent more than 700 letters to election officials across the country as well as letters to members of Congress of both parties containing suspicious substances. The substances have so far tested as nontoxic and are believed to be yeast or flour, the complaint says.

The complaint alleges that Martin started sending letters with suspicious substances ahead of the 2024 election, addressing them to election officials in all 50 states. Some of those letters had messages written on them that could only be shown by exposure to ultraviolet light, the complaint says.

The mailings contained letters that claimed President Donald Trump won the 2020 election and raised concerns about issues with the 2024 count. Tests of the suspicious white substances included with the letters revealed they were nontoxic, the complaint says.

The 2024 letters had a return address of a business office in Maryland, while the 2026 letters had a return address previously tied to a Democratic Socialists of America office. Neither of those addresses were connected to the sender, the complaint says.

The complaint says that DSA provided officials with documents showing that someone identifying themselves as “George Livingston” contacted DSA officials in October and said they would be arrested for “TREASON AGAINST THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.” Those messages contained some similarities to the 2024 letters, according to the complaint.

Investigators later tracked down Martin’s phone to places where the letters were sent from and also tracked his car on surveillance footage. The complaint also says investigators tracked purchases he made, including turmeric and vinegar, that could have been used to create an ink that would be visible under UV light.

The case is separate from one announced last week against an Illinois man accused of sending threatening messages to members of Congress.

In recent animal tests, tiny robots released into the bloodstream showed promise for treating blood clots.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microrobots controlled by magnets can sweep drugs towards hard-to-reach blood clots in the body, boosting the efficacy of these life-saving treatments, early tests in animals suggest.

In tests with pigs, the microbots helped to dissolve clots around 10 times faster than medication alone. The research team is now working on further safety testing to ready the technology for eventual human trials.

"The whole construct is inspired by nature," said lead researcher Simone Schürle, professor of medical microsystems at ETH Zürich. "There are these tiny bacteria that have little magnetic backbones which they use to navigate with the Earth's magnetic field, and we were really struck by the physics and the properties of them when exposed to rotating magnetic fields," Schürle told Live Science.

ETH Zürich announced the research in a statement on Nov. 9. It has not been described in a peer-reviewed study yet.

Left untreated, blood clots can cause life-threatening damage. These blockages can restrict the flow of blood to the body's key tissues, triggering serious cardiovascular events, such as heart attacks or strokes, which starve cells of oxygen.

Doctors can either remove clots manually with tools or deliver clot-dissolving drugs, called thrombolytics, close to the site of the blockage. However, getting these medications through the final few millimeters of their journey is often the hardest part.

"When a pipe becomes blocked in a branched pipe system, the fluid encounters greater resistance and instead flows through alternative routes where it can pass more easily," Schürle explained. "So when you then try to bring in drugs to dissolve the clot, they won't flow into this area because it's occluded [blocked off]."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This is where microbots can help. The bots are tiny particles whose movements can be controlled by external magnets, which send them rotating and tumbling through blood vessels. These bots can redirect the interrupted blood flow and thus carry essential drugs straight to their target, Schürle and her team say.

Each bullet-shaped microbot contains a magnetic backbone of iron oxide nanoparticles, which is surrounded by a protective sheath of hydrogel polymer. When exposed to a rotating magnetic field, the microbots essentially start to somersault through the blood vessel, creating little vortices that help carry the drugs along with them.

Crucially, the bots' rigid backbone ensures that they spin predictably, while the gel body prevents the particles from sticking together and forming a clump.

The researchers introduce the tiny robots into blood vessels where clots are present.

The robots' motion helps to direct blood-clot-dissolving drugs toward the clots in question.

The team first tested the microbots in a silicon model of a blood vessel that contained clots of pigs' blood. Aided by the rotating microparticles, a thrombolytic drug dissolved the blockages around 10 times faster than medication alone did. That's a potentially life-saving difference, the researchers said.

They then repeated the experiment in live pigs, placing clots in vessels in each of the animals' kidneys. "When we introduced our micro-robots with a conventional, state-of-the-art drug, we could reperfuse [restore blood flow to] a much larger area than if only the drug was there," Schürle said. "The next step is doing safety studies over a longer time and in larger animals."

Earlier safety studies in mice showed that both the iron oxide and the gel sheath polymer safely break down in the body within a few weeks. However, the team will now need to demonstrate that the device is safe in larger mammals before it can be trialed in human patients; their latest test in pigs did not look at how the device broke down or how the pigs fared after the clots were dissolved.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that the bots could be injected into the body alongside the thrombolytic medicine. Once inside, they'd be controlled by targeted electromagnets, making the technique easy to integrate into existing clinical procedures for treating clots.

The team's research is still undergoing peer review, but Schürle has applied for a patent for the microbots' production, which uses a droplet-based microfluidics technique to form each individual particle.

"It's a very cheap, high throughput method to produce the micro-robots," she said. "It's about improving the [clot-dissolving] procedure where it is lacking and helping the drugs travel the last millimeters to be really effective."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6268. I Tested SwitchBot’s Tiny Robot Vacuum, and It Reaches Under Couches Where Bigger Bots Can’t

It stands just 3.6 inches tall, picks up pet hair and cat litter, and docks in a station that’s nice enough to leave out.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

I’ve had a SwitchBot robot vac running laps around my home’s lower level for more than a year, so I figured the K11+ Pro wouldn’t hold many surprises. The robot itself is the same compact cleaner I already know from the SwitchBot K10+ Pro Combo, minus the handheld attachments that come with the Combo. Then I unpacked the docking station.

It takes up less floor space than a sheet of printer paper, has a creamy finish with a faux wood top, and looks more like home decor than a cleaning appliance. It’s the perfect way to upgrade the form and function of our guest suite—adding a cute cleaning tool without taking up too much space or making the room feel like a utility closet.

SwitchBot calls the K11+ Pro the world’s smallest robot vacuum, and that diminutive size is the whole appeal. Most robot vacuums stop at the edge of the couch or bed. This one disappears underneath furniture and comes back out with the pet hair, lint, and stray cat litter that I can rarely reach with an upright vacuum or cordless stick vac.

After weeks of frequent cleaning, I’ve come to appreciate this little robot for exactly what it is. It’s not a do-everything flagship, and it doesn’t try to be one. It’s one of the easiest robot vacuums to live with—and its price makes it even easier to like.

I ran the K11+ Pro on hardwood, laminate, tile, and low-pile carpeting, and I sent it under every sofa, bed, and dresser it could fit under. My house supplies plenty of test material, including pet hair, tracked cat litter, crumbs, and lint.

I tested the mapping, no-go zones, mopping pads, and voice prompts, and I watched how it maneuvered around pet toys, shoes, blankets, cords, and my weird little cat who likes to get in the way of every robot vacuum. Since I’ve used the K10+ Pro for more than a year, I also had a long-term reference point for how this robot holds up day to day.

At 3.6 inches tall and just under 10 inches wide, the K11+ Pro fits under furniture that blocks most other cleaning robots. It slides beneath my couch and beds without getting wedged, and it cleans hidden zones just as well as the open floor.

Corners usually give round robots trouble, but SwitchBot’s Anti-Tangle Twin Side Brush helps solve this problem. The brush extends to sweep debris out of corners and along walls, so the K11+ Pro gets closer to full edge-to-edge coverage than I expected from a robot this size.

The smaller footprint pays off in another way, too. The robot weighs about five pounds, so I can carry it to another room, set it down, and let it work. That makes it handy for a single room, a home office, or a spot that needs a quick cleanup.

With up to 150 minutes of runtime, it can handle my home’s entire lower level before heading back to the dock. When I set it to do just our guest suite, it’s back on the charger long before it runs low on battery.

I didn’t expect a whole lot of cleaning power from a robot this compact, but 12,000 Pa of suction gives the K11+ Pro more pull than its size suggests. I watched it collect pet hair, lint, cat litter, and crumbs from hard floors and the surface of low-pile carpet without leaving trails behind. It’s a solid fit for pet-friendly homes that mostly have hard floors and area rugs.

The rubber roller brush resists tangles. I never had to cut hair off the roller itself, though hair can build up at the ends of the brush. SwitchBot includes a combination cleaning and hair-cutting tool, which handles that in a few seconds.

Thicker carpet is a different story. Like every robot vacuum I’ve tested, the K11+ Pro lifts debris from the top of the carpet but doesn’t reach down to the pad. For deep carpet cleaning, I still rely on a full-size machine like the Dyson Ball Animal 3, since upright and canister vacuums reach deeper into thicker piles.

The K11+ Pro’s docking station is where this model separates itself from the K10+ Pro. It takes up even less room, and the extra-large four-liter dust bag fills the whole upper cabinet.

SwitchBot says a bag can last up to 90 days, and based on how slowly mine has filled, I believe it. Lifting off the top to check the bag takes a second, and the dock comes with a bag preloaded, so I had it running within minutes of unboxing.

The one catch here is noise. The robot runs at a comfortable volume while it cleans, but the self-emptying cycle gets loud for such a small machine. It lasts only a few seconds, though, and I just schedule runs for times when I don’t need a quiet house.

The K11+ Pro uses LDS LiDAR to map rooms and plan efficient cleaning routes, and side sensors help it steer around chair and table legs. Drop sensors keep it away from stairs, and it climbs thresholds up to 1.7 cm, which includes every transition strip in my house.

I named rooms on the map and set no-go zones in a few minutes. It steered around pet toys, blankets, and shoes, and kept cleaning even while one of my cats stalked it from room to room. It will swallow cords, though, so check under and behind furniture before a run.

It also lacks the headlight many costlier robots use to spot obstacles and stay visible in dark rooms. LiDAR units don't need light to map or run, so I didn’t notice any trouble with navigation, but it’s worth knowing if having a lighted vacuum matters to you.

The K11+ Pro comes with premoistened mopping pads you attach to the bottom of the unit by hand, and they work for light cleanup on hard floors. But think of it as making passes with a Swiffer rather than a powerful scrub. The pads pick up dust and light spills, and the no-go zones come in handy for keeping the damp pad off rugs and carpet.

If you need deep mopping, you’ll want a different tool for the job. A wet-dry vacuum like the Dreame H15 Pro Heat or G10 Pro tackles sticky spills and dried-on messes, and a robot with a self-cleaning roller mop, such as the Eufy Omni E35, handles hands-off scrubbing.

Setup was a breeze. I just followed the quick-start guide: turn on the switch under the top cover, open the app, and connect it to my WiFi. I already had the SwitchBot app loaded on my phone, and it connected right away.

I’ve always found the SwitchBot app easy to use. Starting a full cleaning run, picking a single room to tackle, or drawing a no-go zone takes a couple of taps. The robot also talks, announcing what it’s doing and when it needs something, which saves me from checking the app.

If you already run a smart home, it’ll fit right in. The K11+ Pro works with Alexa, Google Home, Apple Home, and Home Assistant without an extra hub.

I love the K11+ Pro, and that comes down to expectations. It’s not a full-size robot vacuum and mop with every bell and whistle. If you want a robot that scrubs floors and washes its own mop, a model like the Eureka J15 Pro Ultra fits that role. The K11+ Pro does something different. It squeezes into tight spaces, cleans under and around furniture, and keeps hard floors and low-pile rugs tidy with very little help from me.

While it’s not the top choice as the main vacuum in a larger home, it’s perfect for apartments, smaller homes, individual rooms, and anyone who wants a dependable robot vacuum for pet hair on hard floors. Pair it with a lightweight stick like the Levoit Aero or another cordless stick vacuum for quick spot cleanups, and you’ve got most of your floors covered.

Up to 15 shooting stars per hour may be visible as the Leonids peak under dark skies tonight (Nov. 16 - 17), with the moon setting before the best viewing hours.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of November's best meteor showers peaks tonight (Nov. 16-17) and is expected to bring up to 15 "shooting stars" per hour to a near-moonless night sky.

Although the annual Leonid meteor shower, which is famous for occasionally producing spectacular meteor storms, is active from Nov. 6 to Nov. 30, the peak on Monday into Tuesday is the best time to look, according to the American Meteor Society.

Although the Leonids typically produce around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, they're among the year's fastest shooting stars, reaching 43 miles per second (70 kilometers per second), and often produce bright meteors that leave glowing trails.

The best time to see them is between midnight and dawn Tuesday (Nov. 17), when the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate, climbs higher in the eastern sky. However, shooting stars can appear anywhere in the sky.

A 45%-lit waxing crescent moon will set just before midnight, leaving dark skies for meteor watching. For the best views, find a spot away from artificial lights, lie back with a wide view of the sky, and allow about 20 minutes for your eyes to become adapted to the dark. Don't use binoculars or a telescope during a meteor shower; they will only restrict your view. However, you can try your hand at photographing the shower with your smartphone or a good astrophotography camera.

The Leonids are produced by tiny particles of dust and debris left behind in the inner solar system by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which takes about 33 years to orbit the sun and is about 2.2 miles (3.6 km) in diameter. Tempel-Tuttle last visited the inner solar system in 1998 and is due to return again in 2031.

Although no rapid-fire "meteor storms" are expected this year, the Leonids are famous for occasionally producing outbursts of 1,000 shooting stars per hour. Such storms occurred in 1833, 1866, 1966, 1999, 2001 and 2002, according to the American Meteor Society. The next storm is expected to hit in 2099.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

After the Leonids, the next major meteor shower will be the Geminids, which peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. The Geminid meteor shower, which is caused by an asteroid rather than a comet, can produce up to 120 meteors per hour. This year, the Geminids will peak in dark skies, thanks to a slim crescent moon setting shortly after dark on Dec. 13.

He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.

#6265. 21 Best Places to Visit in December in the USA

We’ll never forget the first time we visited New York City in December. We’d seen it in movies, but standing there, seeing the Rockefeller Center tree all lit up for the first time, with skaters below and festive music in the air… it was pure magic.

But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa. We’ve also spent the holidays escaping to the warmth, trading snow boots for flip-flops.

In fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather. We’ve done so many road trips in the USA and flown almost everywhere, trying to find the best places to either escape the snow or enjoy the winter, you would think we are obsessed. And we want to share all of that knowledge with you.

If you’re looking for the perfect winter getaway, you have a clear choice: either lean into the winter magic or escape it completely. Are you dreaming of a warm-weather escape with sunshine and sand, or a storybook Christmas town that looks like a real-life snow globe?

Based on all those experiences, we’ve put together this list of our favourite places to visit. Whether you’re looking for a festive city, a snowy mountain, or a sunny beach, we’ll help you find the perfect spot.

Here is a quick look at some of the best places for a December getaway in the USA, from festive winter wonderlands to sunny escapes.

December is a month of pure magic and festive energy. It’s the perfect time to use up that last bit of vacation time for the year. The biggest draw is the distinct choice it offers: You can either dive head-first into a winter wonderland, complete with snow and holiday markets, or you can completely escape the cold weather and find yourself on a sunny beach. It’s a month of festive celebrations, incredible decorations, and finding the perfect atmosphere to end the year.

If you’re anything like us, sometimes the best gift in December is a break from the cold. Trust us, we know after living in Toronto, Canada. Those winters are brutal. These are our favourite spots to find sunshine and warm weather, where you can trade your winter coat for a light jacket or even a swimsuit.

We love the laid-back, quirky vibe of Key West, and it’s even more special in December. We have a great memory of biking around the island, seeing the historic inns draped in holiday lights, and then ending the day at Mallory Square for the sunset celebration. It’s a perfect escape from the cold.

Why Visit in December: This is the perfect time to visit. The summer humidity is gone, the weather is sunny and warm (often in the high 70s), and the risk of hurricanes is very low. The whole island is in a festive spirit, with unique events like the “Bight Before Christmas” boat parade.

Where to Stay: We recommend finding a guesthouse or inn in the historic Old Town to be close to the action.

We once went to a holiday luau in Ka’anapali, and it’s an experience we’ll never forget. You’re eating kalua pork and sipping a mai tai, watching a beautiful hula performance… and then Santa Claus arrives on an outrigger canoe. It was the perfect, uniquely Hawaiian way to get into the festive spirit.

Why Visit in December: You get tropical weather, festive holiday luaus, and it’s the official start of the humpback whale watching season. Be aware that this is a popular time, especially around Christmas, so prices can be high and you’ll need to book in advance.

Where to Stay: Look to the resorts in Wailea or Ka’anapali for a classic Maui experience.

We’ll always remember snorkeling the underwater trail at Trunk Bay in St. John. The water was so calm and clear, and seeing all the colourful fish felt a world away from the snow back home. That’s the magic of a Caribbean trip in December, and the USVI makes it so easy for American travelers.

Why Visit in December: It’s the start of the dry season, with fantastic weather and warm, clear water. You get a full-on tropical, warm-weather Christmas experience, all without needing a passport.

Where to Stay: You can choose from large resorts in St. Thomas or more eco-friendly villas and lodges in St. John.

We were not prepared for how magical St. Augustine is in December. We took one of the Old Town trolley tours at night, and seeing the entire historic city, from the old Spanish architecture to the palm trees, draped in millions of white lights… it was breathtaking. It’s a holiday light display unlike any other.

Why Visit in December: The famous “Nights of Lights” festival. The entire city is illuminated, and the mild Florida weather is perfect for walking around and enjoying the atmosphere. It’s one of the most festive and warm places you can visit.

Where to Stay: We recommend a historic inn or bed & breakfast in the downtown district to be within walking distance of all the lights.

While Maui is our go-to for a resort escape, Honolulu is where you go for a vibrant, city-meets-beach holiday. We loved seeing the massive Santa surfing with his reindeer in the fountain at the Iolani Palace. The whole city has this amazing “Mele Kalikimaka” (Merry Christmas) spirit.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect blend of warm beach weather, world-class shopping, and festive displays. It’s also a significant month for history, with the memorial events at Pearl Harbor.

Where to Stay: Waikiki has a huge range of hotels, from historic beachfront properties to modern high-rises.

If your idea of a winter getaway is to truly get away from everything, the crowds, the noise, the stress, then South Padre is a perfect choice. We spent a week there, and our days consisted of long, quiet walks on the beach. It was a total reset and the perfect way to escape the winter blues.

Why Visit in December: The weather is mild, and the crowds are gone. It’s one of the warmest places in Texas and offers a simple, relaxing beach vacation without the high prices or holiday chaos of other destinations.

Where to Stay: You’ll find many beachfront condos and hotels offering great off-season rates.

We thought we knew desert holiday lights, but the “Las Noches de las Luminarias” at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix is on another level. Walking the garden paths lit by thousands of hand-lit luminaria bags, with musicians playing, was a top-tier holiday experience.

Why Visit in December: You get two trips in one: perfect, sunny weather for outdoor adventures like hiking during the day, and stunning, sophisticated holiday light displays at night.

Where to Stay: Choose from upscale resorts in Scottsdale or stylish hotels in downtown Phoenix.

Sometimes, the warm weather destinations just won’t cut it, especially if you are looking for that winter wonderland feel. So, this section is for travellers who want to dive head-first into the holiday spirit. These are the cities and towns that go all-out for December, with millions of lights, Christmas markets, and an atmosphere of pure magic.

We’ve visited NYC many times, but there’s a specific energy in December. We grabbed hot chocolates and walked through the Bryant Park Winter Village, watching the ice skaters zip around the rink under the lights of the surrounding skyscrapers. It felt like being in the opening scene of a holiday movie. There is nothing like New York City at Christmas.

Why Visit in December: It is the quintessential American Christmas destination. From the iconic tree to the world-famous window displays, the entire city is on a different level of festive.

Where to Stay: Midtown is convenient for seeing the main holiday sights, but we also love the West Village for its cosy, neighbourhood feel.

We’d heard Leavenworth was a “Christmas Town,” but we weren’t prepared for the reality. We visited during the Village of Lights festival, and walking through the snow-covered Bavarian-style village while every single building was covered in over half a million lights… it’s not an exaggeration. It’s the closest we’ve ever felt to being inside a real-life snow globe.

Why Visit in December: The entire town transforms into a “Hallmark movie” Christmas village. It’s a full-immersion holiday experience with carolers, festive food, and incredible decorations.

Where to Stay: Book a Bavarian-style lodge or inn right in the village. You must book many months in advance for December.

We love Asheville, but visiting in December is all about the Biltmore Estate. We took the candlelight evening tour, and seeing the main banquet hall with its 35-foot tree, fireplaces roaring, and carolers singing… it felt like we’d stepped back in time into a Gilded Age Christmas party.

Why Visit in December: Christmas at Biltmore is one of the most iconic holiday events in the country. The city itself is a cosy mountain retreat, and the Blue Ridge Mountains are just beautiful with a dusting of snow.

Where to Stay: You can stay on the Biltmore Estate for the full experience or choose a boutique hotel downtown.

Here are the remaining destinations for the “Best Christmas Towns & Festive Cities” section, all written with unique, December-focused content.

We’ve visited a lot of Christmas markets, but visiting the one in Bethlehem, known as “Christmas City USA”, just felt right. We sipped hot cider and browsed the stalls in the old quarter, and you can feel the city’s 250+ years of Christmas tradition. The whole place is lit by the glow of a giant Moravian star on the hillside.

Why Visit in December: This is Christmas City USA. It was nicknamed this on Christmas Eve, 1741. It offers one of the most authentic and historic holiday experiences in the country, blending its Moravian heritage with a European-style Christkindlmarkt.

Where to Stay: Look for a hotel or inn in the historic downtown area to be close to the festivities.

Walking into Solvang in December felt like we’d been transported to a Danish village during its Julefest celebration. We spent the day exploring the half-timbered buildings, windmills, and bakeries, all decorated for the holidays. It’s such a unique and charming way to experience a winter getaway in the middle of California.

Why Visit in December: The town’s month-long “Julefest” (Yule-fest) celebration is in full swing. It’s a one-of-a-kind Danish-style Christmas with parades, markets, and, of course, delicious European pastries.

Where to Stay: Choose one of the charming Danish-themed inns right in the village to be in the middle of the Julefest activities.

We had to see the “Christmas Capital of Texas” for ourselves, and it did not disappoint. The entire historic Main Street is transformed. We loved seeing the vintage railroad, which becomes the “North Pole Express” for the month. They take the “Christmas Capital” title seriously; there are over 1,400 events in 40 days.

Why Visit in December: It is the officially designated “Christmas Capital of Texas”. The sheer number of festive events, light displays, and activities is staggering, making it a top-tier destination for families and holiday lovers.

Where to Stay: The Gaylord Texan Resort is an attraction in itself, or you can stay near the Historic Main Street to be close to the events.

A New Orleans Christmas is an experience all its own. We did a “Reveillon Dinner,” a modern take on a Creole holiday tradition, and it was one of the most memorable meals we’ve ever had. Afterwards, we walked to Jackson Square to see the St. Louis Cathedral all lit up while carolers sang.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience unique Creole Christmas traditions you won’t find anywhere else. The weather is mild, the food is incredible, and the city’s lobbies (like at The Roosevelt) have some of the most elegant decorations we’ve seen.

Where to Stay: We recommend a hotel in the French Quarter to be in the middle of the action and see the decorated lobbies.

We went to Natchitoches (pronounced Nak-a-tish) specifically for its Christmas Festival, and it was a total joy. It’s one of the oldest and biggest in the country. The whole city, which is the oldest in Louisiana, lights up with over 300,000 lights along the Cane River, and the weekly fireworks shows are fantastic.

Why Visit in December: It hosts one of the oldest and most celebrated holiday festivals in the US, running for six weeks. It’s a classic, Southern Christmas experience in a beautiful historic district.

Where to Stay: Book a room at a historic bed & breakfast in the downtown area.

Visiting Colonial Williamsburg in December felt like walking through a living history Christmas card. We joined a candlelight tour, and seeing the historic buildings lit by real candles in the windows, with carolers in period costumes and the smell of woodsmoke in the air… it was absolutely magical.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience a traditional, 18th-century “Colonial Christmas”. The decorations are all-natural (no plastic lights), and the atmosphere is incredibly authentic and charming.

Where to Stay: Stay in one of the historic Colonial Houses or a tavern right in the restored area for the full immersive experience.

Here is the final category of destinations. This section is all about embracing the snow and finding that perfect winter wonderland.

For many, holiday season travel is all about finding that perfect, snowy scene. These are the places to go for world-class skiing, cosy lodges, and that magical feeling of a true winter escape.

We’ll always remember our first “après-ski” in Aspen. We had spent the day on the mountain hitting fresh powder whenever we got the chance, and as the sun went down, the sky lit up with this incredible pink and orange light they call “Aspenglow.” Sitting by a fire, enjoying a glass of Christmas cheer, and watching the snow fall on the historic town, it just felt like the peak of a luxury winter trip.

Why Visit in December: It’s one of the world’s most famous upscale ski destinations, and the town is just as much an attraction as the mountains. The festive atmosphere, high-end shops, and restaurants are all decked out for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Aspen is known for its luxury hotels and ski-in/ski-out resorts.

One of our favourite things about Park City is its history. We loved skiing down to the historic Main Street, popping off our skis, and walking straight into a saloon that’s been there since the silver mining days. It feels like a real Western town, not just a ski resort.

Why Visit in December: It’s a historic mountain town with two world-class ski resorts (Park City and Deer Valley). The historic Main Street is incredibly charming, and the “Snow Globe Stroll” features life-sized snow globes you can walk through.

Where to Stay: You can find ski-in/ski-out hotels or stay at an inn on the historic Main Street.

Jackson Hole in December is just dramatic. We took a sleigh ride through the National Elk Refuge, and seeing thousands of elk gathered against the backdrop of the snow-covered Teton mountains… it was a powerful and wild winter experience we’ve never forgotten.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect mix of rugged “cowboy Christmas” charm and some of the most challenging ski terrain in North America. The town square, with its famous antler arches, is beautifully lit for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Stay at a slopeside resort in Teton Village or in a hotel in the town of Jackson.

We love Whitefish because it feels like a real, down-to-earth ski town. We spent a day snowshoeing in nearby Glacier National Park, enjoying the total silence and incredible snowy landscapes, and then came back to town for a casual dinner. It’s all the beauty, without the glitz. Just what we were looking for in a winter vacation.

Why Visit in December: It’s a laid-back, charming mountain town with a top-rated ski resort and stunning scenery. It’s also right next to Glacier National Park, which is a spectacular place to explore in the winter.

Where to Stay: You can find lodges on the mountain or stay in one of the friendly inns in downtown Whitefish.

This was a trip purely for the fun of it, and it was 100% worth it. You drive down streets named “Santa Claus Lane” and “St. Nicholas Drive,” the streetlights are shaped like candy canes, and you can visit the Santa Claus House and see his reindeer. It’s a surreal and joyful experience.

Why Visit in December: It’s the ultimate Christmas fantasy come to life. The entire town is Christmas-themed, 365 days a year, but it’s most magical in December with real snow on the ground and the added bonus of possibly seeing the Northern Lights.

Where to Stay: North Pole is very small; most visitors stay in the nearby city of Fairbanks, which has a wide range of hotels.

For the best warm weather, your top choices are Southern Florida (like Key West), Hawaii (like Maui and Honolulu), and the desert Southwest (like Phoenix and Palm Springs). The U.S. Virgin Islands are also a fantastic passport-free tropical option.

Leavenworth, Washington, is often considered the ultimate “Christmas town” as it looks just like a Bavarian snow globe. Other top choices include Bethlehem, PA (known as “Christmas City USA”), Solvang, CA (for a Danish-style Julefest), and Grapevine, TX (the “Christmas Capital of Texas”).

Yes, but it depends on the park. It’s the perfect time to visit desert parks like Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend, where summer heat is unbearable. However, many mountain parks like Glacier, Yellowstone, and parts of Yosemite are mostly inaccessible due to heavy snow and road closures.

You are almost guaranteed to find snow in the mountain towns of the Rockies, like Aspen, CO, Park City, UT, and Jackson Hole, WY. You’ll also find snow in the Cascade Mountains (like Leavenworth, WA), Alaska, and the mountains around Lake Tahoe.

December is a magical month to travel. Whether you’re chasing the sun, seeking out that perfect snowy scene, or looking for a town that’s full of holiday magic, the US has the perfect spot for you.

We hope this list, based on our own winter travels, helps you plan your next getaway. Save this on Pinterest for your holiday planning! Where is your favourite place to go in December?
