More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.

Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:

Voters in Maryland on Tuesday approved an amendment to the state’s constitution that will make it easier for the state’s Democrat-controlled legislature to redraw the congressional map for the 2028 elections.

The outcome was a victory for Democrats, who could potentially eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat – the 1st District on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, represented by Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of the hard-line conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The Old Line State emerged as a bright spot in Democrats’ plan to counter the redistricting wars initiated by President Donald Trump and turbocharged by the spring Supreme Court ruling that diluted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and set off a slew of Republican-led map-remaking across the South.

But those GOP-led efforts appeared to backfire this week, with Democrats holding many of the redrawn seats in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina.

Still, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters Wednesday that he was “ready to engage” with the legislature on a new map, citing the threat of further redistricting in Republican states.

“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states, to go after places like Mississippi and South Carolina and Indiana,” Moore said, according to video posted by WBAL-TV 11 News.

Following an unsuccessful attempt to redraw the Maryland map in February, Moore called a special August legislative session during which state lawmakers voted to put the redistricting amendment, known as Question 3, on the November ballot.

The move faced immediate legal challenges from Republicans. Two Maryland courts ruled to block the measure from appearing on the ballot, finding that lawmakers had missed the legally imposed deadline to refer the ballot measure. The state’s Supreme Court, though, allowed the redistricting amendment to go before the voters, with changes to the ballot text.

State and national Democrats campaigned heavily for Question 3 as some public polling pointed to skepticism among voters. Former President Barack Obama even appeared in an ad urging voters to approve it.

Voters in the Show-Me State overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map that sought to dismantle a safely Democratic seat in the Kansas City area.

Missouri Republicans enacted the new lines in 2025, aiming to give them an advantage in seven of the state’s eight House districts, including the 5th District held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver II.

A protracted legal and political tussle over the map ensued.

The group People Not Politicians Missouri started a citizen petition to put the adoption of the map to a statewide vote. While the petition effort was pending, the state held its August primaries under the new lines. But in September, the state Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map could not be used in the general election because of the pending ballot measure and ordered state officials to hold November’s election under the previous boundaries, first enacted in 2022.

Attempts to challenge the ruling in federal court ultimately proved unsuccessful, with the U.S. Supreme Court issuing an order that reinstated the 2022 map.

Groups on both sides of the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, reportedly spent millions to persuade voters. But St. Louis Public Radio reported last week that while opponents of the 2025 map were actively campaigning against it, organized efforts in favor of Proposition A appeared “nearly nonexistent.”

Republican efforts to try again and enact a new congressional map for 2028 could be complicated by a constitutional amendment, approved by voters Tuesday, that curtails the power of state legislators to override the result of a voter-approved initiative.

Voters in Massachusetts opted this week not to join states such as California and Washington and adopt a nonpartisan primary system.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, would have replaced the state’s partisan primaries with an open primary under which all candidates would appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to the general election.

The outcome was a victory for the chorus of labor unions and progressive groups, including the Working Families Party, that opposed the measure. Holding so-called jungle primaries, the groups argued, could make it harder for candidates without financial resources or high name recognition to run for office.

A bipartisan coalition that included the NAACP of New England and Republican former Gov. Charlie Baker supported the measure, arguing that open primaries would give voters more choice and create more competitive elections in a state dominated by Democrats.

Alaskans weighed in this year for the second time as many cycles on a ballot measure to revert to partisan primaries and repeal the state's top-four ranked choice voting system.

With over 70 percent of the vote in, The Associated Press had yet to call the ballot initiative, known as Measure 2, which would also roll back certain campaign finance disclosure requirements. As of Thursday evening, the “no” side, which supports keeping the current election system, was narrowly ahead. The state has until Nov. 18 to finish counting outstanding ballots.

Under Alaska’s voting system, all candidates run on the same ballot during the primary. Then the top four candidates, regardless of party, advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes a majority of the vote.

In 2024, Alaska voters narrowly voted to keep the current system in place.

National Republicans, though, have largely opposed ranked choice voting, including Trump, who has characterized Alaska’s voting system as a “scam.”

The state’s use of open primaries and the top-four ranked choice system has drawn fresh scrutiny this year.  Outside groups spent big sums trying to boost underdog candidates during the Senate primary in an effort to hurt the front-runners. And several candidates in the Senate, House and governor’s races dropped out before the deadline to finalize the general election ballot, again trying to prevent splitting votes with their party front-runners.

Then last week, the Senate race was upended by a New York Times investigation that revealed operatives aligned with the Senate campaign of Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate with a similar name to GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in an attempt to stack the ballot with two Republicans with the same first and last names. The revelations have fueled an ongoing debate in the state about whether ranked choice voting encourages this kind of alleged campaign chicanery.

“We would not be having this conversation at all if we didn’t have a thing in place called ranked choice voting,” Mike Dunleavy, Alaska's outgoing Republican governor, told Fox News last week.

Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the revelations, as has the Justice Department. The DOJ also sought to block the certification of the Senate result if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Last weekend, a federal court dismissed the lawsuit.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states that currently use ranked choice voting in regular federal elections, along with the District of Columbia.

Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#6179. The Best Places to Go in Africa in 2027

While editing this year’s list, one thing quickly became very clear: 2027 is poised to be a banner one for cultural experiences across Africa. While chatting with our writers, I kept finding compelling reasons to go back to my favorite corners—the Kigali Triennale’s return to Rwanda in February, Jazzablanca’s 20th anniversary in Casablanca, and an even more vibrant creative landscape in Tunis than the one I reported on six years ago. But now I’m adding Benin to my list, thanks to four—yes, four—eagerly anticipated new museums debuting in the year ahead that will showcase everything from modern art to critical artifacts recently repatriated from Europe. Elsewhere on the continent there are fresh ways to experience some of its familiar pleasures, owing to a high-end resort boom on the beaches of Zanzibar, a host of safari lodge openings in Zambia, eight new marine reserves in São Tomé and Principe, and a groundbreaking five-country trans-frontier conservation area. Be sure to make some time for rarer incentives to travel too, like a once-in-a-generation “superbloom” in South Africa and the “eclipse of the century” over Luxor, Egypt (it also helps that there are some swish new places to stay at these places).But one of the most endearing stories of an African destination of the past year may be Cape Verde: Is the “World Cup effect” going to bring a wave of curious travelers to the archipelago? Read on to decide for yourself. —Sarah Khan

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: a museum boom and a vibrant cultural milieu

Home to ancient Kingdom of Dahomey, Benin has transformed into a destination for heritage tourism.

Benin is a place where history runs deep: It’s home to the ancient Kingdom of Dahomey, the spiritual traditions of Vodun, and Ouidah—one of West Africa’s significant ports in the transatlantic slave trade. Now the country is turning that history into a new era of cultural tourism, while creating ways for travelers, particularly people of African descent, to reconnect with their heritage.

Ouidah, an especially important destination for those tracing their ancestry, is central to that effort. In 2025 the government announced plans to invest $1.4 billion in tourism and cultural development, including for infrastructure, heritage restitution, and indigenous traditions. In 2027 that transformation is expected to become more visible with a host of new museum openings, like the Museum of Modern Art in Cotonou; the International Museum of Memory and Slavery in Ouidah; and the Museum of the Epic of the Amazons and Kings of Dahomey in Abomey. The latter of which is expected to house 26 royal artifacts repatriated by France in 2021.

Vodun Days, an eight-day celebration of Benin’s indigenous spiritual traditions taking place January 2–9, 2027, will showcase ceremonies, music, and dance. Meanwhile, Villa Karo in Grand-Popo—a bridge between artists and researchers from Finland, Sweden, and West Africa—will continue its residency program, which brings artists to its seaside research center to connect with the local community through workshops, concerts, and exhibitions. The famous stilt village of Ganvié, meanwhile, remains open to visitors as its Reinventing the Lakeside City of Ganvié project upgrades tourism infrastructure. Benin is also beginning to make appearances on cruise itineraries. Two new Swan Hellenic sailings in 2027 sailings feature the country, including an April voyage from Luanda to Accra and an October sailing from Ghana to Angola. —Harriet Akinyi

Go for: beaches, festivals, and new-found buzz

New Cabo Verde Airlines flight routes launched in May 2026, and coupled with the “World Cup effect,” will make travel to Cape Verde more appealing than ever.

During FIFA World Cup 2026, one of the most impressive performances came from Cape Verde, an archipelago of 10 islands off Africa’s Atlantic Ocean coast. Now the “World Cup effect” has gotten travelers curious about what the destination has to offer. It helps that getting there is easier than ever, thanks to new direct flights launched in May 2026 from Rhode Island’s T.F. Green International Airport on Cabo Verde Airlines. On the island of Sal, which boasts white-sand beaches and over 350 days of sunshine a year, adrenaline-driving activities range from swimming with lemon sharks to kite- and windsurfing, while those seeking a more relaxed experience can float in the saline pools of Pedra de Lume. The island’s luxury accommodation options are also getting an upgrade with Hyatt Regency Cape Verde Sal as well as a family-friendly all-inclusive Bahia Principe set to open in 2027. In March the 322-room Robinson Boa Vista will welcome its first guests to the easternmost island of Boa Vista, known as the Sahara in the Atlantic due to its desert-like flat plains. São Vicente and Praia are the islands to hit for local music—the samba-inspired São Vicente Carnival features dance performances, fireworks, and floats, while Praia hosts the annual Kriol Jazz Festival and the Atlantic Music Expo. Africa’s first Four Points by Sheraton resort opened in the port city of São Vicente last March, with 105 rooms and 22 suites overlooking either Laginha Beach, known for its turquoise waters, or the Monte Verde mountains. —Mazuba Kapambwe

Go for: a vibrant cultural and design scene

Casablanca's 2027 roster of cultural events include the 20th anniversary of Jazzablanca in July and the newly launched Morocco Design fair.

Casablanca stealthily enters 2027 as Africa’s most creative urban reinvention. It’s an apt year to visit, given the pioneering Royal Air Maroc flights, launched in June 2026, linking Casablanca with Los Angeles—the first African connection to America's Pacific Coast. It is a poetic bridge, connecting the dream factory that conjured Casablanca’s mythic character with the modern metropolis redefining itself as a vanguard of contemporary Maghrebi culture. A cornerstone of this cultural renaissance is the 20th anniversary of Jazzablanca in July: Once an intimate gathering, it has evolved into North Africa's best boutique music festival, hosting emerging Afrobeat, jazz, and urban artists beneath the modernist skyscrapers in Anfa Park and on stages in the palm-lined Arab League Park beside the Nevada skate park. Design lovers, meanwhile, can admire the Museum of Photography and Visual Arts, which was inaugurated in June in the medina and is Tadao Ando’s sole architectural project on the continent. The museum and the recently launched annual Morocco Design fair, which spotlights high-end design studios, establish Casablanca as an emerging destination for cutting-edge design, music, and art. The city's heritage sites are getting a revamp too. The iconic 1916 Neo-Moorish Lincoln Hotel by Radisson Collection is being masterfully revived by French Moroccan architects OUALALOU + CHOI, who are pairing its historic façade with an über-minimalist interior. From the hotel’s doorstep, a new tramline whisks you to the Casablanca Finance City (CFC), a glittering new commercial district composed of futuristic, climate-resilient buildings that pay homage to Casablanca’s legacy of concrete experimentation. Nearby, bougie restaurants like Le 7ème Ciel draw crowds and a new Radisson Red will open in 2027 to join an existing Radisson Blu. CFC is built on the old Anfa Airport, from which The Little Prince author and architecture school dropout Antoine de Saint-Exupéry flew a perilous mail route to Dakar in an open-cockpit Bréguet 14 biplane, returned for drinks at Le Petit Poucet, and lived with his fiery Salvadorean muse, Consuelo Suncín. Then, as now, the city was a nexus connecting continents and a frontier to the future. —Paula Hardy

Go for: a ground-breaking cross-border safari project and birding adventure

The Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area, or KAZA TFCA, is the world's largest terrestrial transboundary conservation area.

Zambia, which has forgone visa requirements of 53 countries and has increased international flights, will be the center of attention.

In a world where ecological degradation and global discord are reasons to despair, Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area, or KAZA TFCA, is more rising sun than ray of hope. Supported by five countries—Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, the world’s largest terrestrial transboundary conservation area encompasses a region roughly the size of France and is watered by the Kavango, Zambezi, Chobe, Kwando, and Kafue river systems. Officially launched in 2012, it languished as a plan on paper for years, but recent initiatives have seen it shake off bureaucratic paralysis: Green Growth for KAZA, the umbrella initiative, directly links community benefits to conservation. Several depleted parks have been rewilded; Africa’s first cross-border avitourism project, the Great Kavango Zambezi Birding Route, was recently launched; and connectivity improved—Shearzone Safari launched a charter service in Zambia in early 2026. Notably, Angola has entered the guided-safari arena with Luiana Plains Expedition Camp, the first to open in the 10.3-million-acre Luengue-Luiana National Park in July 2026. It will soon be followed by Natural Selection, which is developing a new 500,000-acre game reserve around Angola’s existing Cuatir Reserve. In Namibia’s unsung Zambezi Region, Thitake River Lodge opens on the banks of the Kwando in Bwabwara National Park late in 2026, while Nkasa Linyanti is the fabulous new linchpin in Nkasa Rupara National Park. But the KAZA TFCA region that’s experiencing the biggest proliferation is Zambia, buoyed by the scrapping of visa requirements of 53 countries and increased international flights. Ker & Downey launched its Zambia division with King Lewanika Lodge in remote Liuwa Plains National Park, the first luxury base from which to witness Africa’s second-largest wildebeest migration; its second location, Musesenji River Camp, opens in April 2027. And luring the well-heeled to 5.5-million-acre Kafue National Park are Anantara with Tented Camp Kafue River, and Classic Zambia with new Lwenge River Camp; both opened this summer. —Pippa de Bruyn

Go for: a wave of gallery and festival openings turning a gorilla trek stopover into an art capital

Kigali's art scene is ramping up as institutions like Kigali Triennial and Gihanga Institute of Contemporary Art platform Rwandan and East African artists.

New Kigali properties are showcases for art, such as the nine-room Pinnacle hotel and members' club.

For years Kigali has been seen as little more than a pit stop before going gorilla trekking. Now the city is making a compelling case for staying awhile. The city’s vibrant food and fashion have already been putting it on the map, and now the art scene is getting noticed as several institutions build platforms for championing Rwandan and East African artists. February 2027 marks the second edition of the Kigali Triennial, which is primed to rival some of the continent’s more established art festivals, like ART X Lagos and Dak'Art Biennale. The Gihanga Institute of Contemporary Art, which opened at the end of 2025, highlights artists across East Africa with two exhibitions: “Space Encounters,” exploring human connection and memory, which is currently on through December 2026; and a collection of contemporary work by Sudanese artists opening in January 2027. This follows the debut of the Inyuguti Art Hub this year, which brought together 19 artists from across Africa and the UK, including Rwandan Elisa Niyogisubizo (also the gallery’s founder), Burundi-based Peter Kamale, and Nigerian Pascal Ejiofor. The lines between the art and hotel scenes are beginning to blur too, with a new generation of properties doubling as cultural showcases. Among them is the nine-room Pinnacle hotel and members club that opened in early 2026 as Rwanda’s first women-led ultraluxury boutique property, showcasing the owner’s private art collection. Creative events are rippling beyond the capital, as Rwandan artists Willy Karekezi and Cedric Mizero are each launching new spaces in Musanze, the gateway town for gorilla trekking, in 2027: Karekezi will open a residency alongside his Indiba Arts Space in Kigali, and Mizero will open Umugenzi, an addition to the multisite Ikinyugunyugu art residency. —Vivienne Dovi

Go for: the eclipse of the century and nostalgia-soaked Nile cruises

Astrotourism is coming for Luxor and the Nile on August 2, 2027, thanks to the six-minute “eclipse of the century" and a wave of new boats promising prime viewing spots along the ancient waterway.

Dubbed the eclipse of the century, 2027’s much-anticipated celestial event will reach its zenith in Luxor, Egypt, on August 2, when the moon will block out the sun for a record-breaking 6 minutes and 23 seconds. Fitting, perhaps, for a place where the mystical has always loomed large, the mountains hold secret treasures, the temples and tombs have been perfectly preserved roughly 3,000 years after they were built, and the Nile exudes a life force of its own. Travelers have come to this transcendent stretch of Upper Egypt, nearly 400 miles south of Cairo, for millennia. Luxor itself served as Egypt’s capital from 1570 BCE to 1069 BCE, but today is better known as the home of the Valley of the Kings, and the start or end point of nostalgia-infused Nile cruises to and from Aswan, a leisurely four- or five-day sail away. Both destinations are primed for a momentous 2027: In Luxor the much-loved Winter Palace—archaeologist Howard Carter’s base during his 1922 Tutankhamen tomb discovery—will reopen in July as a Mandarin Oriental after an extensive renovation exactly 120 years after its official inauguration. Aswan’s own grande dame, the Old Cataract, which famously inspired Agatha Christie’s best-selling novel Death on the Nile, has also been taken over by Mandarin Oriental and will reopen its Nile Wing in 2027 after a thorough upgrade. Mandarin Oriental will launch its first Nile cruise that connects the two, joining a flurry of other new boats taking to the ancient waterway. Among them Oberoi’s Melouk and Malekat dahabiyas, with only seven cabins apiece, and homegrown operator Kemetale’s second boat, Deshret, with its Nile-view sauna, plunge pool, and spa treatments. —Selina Denman

Go for: a rare ‘superbloom’ of endemic flora and world-class wines at Africa’s southern tip.

Cape Agulhas, Africa's southernmost tip, offers a new interpretation center focused on the history and geology of Agulhas, as well as a 177-year-old lighthouse.

Chef Michael Broughton, formerly of Terroir in Stellenbosch, now leads the kitchen at historic Fisherman’s Cottage, putting seafood centerstage.

Cape Town. Winelands. Then head off on safari. That’s the typical circuit for travelers jetting into South Africa. But in 2027 look beyond to the Overberg—“over mountain” in Afrikaans—region, where wildfires have triggered a floral extravaganza not seen in decades. Base yourself in Hermanus for memorable whale watching from the seven-and-a-half-mile Cliff Path. The Marine Hotel, a seafront landmark since 1902, has unveiled a fynbos-inspired revamp of its public spaces and seafood-driven Pavilion Restaurant. There’s a new culinary energy in town too: Chef Michael Broughton, previously at Terroir in Stellenbosch, has turned the historic Fisherman’s Cottage into a hotbed of polished Cape coastal cuisine (don’t miss the spaghetti aglio e olio with local rock lobster). Broughton’s wine list leans into estates from the nearby Hemel-en-Aarde (Heaven and Earth) valley, where cellars are known for exceptional Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Creation Wines offers a new sculpture-led vineyard walk, and opens a private tasting room in May 2027 aimed at wine lovers looking for a deep dive into the cool-climate terroir. Bouchard Finlayson, one of the oldest estates in the valley, reopens in late 2027 after an extensive renovation, with a new tasting space and art collection.

Set in the heart of the Cape Floristic Region, Grootbos Private Nature Reserve is a biodiversity hot spot. Wildfires that swept the area in 2025 sparked a superbloom of new growth, including dormant species that haven’t flowered in decades like wild orchids and the fire-dependent Gladiolus overbergensis. Guided botanical walks and drives get you in the thick of the fynbos, but a new equestrian center also makes this a great choice for horse-riding holidays. Long popular with families, Coot Club, on the nearby Klein River Lagoon, expands in 2027 with a pair of new two-bedroom boathouses and brings a new wellness focus with outdoor yoga sessions and in-room wellness treatments. Toast it all with a sundowner in the refreshed Flamingo Bar upstairs in the original homestead. An hour’s drive east, Cape Agulhas, the southernmost tip of Africa, is a fitting finale. A new interpretation center delves into the history and geology of Agulhas, after which you can climb the 177-year-old lighthouse and stand on the rocky shoreline where the Indian and Atlantic Oceans meet. —Richard Holmes

Go for: new marine reserves and World Heritage Sites

Often known as the African Galapagos for its high concentration of endemic species, the island nation of São Tomé and Principe is surrounded by clear waters full of manta rays, sharks, and migrating humpback whales.

On the islands of São Tomé and Príncipe, more than 155 miles off the coast of Gabon in the Gulf of Guinea, a thick rainforest punctuated by needle-like rock formations meets shores of white and volcanic black sand. One of the world’s least visited countries, and known as the African Galapagos for its high concentration of endemic species, this island nation is surrounded by clear turquoise waters brimming with manta rays and reef and nurse sharks. Humpback whales migrate through seasonally, and turtles begin to nest on the beaches in November before hatching between February and April. In 2025 the first two of eight new dedicated marine reserves, Santana and Ilhéu das Rolas, were approved; in 2026, six roças, or former Portuguese plantations, were designated UNESCO World Heritage Sites, recognized for their role in shaping the social, economic, and cultural history of the nation, which was once the world’s preeminent supplier of cacao. Two of these roças are a part of the Príncipe Collection—the hospitality arm of sustainable development group HBD Príncipe—meaning you can stay at these historically significant sites. One of the properties on offer is Hotel Belo Monte, which opened in June and sits high up on a hillside overlooking the rainforest and sea. A stay in this eco-hideaway, chicly styled with splashes of bold color, comes with cultural insight and an immersion into the wild surroundings. Another outpost, Sundy Praia, is set within what was once part of Príncipe’s second-largest cocoa plantation on the remote northwest tip and hosts guests in tented villas backing the golden shores on the remote northwest tip of the island. —Lauren Burris Hill

Go for: ancient treasures and contemporary culture by the sea

Villa Kahina, an intimate guesthouse that opened in September in Tunis.

In the blue and white village of Sidi Bou Saïd, the six-room Villa Kahina offers views of the Mediterranean.

Designated 2027’s Arab Capital of Tourism, this languid North African city now pulses with the energy of a new generation of Tunisian creatives and entrepreneurs. Events planned in the historic Medina range from TedX Pasha Street talks and musical retreats to artisanal workshops, many organized by the beloved Dar Ben Gacem boutique hotel and cultural hub, which will also host a rooftop event for August’s solar eclipse. Across the Medina, near the Great Mosque of Zitouna, Dar Ben Turkia's early 2026 opening expands the luxury-hotel options that preserve the area’s history. The elegant eight-suite hideaway has an in-house hammam and spa, so it doubles as a wellness retreat in the heart of the Medina. Beyond the medieval city’s labyrinths, the sun-kissed ruins of ancient Carthage spill toward the coast. Anchoring these archaeological riches is the Carthage National Museum, slated to reopen by year-end after an eight-year overhaul. For more contemporary treasures, head downhill to the city’s leading art gallery, Selma Feriani, which in 2027 will exhibit major Tunisian artists Mohamed Amine Hamouda and Rafik El Kamel.

Nearby, sleek seaside city La Marsa gives way to the historically working-class neighborhood of Bhar Lazreg, where artists and makers have been repurposing spaces. Anchors like the B7L9 Art Centre (built by and for the area’s community), and Phosphor Creative District—showcasing local talent who specialize in everything from fine art to design—are transforming the area into a meeting place for artists, demonstrating why the neighborhood has become known as one of Tunis’s coolest. Meanwhile, fashionable La Marsa remains a firm favorite with the stylish set, and mid-2026 restaurant openings like Oto, a Japanese izakaya, and Sujet, a hybrid café and design store, keep things fresh. When you’re ready for a break, make your way up the coast to Birdie at The Clubhouse in Gammarth, which opened in August 2026, or south to Villa Kahina, an intimate guesthouse that began welcoming guests in September. Perched on the forested edge of the iconic blue and white village of Sidi Bou Saïd, this whitewashed six-room sanctuary with sweeping Mediterranean views feels almost untouched by time. —Lee Middleton

Go for: a host of new hotels from which to experience some of Africa’s best beaches

Beyond its beaches, Zanzibar is set to welcome two new luxury properties: Anantara Zanzibar Resort and Residences in 2027, followed by Four Seasons Resort Zanzibar at Pongwe in 2028.

Most visitors arrive in Zanzibar with postcard perfection already in mind—turquoise shallows, swaying palms, and dhows tipping into the sunset—but the island’s enduring drawcard is still Stone Town: a UNESCO-listed tangle of coral-rag limestone alleys, carved Omani doors, and clove-scented air, where Africa, Arabia, and India have intersected for centuries. In 2027 Zanzibar gets its most serious branded hotel wave yet with the 181-key Anantara Zanzibar Resort & Residences on the north coast, and in 2028 it will welcome, the 60-villa Four Seasons Resort Zanzibar at Pongwe, widely regarded as the loveliest beach on the east coast. The latter is a short flight from the brand’s Serengeti lodge and has been built with a bush-and-beach pairing in mind. The freshest energy is homegrown, though, and it has moved away from the overdeveloped north. In Jambiani, on the sunrise-facing southeast coast, the seven-villa Ma’a Salama (“go in peace”) opened in mid-2026 as a nonprofit that doubles as a hospitality school, training island youth in exchange for a year’s free education. Ma’a Salama’s spacious villas are named for spices and are cooled by bioclimatic design rather than air-conditioning, and four are crowned with rooftop teahouses, designed in Stone Town’s famous Emerson’s teahouses. On the quiet southwest coast at Kizimkazi, Kizikula is the antithesis of a resort: no sign, no jetty, just a jungly pathway leading to what feels more like a private home or artist’s enclave than a hotel. At low tide, guests access the beach through a secret gap in the coral cliff. Designed by Mumbai’s Case Design, its coral-limestone rooms sit in wild permaculture gardens. In 2026 the resort added 19 rooms, and in December it will open a new rooftop sunset bar and a three-floor wellness center, where treatments incorporate ingredients like Zanzibari cinnamon, turmeric, and cardamom. As of October 2026 Airlink flies the first-ever nonstop route between Cape Town and Zanzibar, with low-cost FlySafair rumored to be expanding its regular Johannesburg service to include Cape Town too. The UK gets its own first direct link in November 2027, courtesy of TUI Airways’s Gatwick service, along with a direct London flight from Air Tanzania. —Jane Broughton

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6178. Foster bill would bolster tech use to monitor AI financial risks

A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.

The draft bill, from Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond quickly to cybersecurity and other threats.

The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with new risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.

The legislation is intended to help regulators provide financing to banks during crises and wind down failing banks. The model software would reduce the amount of manual compliance work that smaller financial institutions would have to do by providing standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and transmit the information to regulators, according to a Foster spokesperson.

“With advances in AI creating new cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it's more important than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster said in a statement. “We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.”

Foster, who has a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leader on AI issues on the Financial Services panel, is in line to become chair of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year.

He has been mulling a challenge to ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., to chair the full committee in the new Congress. But Foster is now “leaning toward not running,” a person familiar with his thinking said.

Waters already has a confirmed challenger in Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., who on Thursday circulated a "Dear Colleague" letter seeking the support of House Democrats for his bid.

Casten touted his “career at the intersection of business, science and public policy." Before entering Congress, he worked in clean energy and co-founded a company that converted industrial waste energy into usable power.

In his letter, Casten cited the need to lower housing and insurance costs, protect consumers from fraud, address risks posed by cryptocurrency and prediction markets and guard against the next financial crisis. He also promised to hold the Trump administration accountable for ethical lapses.

He's got a tough road ahead of him, however. Every Financial Services Democrat except Casten, Foster and Rep. Sam Liccardo of California signed an Oct. 21 letter to House Democrats in support of Waters. That show of support came after Casten made it known he was interested and it was clear that Foster had been considering his own bid.

Although Foster may not compete for the chairmanship, he has recently talked to Waters about changing how the committee operates.

“He wants a variety of members to play a role in legislation brought up in committee,” the source familiar with his thinking said. He’s also seeking more input on witnesses who testify at subcommittee hearings.

The draft bill he released on Thursday covers a topic that Foster is likely to pursue throughout the 120th Congress. He often asks the most questions about the use of AI in financial services at hearings and offers the most amendments related to the issue at markups.

Under the bill, model software would be developed for banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, AI risk monitoring and other activities.

The software must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, according to the summary. It would be tested using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than actual customer accounts. Regulators would not take financial or supervisory actions during the study.

The software developed during the study would not have to be adopted; rather, it “should be viewed as a starting point for further modernization,” the summary says.

All software models would have to be published within one year of enactment of the bill and a final report assessing feasibility, costs and savings, competition and other criteria, would be due to Congress within two years.

You might think that the best all-inclusive resorts are only found dotting the beaches of Mexico and the islands of the Caribbean. While there are certainly plenty of incredible options in the sunny tropics, there are also plenty of great all-inclusive resorts in the U.S.

Believe it or not, from the Florida Keys all the way to the California coast, there are incredible all-inclusive resorts and hotels where the price covers all (or most) of your food, drinks and activities, and you won’t get sticker shock from the final bill. And they're different from what you'd expect, including dude ranches serving elevated Western fare and wellness-focused retreats in the desert.

Booking an all-inclusive resort in the U.S. is slightly different from booking the more traditional ones in tropical destinations. So, while researching, make sure to read the fine print about what exactly is included in your rate because many of the properties listed below might cover all your meals but not alcohol (or just wine with dinner, for example).

You'll also want to consider what extra activities are included in the price and what activities (like horseback riding or fly-fishing) cost extra so you have a clear idea of how much you'll actually experience on your dream vacation.

One other difference to note is that some all-inclusive resorts in the U.S. (especially dude ranches and wellness retreats) have minimum stay requirements or select check-in days (like Monday or Thursday), so consider being flexible with your travel dates.

Ahead, find our top choices for all-inclusive resorts located within the U.S.

Just an hour’s drive from Phoenix, Castle Hot Springs is a luxury desert oasis in a lush, almost tropical setting with sky-high palm trees and over 1,000 acres of land to explore and relax. The resort, which dates back to the 1800s, has a series of natural hot springs that start at 86 degrees Fahrenheit and top out around 106 degrees.

For meals, the resort’s property-grown ingredients are the star of the show, with breakfast, lunch and a multicourse tasting menu in the evening. Note: alcoholic drinks aren’t included in the rate.

Besides soaking in the natural hot springs (reserved exclusively for those staying at the resort), guests can find Zen through meditation, take a farm tour to see where the food is grown, experience nature through a guided hike or pay extra for spa treatments and adrenaline-inducing activities like an elevated adventure course and utility task vehicle tours.

Rates at Castle Hot Springs start at $1,250 per night, based on double occupancy. Two- and three-night minimums are required for most dates, and the resort is closed for most of July and August.

An adults-only resort hugging the coast of Big Sur, California — arguably one of the most scenic areas in the U.S. — this resort has long been a favorite of readers and staffers of TPG, even before it was converted into an all-inclusive property in 2020.

At this property, one of three Alilas in California, guests are invited to relax in one of 54 rustic-chic rooms and suites that are as comfortable as they are luxurious; all of them include walk-in showers, soaking tubs, stocked minibars, great views and either balconies or private decks. To take it up a notch, reserve a room with a fireplace to snuggle up next to or one with a hot tub for an even more intimate place to relax.

Produce grown on the property, alongside locally sourced ingredients, is front and center at the modern American restaurant, The Sur House; just note that alcohol is supplemental to this Alila’s inclusive package.

During a visit, explore the great outdoors on a hike, hit up the indoor and outdoor wellness studios for some mental and physical stimulation and take a moment to breathe during a yoga class. Just don’t forget to schedule time in the Japanese hot baths to soak up the power of invigoratingly hot water, or, for an added fee, visit Spa Alila for a special treatment like the Jade Body Ritual, which uses basalt stones and Swedish massage techniques to eliminate life’s stress.

Rates at Alila Ventana Big Sur start around $1,800 per night for double occupancy and include all meals and various activities. World of Hyatt members can book this Category 8 property from 35,000 to 75,000 points per night.

A working farm, a luxury resort and an internationally acclaimed dining destination, Blackberry Farm — a gem of a resort set on 4,200 acres near the majestic Smoky Mountains — is a truly special place to get away. The resort’s signature “Foothills Cuisine” will change everything you thought you knew about American food. From dinner on the day of arrival through the very last breakfast before checkout, expect meticulously prepared meals crafted with seasonal ingredients foraged from the on-site 4-acre garden, plus other locally sourced ingredients.

With 69 different accommodations, there’s room for everyone, from three- to five-bedroom houses with space to spread out to 1,080-square-foot Hill Cottages with typical Tennessee front porch rocking chairs, private golf carts and warm fireplaces. On the smaller side, the farm’s Historic Rooms are intimate, cozy and decorated with antiques that are classy and classic at the same time.

Come for the food but stay for the seemingly countless activities like hiking, yoga, horseback riding and fly-fishing, among many, many others (though many of them have an additional cost outside of the inclusive offerings). There are also top-tier concerts populating the farm’s entertainment calendar, alongside a spa, wellness treatments and special programs designed to entertain and educate children.

Rates at Blackberry Farm start at $1,200 per night and require a three-night minimum stay. Alcohol is an additional fee.

With three adults-only, wellness-focused resorts across Arizona, Texas and Massachusetts, any of Hyatt’s Miraval locations is worth considering for a visit. Though it’s no easy contest among them, we’d have to argue that Miraval Berkshires is truly one of the best all-inclusive resorts in the U.S.

A “digital device-free resort,” guests check their phones at the door, and instead of checking emails and Instagram likes, they’re invited to check in on themselves through wellness and well-being programs that are designed to enhance their lives and their health. That includes deep dives on nutrition, fitness activities like a barre class in the pool, connecting with nature through hiking and limbering up as you practice your lotus pose during yoga.

Other activities, at an additional cost, include learning the art of pottery, mastering the bow and arrow in archery and getting up close and personal with horses in specially designed therapeutic sessions with gentle equines.

Inclusive rates at Miraval Berkshires cover breakfast, lunch and dinner at the health-focused restaurant, Harvest Moon, or ordered directly to the room. Though the entire experience is top-notch, a further elevated experience (for an additional fee) can be had at 1894, offering four-course, prix fixe menus served as part of an interactive experience.

And as for where you’ll rest your very relaxed head, choose from a range of options like a room in the Gilded Age Wyndhurst Mansion, a 600-square-foot suite with a balcony, or a room in a historic cottage, all of which are stocked with Tibetan singing bowls and meditation cushions.

Rates at Miraval Berkshires start at $1,100 or 60,000 World of Hyatt points per night, both based on double occupancy. Note that every award booking includes a $175 resort credit per person.

Imagine taking a water taxi from the hustle and bustle of a busy downtown to a charming spa and wellness resort set on 19 acres of lakefront property. If your intention is to leave it all behind for a few days of blissful relaxation, you’ve come to the right spot: Lake Austin Spa Resort.

Located just 30 minutes from downtown Austin (and also accessible by car), this spa resort is an intimate experience, offering just 40 bright and airy rooms with private porches, soaking tubs and 12-foot ceilings, plus a few cottages with hot tubs.

The all-inclusive pricing covers three meals per day, including via room service, along with snacks and unlimited fresh smoothies and juices. It also offers guests access to 24-hour fitness facilities, unlimited use of lake equipment like stand-up paddleboards and kayaks, a lakeside beach with swings and hammocks, and two outdoor pools, plus a heated indoor lap pool and 20 daily activities, ranging from hiking to belly dancing.

Considering this is a spa resort, you might be happy to hear the spa itself is a whopping 25,000 square feet, and guests have access to its steam rooms, saunas, whirlpools, gardens and relaxation areas.

Rates at Lake Austin Spa Resort start at $1,206 per night, based on double occupancy.

You don’t have to be a cowboy or cowgirl to appreciate a luxury ranch — or to simply bask in the wonder of Montana’s natural beauty. The Ranch at Rock Creek gives visitors the best of it all — a truly luxe experience, incredible activities and even the chance to ski — with inclusive pricing that means (mostly) everything is taken care of before you even take off on the trip.

With 31 accommodations on offer, there are options as vast as the Montana sky, from hybrid luxury glamping tents to historic converted barns to multiroom homes with space for the entire family.

Ranch-style food is the name of the game here, with a handful of dining options offered across breakfast and lunch, though the star of the show is the rotating seasonal dinner schedule that’ll have guests do-si-do-ing under the stars at a barn dance and enjoying a barbecue with a side of a summer rodeo. And for an even more upscale experience, make sure to visit during the weekly chef’s tasting menu experience on Fridays.

Outside of dining, guests can plan every activity through a dedicated “Ranch Ambassador,” who might suggest seasonal activities like snowboarding, skiing or tubing or other memorable experiences like horseback riding, archery and fly-fishing. And when all that makes you feel a little tuckered out, hit up the spa for a rejuvenating treatment so you’re refreshed, revived and ready to do it all again the next day.

Rates at The Ranch at Rock Creek start at $2,800 per night, based on double occupancy.

More like a traditional all-inclusive experience, though, all meals plus alcoholic beverages (including spirits) are offered in the restaurant or served directly in your cottage or suite. For a very special lunchtime treat, request a picnic-style lunch that can be set up anywhere on Twin Farms’ 300-acre grounds.

Despite its seemingly slow and leisurely pace, there’s no shortage of things to do at this luxe retreat. In the winter, take advantage of sledding, snowshoeing or visiting the farm’s private mountain for skiing. When it’s warm, canoeing, fly-fishing, kayaking, tennis and swimming in a picturesque pond are all on offer. Or, if relaxing is the only thing on the agenda, the Bridge House Spa therapists will come directly to you for an in-room ritual or invite you into a treatment room for a facial or massage (for an extra fee).

Rates at Twin Farms start at $2,950, based on double occupancy.

The magic number at Little St. Simons Island, off the coast of Georgia, is 32 — because that is the maximum number of guests who can stay at the resort at any given time. Intimate and almost like stepping out of the modern world and into a gentle wilderness, the island offers 11,000 acres of unspoiled beauty to explore, with 7 miles of beaches.

To get to the island property, which dates back to 1979 and is located between Savannah, Georgia, and St. Augustine, Florida, guests must catch a ferry from Hampton River Marina on St. Simons Island, which is accessible by car.

On the island, there are six cottages with one to four bedrooms that can be booked by the room or cottage (or, if you want to take over the whole place, the entire island is available to book starting at $8,000 per night). The cabins are rustic but well appointed with cedar furniture, gathering areas — like screened-in porches or living rooms with fireplaces — and postcard-worthy views of the island’s many live oak trees. The various arrangements make mixing and matching room or cottage types based on your group’s needs a breeze.

All meals are included in the nightly rate and feature shared plates made with ingredients grown on the island and procured from the area, like locally dredged oysters, served in The Lodge. Hors d’oeuvres and snacks are also available throughout the day. (Just note that alcohol is not included in the price.) As for activities and amenities, there are fishing experiences with all equipment provided, 26 miles of hiking trails, kayaking through the marsh, a saltwater swimming pool, open-air truck safaris and loaner bikes you can take out to the beach.

A family-friendly experience, the island welcomes kids of all ages between Memorial Day and Labor Day but is limited to kids age 6 and up the rest of the year.

Rates at The Lodge on Little St. Simons Island start at $800 per night for double-occupancy rooms. A two-night minimum stay is required.

Bungalows Key Largo is the Florida Keys’ take on a more traditional beachfront experience, with all the attributes that folks look for in an all-inclusive concept — meaning a true beach you can visit ... with an included drink in hand.

This adults-only resort for those age 21 and up has it all, starting with 135 900-square-foot bungalows with verandas featuring outdoor showers, soaking tubs in the bathrooms and private porches. Restaurants and bars include a beachfront Mexican-style seafood grill, a fine dining experience for an extra fee, a classy cocktail bar and even a sunset tiki-themed bar where tropical drinks are a must-order. And don’t worry about paying extra for drinks, as most top-shelf liquor, beer and wine is included.

Also included are daily group yoga classes, live entertainment, karaoke nights and water sports like stand-up paddleboarding and kayaking. Guests can also ante up for some paid excursions that are well worth the money, like taking the crew out for drinks on a floating tiki boat, going on a sunset cruise or heading to the Key Largo Spa for a massage in a waterfront tiki space.

Rates at Bungalows Key Largo start at $899 per night, based on double occupancy. Garden Bungalows have a two-night minimum stay, while Waterfront Bungalows have a three-night minimum stay.

All meals are included for everyone in the group and served buffet-style at breakfast (with 40 options) and lunch (featuring a large salad bar), while dinner is a rotating a la carte menu with items like strip steaks and barbecue. Though alcoholic drinks aren’t included in the rate, the Silverado Saloon is open for adult beverages and Shirley Temples for the young ones.

At the resort, nearly all activities are included in the nightly rate, from horseback riding to tractor rides to indoor and outdoor water park visits for fun on slides and at splash pads. Winter activities include sledding and tubing. There are also water activities on a private lake, magic and comedy shows, fireworks displays and laser tag. Whether you want to escape the snow for the heated indoor water park or beat the summer heat with a fun day on the lake, this all-American, all-inclusive resort really does have it all.

Rates at Rocking Horse Ranch Resort start at $599 per night, based on four guests occupying a room.

For the young and young at heart, Fair Hills Resort is an oasis of fun in Minnesota that’s open from May to September and harks back to the glory days of a typical American vacation: one with goofy games, waterslides, campfires and cabins. Speaking of cabins, this isn’t a Four Seasons, and the resort is quick to let you know that its one- to four-bedroom cabins are basic and have no air conditioning — but that just adds to the camp vibe.

Stays include three meals daily and, fittingly, are announced by the clang of a bell echoing throughout the resort. Breakfast is a buffet, while lunch is lighter, with a salad bar and twice-weekly picnics. Dinner is a rotating three-course menu that can include dishes such as steak, prime rib or Minnesota walleye fish. Off-menu cold items are also available for picky eaters.

The activities are wide-ranging, too. In fact, the 94-year-old resort has a detailed calendar showing exactly what the family can expect. Treasure hunts, Zumba classes, capture the flag, river tubing, scavenger hunts and talent shows are all on offer. But don’t fret, parents: Adult activities like poker night are scheduled, too. Sports include tennis and an 18-hole golf course, and lake activities are also available if the calendar gets a little too overwhelming.

All-inclusive rates at Fair Hills Resort start at $309 per night for adults and $169 per night for kids between 6 and 12; kids who are 4 and 5 years old can stay for free on most dates, and children 3 and younger are always welcome for free. A detailed calendar of rates, including specials if booking for seven nights, is available online.

Rawah Ranch, a luxe guest ranch in Colorado’s Laramie River Valley, is a member of Small Luxury Hotels of the World and is now available to book with Hilton Honors points.

During the day, go horseback riding without worrying about packing cowboy boots, as the resort provides them for kids and adults, and build a connection with the horse you’re assigned since you’ll be riding the same one throughout your stay. You can also spend time at the river fly-fishing (a half-day session is included in the rate) or paddleboarding, learning how to shoot clay traps and arrows, or simply get lost in the beauty of it all on a hike.

Each day, guests are treated to three meals of “Colorado Ranch Cuisine,” starting with a la carte breakfast, a hearty lunch buffet and a cocktail hour followed by a family-style dinner all crafted by chef Jennifer Sanchez.

A seasonal resort open only from June through September, Rawah Ranch rates start from $833 per night, double occupancy, and require a three-night minimum stay. Award pricing starts at 240,000 Hilton Honors points per night.

At RiverView Ranch, an all-inclusive luxury private ranch in Montana, there are only eight lodge suites to book, making for an intimate experience. Each of the suites has a private deck with a fire pit and views of the ranch’s private lake, as well as cozy slippers and robes to relax in. They also receive twice-daily housekeeping. Rooms range from a stately king-size suite with a deep soaking tub down to a four-bedroom option with double bunk beds that can sleep up to 10 people.

All on-property experiences are available for no extra charge with the all-inclusive rate — even the more extravagant options like snowmobiling in the colder months and Jet Skiing and taking a hoverboard for a glide in the warmer months. But since it’s a ranch resort, make time for some horseback riding, going for a trail ride and fishing.

Meals are a magical affair, rotating between the Great Room in the main lodge and barbecues at the lake house and out on the deck. The meals consist of “ranch-to-table” menus that feature Angus prime steak and ribs, fresh fish caught on the lake and even bison with sides of hearty vegetables cultivated on the ranch. And for wine, consult with the house sommelier for the perfect pairings.

Rates at RiverView Ranch start at $4,800 per night for a minimum three-night stay, based on double occupancy. Hilton Honors members can book from 220,000 points per night.

Nearly the opposite of a typical all-inclusive resort experience that’s heavy on booze and big on entertainment, a stay at Canyon Ranch Tucson is all about finding, reviving and cultivating yourself through wellness practices and lifestyle changes.

Guests are invited to choose between different “pathways,” or programs, that guide their experience. These pathways can be simple and laid-back or extremely regimented, with focus areas including weight management, learning and breaking habits, and even options that cover medical scanning followed by guidance from clinical practitioners to shape the experience.

Scheduled activities include yoga and Pilates, meditation, aqua Zumba, cardio training, cooking classes and photography hikes. Meals are served at the Vaquero Canyon Ranch and feature healthy dishes “free of additives and unhealthy extras,” like sunflower seed tacos, turmeric cauliflower steak and grass-fed short rib. Grab-and-go options are also available from a cafe.

At the end of a busy day of centering yourself, crash into a room or suite with Mascioni Italian linens and a personally selected pillow from a menu with more than 20 options.

Outside the room, enjoy three outdoor pools plus an indoor one, a spa, multiple fitness centers and 150 acres of outdoor space to explore.

Rates at Canyon Ranch Tucson start around $2,250 per night, based on double occupancy.

Ghost towns are supposed to be creepy, right? Not in Dolores, Colorado, where the mining town dating back to the 1800s has been converted into a luxury resort full of life. Individual hand-hewn log cabins, some built by the original miners (the resort claims), plus a luxury tent, are full of Western character and design — as well as en suite bathrooms and high-speed Wi-Fi.

The hot springs, which range from 85 to 106 degrees Fahrenheit, can be enjoyed in a restored bathhouse, in a number of pools, with water bubbling up directly from the source and in the Well House cabin accommodation. At the spa, aestheticians offer facials while massage therapists can work out knots with a deep-tissue rub.

Seasonal activities include horseback riding, mountain biking and fly-fishing in the summer and snowshoeing, cross-country skiing and horse-drawn carriage rides in the winter.

An all-inclusive experience, meals plus alcoholic beverages (except premium drinks) are served at a long table in the old-school saloon. Chefs cook in an open kitchen using ingredients grown on the property to create dishes like roasted Bountiful Ridge pork with charred leek grits and preserved green apricots, for which the suggested pairing is a glass of 2018 Cos Frappato wine from Sicily, Italy.

Rates at Dunton Hot Springs start at $1,165 per night, based on double occupancy.

#6176. Air India Cuts Up To Five Hours From New York Flights By Flying Over Iraq

Air India has eliminated fuel stops in Rome on its flights from Delhi and Mumbai to New York, cutting some journeys by five hours. The surprising key to restoring nonstop service was not Russian airspace, but the reopening of a shorter corridor over Iraq.

Air India has restored nonstop service on all four of its routes linking Delhi and Mumbai with New York JFK and Newark.

Flights that had taken approximately 22 hours with a technical stop in Rome are once again operating in about 17 hours.

The Delhi flights are operated with Airbus A350-900 aircraft featuring business class suites, premium economy, and economy class. The Mumbai routes use refurbished Boeing 777-300ERs with first class, business class, premium economy, and economy class.

Removing five hours from an already very long journey represents the difference between a difficult nonstop flight and a 22-hour saga involving an annoying fuel stop.

Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian-operated aircraft, eliminating the most direct westbound corridor from India toward Europe and North America.

The conflict involving Iran then created further restrictions across the Middle East. Air India was forced to operate a much longer route through Jordan and Egypt before continuing across Europe and the Atlantic. That routing pushed the limits of what the aircraft could operate with a commercially useful payload. Air India consequently added a technical stop in Rome to refuel before continuing to New York.

The reopening of Iraqi airspace changed the calculation. Air India can now fly a shorter route across Iraq and Turkey before continuing through Europe and across the Atlantic.

The airline says this has reduced total journey time by as much as five hours. Additionally, the shorter route will reduce fuel consumption by approximately 10% and also ease crew scheduling pressures associated with flight-duty limits. Considering the cost of operating a fully loaded Airbus A350 or Boeing 777 for several additional hours, this is a substantial operational improvement for Air India as well as a welcome one for passengers.

Air India remains permitted to use Russian airspace and has done so on certain North American routes, particularly services connecting India with the West Coast of the United States.

That has given Air India an advantage over U.S. and European airlines that avoid or are prohibited from using Russian airspace. But it would be incorrect to assume that Air India routinely flies over Russia when traveling between India and New York.

The available flight-tracking data suggests otherwise.

Recorded routes displayed by FlightPaths.com for Delhi–JFK show no use of Russian airspace in its sample of 20 flights. Among seven recorded Mumbai–JFK flights, just one crossed Russia. The pattern is even clearer in the opposite direction. Russia did not appear in the displayed samples of 20 JFK–Delhi flights or 10 JFK–Mumbai flights.

(Those samples are not a comprehensive record of every Air India flight, and routings can change based on winds, restrictions, and operational requirements. But they demonstrate that Russian airspace is not the normal solution for Air India’s New York service).

These flights generally travel westward through the Middle East and Europe, which why access to Iraqi airspace has such a large effect.

Air India has restored nonstop flights from Delhi and Mumbai to New York JFK and Newark, cutting journey times by as much as five hours.

The change was made possible by renewed access to Iraqi airspace, not by shifting these flights over Russia. Although Air India uses Russian airspace on some routes, flight-tracking data indicates that it is not routinely used for New York service.

A 17-hour flight remains very long, but it is much better than a 22-hour journey with an unwanted fuel stop in Rome. For passengers traveling between India and the New York area, this is a genuine and substantial improvement…and ironically might allow Air India to charge a higher premium for its nonstop service, despite the fuel and labor savings this shorter flight time will produce.

Thanks for covering this! Was wondering about the routing as the press release was a bit vague about it.

Thank you for covering this. Even on the routes from Delhi and Bombay to and from London Heathrow they have been cut by about 30 minutes as well. A bit shorter than flying over Northern Saudi Arabia

Air India is really knocking it out of the park based on an ongoing trip. Wonderful cabin, food and service (to/from LHR).

Of course, the flights to North America still have to the outdated cabins.

And the Jamun juice served on your domestic Indian leg from DEL – BOM is a popular Indian summertime refreshment made from Indian blackberries and salt – I think you were wondering what it was.

I thought it was far too peppery (also tasted like there was turmeric in it), but different strokes for different folks!

Question for you – I have a flight booked DEL-JFK in February. It was always listed as non-stop and I haven’t gotten any updates regarding a fuel stop or arrival time change. Looks like that isn’t an issue now but was their DEL-JFK A350 flight ever stopping for refueling or has it remained non-stop through this time? If it ever had a stop and 4-5 hour delay arriving at JFK then Air India (or United who I booked the J award through) sure didn’t communicate it.

Ironically, AI101 from DEL-JFK made a stop in FCO today.

It arrived in Rome at 0115 and took off at 0305.

From what I can tell, they ended up cancelling today’s technical stop in FCO – I could be wrong.

The last communication actually had us leaving earlier (just after midnight) from DEL and getting to JFK at 6:55 AM which was an improvement of almost 2 hours from original schedule.

#6175. Update: FAA Lifts Ground Stop

After a roughly five-hour freeze on virtually all commercial aircraft departures, the FAA has lifted its nationwide emergency ground stop.

The FAA canceled the ground stop around 8:20 p.m., and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed it at a press conference at the White House Friday night. He said it will take some time for flights to restart but emphasized that the air space is safe.

According to Duffy, FAA personnel began to see inconsistencies in air traffic data around 3:30 p.m. Friday, and, out of an abundance of caution, the decision was made to ground flights not already in the air. He said old analog ATC communications switches were overwhelmed and “went down,” causing the inconsistency.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the failure was triggered by an attempted technology update, which caused the system to reboot and crash.

There is no evidence of a cyberattack or terrorism, Mullin emphasized, and passengers were never in any danger.

Duffy said travelers should contact their airline for information about potential cancellations and delays. He said his department is in contact with the major carriers and will work with them to restore normal operations.

A small number of mostly international flights were cleared for takeoff at airports such as New York-JFK, Washington Dulles, Reagan National, and Detroit Friday afternoon during the ground stop, but most remained grounded until the FAA reversed its order.

#6174. Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous New York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

“Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”

West Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and New Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

Rockefeller was born in New York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

He returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

In West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness."

He had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

Rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

But defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension plans.

In 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him said the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

He believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

He viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

But industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

“The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

He had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller announced he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

Rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance plan, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”

"These are people," Rockefeller said, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice."

The amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

Rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

Rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.
